value.text: An autistic child, covered in fire ants, was saved by a group of Port St. Lucie residents after he tried wandering into a retention pond on Saturday morning. Lucie Police Department says a group of Port St. Lucie residents were on their way to grab coffee when they noticed a child wandering alone near a retention pond. Feeling that something was off, the group of Good Samaritans stopped to help. PSLPD says the group tried to guide the child to safety, but when he tried to enter the pond, they followed him into the water and dragged him to safety. See also: DeSantis says Florida will begin testing air taxis in Central Florida by year's end The group of PSL residents immediately called 911 and stayed with him until officers arrived. Body camera video shared by the Port St. Lucie Police Department shows deputies talking to the residents who rescued the child. Video continues to show deputies wiping the fire ants off the weeping child. PSLPD warns residents that if they see someone who could be in danger, they are advised to follow their instincts

The Border Collies rescued from a Palm City home where authorities found deplorable conditions are now receiving medical care, nourishment and grooming as they begin their recovery. The Humane Society of the Treasure Coast said it has taken in the dogs rescued by the Martin County Sheriff's Office Animal Services Unit and is assessing their needs while determining the best path forward. These innocent dogs were inhumanely kept in deplorable conditions, and while they are finally safe, their journey to recovery is just beginning, the shelter said. Authorities said 36 Border Collies had been removed from the home as of Monday, while crews continued working to safely remove the remaining dogs. Investigators said it was initially unclear exactly how many animals remained inside because some were skittish and hiding. See also: Homeowner in custody after 36 Border Collies found in Palm City hoarding case The shelter said its immediate focus is on the well-being of the dogs and asked for the public's patience as it works through the complex situation. It is also asking for donations to help cover the cost of caring for the neglected animals, saying the financial burden comes at a time when the shelter was already facing significant challenges. Every dollar makes a difference, the shelter said. Together, we can give these dogs the second chance they deserve. The dogs were rescued after deputies with the Martin County Sheriff's Office and animal services officers served a search warrant Monday at a home on SW Alligator Street in Palm City. Sheriff John Budensiek described the conditions inside the home as extremely concerning, saying the dogs were covered in feces and the residence was filled with feces, urine-soaked materials, boxes and other debris. The animals themselves, the dogs, which are supposed to be Border Collies, beautiful dogs, are covered in feces. They're supposed to be white and black dogs, and they're solid black from the feces, Budensiek said. Deputies and animal services workers wore Tyvek protective clothing while working inside the home. Budensiek said the house was extremely hot and may not have had air conditioning. He also said about a foot and a half of drywall was missing, furniture had been destroyed and food and water bowls were covered in feces. It's really sad to see them in such rough shape. But also I'm very happy to see them finally getting out, neighbor Kelsey Weidenheimer said. Meanwhile, Paige O'Donnell, 62, was booked around noon Monday in connection with the case, according to jail records. O'Donnell faces 72 charges 36 third-degree felony counts of torture involving pain, serious physical injury or death and 36 first-degree misdemeanor counts of keeping animals in an enclosure without exercise and air. All 72 counts are listed as no bond. The investigation remains ongoing as authorities assess the condition of the dogs and determine the full scope of the case. The case comes weeks after a U.S. Postal Service carrier was arrested after more than 100 dogs and cats were found inside her Palm City home.

A vehicle fire has shut down all northbound lanes of Florida's Turnpike in Martin County near Becker Road. Officials say all occupants safely exited the vehicle before it became engulfed in flames. A vehicle fire has shut down all northbound lanes of Florida's Turnpike in Martin County near Becker Road. Officials say all occupants safely exited the vehicle before it became engulfed in flames. All northbound lanes of Florida s Turnpike are currently shut down in Martin County after a vehicle caught fire and became fully engulfed Tuesday, authorities said. The fire was reported at the 137-mile marker, about one mile south of Becker Road. According to officials, everyone inside the vehicle was able to get out safely, and no injuries have been reported. Motorists traveling through the area should expect delays and seek alternate routes while emergency crews work to extinguish the fire and clear the roadway. The cause of the fire has not yet been released. The Martin County Sheriff s Office shared a photo from the scene showing the vehicle engulfed in flames. Officials are urging drivers to use caution and avoid the area if possible as the closure remains in effect.

Before backpacks are packed, alarms are reset, and weeknight routines return, Florida’s Treasure Coast families still have time for one more summer adventure. The Locals Only program makes planning that last getaway a little easier, with exclusive seasonal offers for residents of Indian River, St. Lucie, and Martin counties. A family living anywhere within those three counties can use eligible deals throughout the entire region. That means a resident of one county can cross county lines, explore somewhere new, and still receive local savings. A valid ID showing a Treasure Coast address may be required when redeeming an offer. There is no need to plan a long road trip or spend the final days of summer sitting in traffic. Families can turn an ordinary afternoon, weekend, or overnight stay into a close-to-home escape. The available accommodations include hotels, resorts, inns, cottages, suites, vacation rentals, waterfront properties, and beachfront stays. Depending on the offer, families may find discounted room rates, percentage-based savings, special multi-night pricing, complimentary extras, or reduced rates for longer stays. Some accommodations include family-friendly conveniences such as kitchens, free breakfast, pools, sleeper sofas, outdoor spaces, and easy access to beaches and nearby attractions. Families hoping to fill the final stretch of summer with activity have plenty of choices, too. Locals Only deals cover museum and attraction admission, waterparks, beach equipment, fishing trips, kayaking, sailing, cruises, eco-tours, boating experiences, botanical gardens, golf activities, horseback riding, and other outdoor adventures. There are also dining and shopping offers that can help turn a day trip into a full family outing. A morning on the water can lead to an afternoon by the pool. A beach day can end with dinner, ice cream, or a walk through a local attraction. Even a single overnight stay can give children one more summer memory to talk about when they return to class. The offers are available for limited periods, and dates vary. Many summer lodging, dining, and activity deals continue through August or September 2026, while some accommodations remain discounted through October or December. Indian River County also lists a back-to-school special running Aug. Families should review each offer carefully before booking because expiration dates, availability, minimum stays, reservation requirements, and blackout periods may apply. Labor Day weekend and other busy travel dates are excluded from some promotions. Summer always seems to move faster once the school supplies appear in stores. The Locals Only program offers families a reason to pause before the season slips away completely. Whether the plan includes sandy feet, a boat ride, a museum visit, a pool day, or a quiet night near the water, one final adventure can make the transition back to school feel a little sweeter. Explore the current Locals Only deals at Florida’s Treasure Coast and plan one more family escape before the first bell rings at floridastreasurecoast.com/locals-only-deals . This article is sponsored by Florida’s Treasure Coast.

Keeping track of your child’s school bus is about to get easier for families in Indian River County. The School District of Indian River County is rolling out a new feature in its free app this school year that allows parents to track their child’s bus in real time. Parents can tap the bus icon in the district’s app to see where the bus is and get an estimated arrival time. The app will also send push notifications when a bus is running late. See also: Palm Beach County students return to school Monday with changes to free meal program Superintendent David K. Moore says the new feature is designed to give parents more peace of mind. You feel good as a parent, speaking as a parent, when your kid’s in school. But when they are on the bus, there’s just a little bit of angst until they get off that bus and walk in that front door, Moore told CBS12 News. Now parents have greater access when they are walking in that front door. The district is also adding another layer of security for students. Students will scan their school ID when they board the bus, allowing the district to keep better track of who is riding each bus. Moore says every school bus driver position is filled, meaning the district is fully staffed. The new tracking feature is expected to give parents another way to stay informed about their child’s ride to and from school especially on days when buses are delayed.

Lucie County Sheriff's Office is asking for the public's help finding a 2-year-old horse believed to be stolen from a Port St. Strait from Above, an American Paint Horse , was last seen around 3 p.m. The black-and-white Tovero stallion was born May 18, 2024, and has a white forelock and mane, black-and-white tail hair and a distinctive pinto coat with black-and-white spots. His registration number is 01206069. See also: Targeted in broad daylight: Boca Raton police search for multiple gunmen Deputies are asking residents, property owners, horse enthusiasts and members of the agricultural community to keep an eye out for the horse or anyone who may have been offered a horse matching his description. Anyone with information is asked to call the St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office at (772) 462-7300 or email PatrolTips@stluciesheriff.com . The sheriff’s office is urging anyone with even a small detail to come forward, as it could help bring Strait from Above home safely.

A 45-year-old dump truck driver was killed after being hit by another construction vehicle inside a work zone on I-95 just south of Tradition on Monday night, according to the Florida Highway Patrol. The driver stepped out of their dump truck on the northbound lanes and was struck by a tractor with a sweeper traveling south, repaving the area as part of an improvement project. The construction worker was transported to Cleveland Clinic Tradition Hospital, where they later died. The driver of the other truck was arrested on an unrelated warrant, FHP said. FHP s Traffic Homicide Investigation is ongoing.

A Palm City woman is facing dozens of animal cruelty charges after Martin County deputies say they found more than three dozen Border Collies living in deplorable conditions inside her home. But animal welfare experts say cases like this are often more complex than simply owning too many pets. According to investigators, 62-year-old Paige O'Donnell was arrested Monday after deputies executed a search warrant at her Palm City home. Authorities said at least 36 Border Collies were removed from the property, where deputies described conditions as unsanitary and dangerous for both the animals and anyone entering the residence. "The animals themselves, the dogs, which are supposed to be Border Collies, beautiful dogs, are covered in feces," Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek said. "They're supposed to be white and black dogs, and they're solid black from the feces." See also: Homeowner in custody after 20+ Border Collies found in Palm City hoarding case For many people, cases like this prompt a difficult question: How do conditions become so severe? Experts at the ASPCA say animal hoarding is often much more complicated than a love of animals. While some people intentionally neglect animals, others begin with good intentions and eventually become overwhelmed by the number of pets in their care. "We do see a few different subtypes of hoarding," said Dr. Maya Gupta, Vice President of Research at the ASPCA. "One is the person who is caring for animals, maybe caring for other people and just gets overwhelmed." Another common type involves what experts call a "rescuer hoarder" someone who believes they are helping animals but gradually loses the ability to care for them or place them in new homes properly. The latest Palm City case may fit into that discussion. Investigators said O'Donnell previously operated as a Border Collie breeder, and all of the dogs recovered from the home appear to be Border Collies. Gupta says one of the most powerful factors in animal hoarding is what she describes as a rescue mentality. "When somebody starts to believe that they are the only one who can provide care for the animals, that's where it can get dangerous," Gupta said. Researchers say mental health can sometimes play a role in animal hoarding cases. The Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders identifies animal hoarding as a feature that can be associated with hoarding disorder. However, experts caution that not every person who hoards animals has a diagnosable mental health condition. Instead, hoarding often involves a combination of factors, including social isolation, emotional attachment to animals, and a diminished awareness of how serious conditions have become. "Something has gone wrong in the relationships that that person has with others around them," Gupta said. "That's not something we can definitely apply to every case, but it's something we see more often than not." Experts say another challenge is that many animal hoarding cases remain hidden for years. Individuals often avoid allowing visitors into their homes, and neighbors may only become aware of a problem after noticing strong odors, excessive numbers of animals, or concerns about the animals' welfare. The latest case comes just weeks after another major animal hoarding investigation in Martin County, where more than 100 dogs and cats were rescued from a different Palm City home. Authorities said that the owner claimed she was rescuing animals she encountered along her mail route. While the rescued Border Collies are now receiving care, Gupta says it's important to remember these situations impact more than animals. "This is not 'just' an animal problem," she said. "The welfare of the people living in these homes is often really compromised." Animal welfare experts say recognizing warning signs early and reporting concerns to local authorities can help prevent situations from escalating before animals and people are put at risk. O'Donnell is expected to make her first court appearance Tuesday. Deputies said the investigation remains ongoing.

One person is in custody as Martin County sheriff’s deputies investigate what authorities describe as a serious animal hoarding case involving Border Collies at a Palm City home. The Martin County Sheriff’s Office said deputies were serving a search warrant Monday at a home at 1245 SW Alligator Street. The search follows an ongoing investigation by Martin County Animal Services officers and sheriff’s detectives, who have been working to determine the scope of the situation and the condition of the animals. "The animals themselves, the dogs, which are supposed to be Border Collies, beautiful dogs, are covered in feces. They're supposed to be white and black dogs, and they're solid black from the feces," said John Budensiek, Martin Co. Authorities said 36 Border Collies had been removed from the home so far, while deputies and animal services officers continued working to safely remove the remaining dogs. Investigators said it was unclear exactly how many animals remained inside because some of the dogs were skittish and hiding in the home. The woman who was arrested was identified as Paige O'Donnell, 62. She is being charged with felony animal cruelty and improper confinement. "She, on purpose, kept these dogs trapped in this jail that she has behind us and abused them for lack of a better word," Sheriff Budensiek said. The conditions inside the home were described as extremely concerning. Deputies and animal services officers were required to wear Tyvek protective clothing because of extensive accumulations of feces, urine-soaked materials, boxes and other debris throughout the residence. Authorities said those conditions were making it difficult and time-consuming to locate and safely remove the animals; they also said it was extremely hot and that she may not have had A/C. "It's just stacked with garbage. There's feces over every square inch of the house," Sheriff Budensiek said. "It's really sad to see them in such rough shape. But also I'm very happy to see them finally getting out," said Kelsey Weidenheimer, a neighbor. Investigators and animal services personnel are continuing to assess the condition of the dogs and determine the full scope of the case. He said the dogs were running loose in the house and conditions in the house were very bad. "The house is so deteriorated that about a foot and a half of drywall is gone. The furniture is destroyed and the animals are in deplorable condition. The food bowls, the water bowls in there are covered in feces," Sheriff Budensiek explained. Budenseik says O'Donnell will face at least 40 charges. She is expected to make her first appearance before a judge on Tuesday. She's supposed to be an animal breeder and she's gonna let the animals live like that? That's just, there's something wrong with her," said Kimberly Todd, another neighbor who lives on SW Alligator Street.

A different approach to public education is taking shape in Indian River County this school year as district leaders expand school choice and reorganize several campuses. Families in the district have more flexibility in where their children attend school. Parents can choose to enroll their children at schools across the district, rather than being limited to the school assigned to their neighborhood. The district has also converted several campuses into K-8 schools and operates five charter schools. One of the biggest changes this school year involves the district’s former all-freshman high school. See also: Indian River County launches new feature to track school buses in real time The Freshman Learning Center has been converted into Vero Beach Middle School. Moore says the freshman center was expensive to operate and did not provide students with high-quality educational programs. He says moving ninth-graders back to traditional high schools will also give them earlier access to more academic opportunities. From a student’s perspective, it allows them access to programming that was only being offered at the high school. You shouldn’t have to wait until you’re in 10th grade to take some of those courses, Moore told CBS12 News. District leaders say the two high schools, Sebastian River High School and Vero Beach High School, have enough capacity to accommodate incoming freshmen. That means all incoming ninth-graders this school year will attend either Sebastian River High School or Vero Beach High School. The changes are part of the district’s broader effort to give families more educational options while restructuring how its schools serve students.

School lunch is getting a makeover in Indian River County. District leaders say new, fresher menu options are coming to cafeterias this year. According to District Superintendent David Moore about 70 percent of Indian River County students qualify for free or reduced-price meals. See also: Palm Beach County schools continue layered approach to campus safety as school year begins This school year, the district is investing in more meals made fresh in school cafeterias instead of simply reheating food. Moore says students will also see more build-your-own options as they walk through the cafeteria line, including salads and tacos. Some of the items coming up, and some of the items coming off, come at the direct response of the students who say, That’s no good. We want fresher options,'" Moore told CBS12 News. Moore says he’s been taste-testing many of the new menu items himself and believes students will notice the difference when they head through the lunch line this school year.

The Martin County Sheriff's Office conducted a search warrant Monday at a Palm City home in connection with an alleged animal hoarding case.Sheriff’s deputies rescued 36 dogs from a home in the 1245 block of Southwest Alligator Street following a WPTV investigation. WPTV was told that the hoarding case involves Border Collies.WATCH BELOW: Dogs rescued after WPTV investigation into suspected animal hoardingMartin County Sheriff John Budensiek said the owner of the home, Paige O'Donnell, will face 72 criminal charges — 36 felony torture charges and 36 misdemeanor charges. She's accused of keeping animals enclosed without exercise and air. This comes after investigators said she never let the dogs outside — something that neighbors previously told WPTV had been occurring."The house is so deteriorated that about a foot and a half of drywall is gone. The furniture is destroyed, and the animals are in deplorable condition. The food bowls, the water bowls in there are covered in feces. The animals themselves, the dogs, which are supposed to be border collies, beautiful dogs, are covered in feces," Budensiek said.Monday's search warrant comes after WPTV's investigation revealed that Martin County Animal Control officers and sheriff's deputies had visited homes in the area at least 11 times since 2020 — all related to concerns about dogs and their owners.As law enforcement continued to respond, the homeowner built a fence and stopped letting deputies in — making it hard to find probable cause for a warrant.But after WPTV started asking the sheriff’s office about the house, they decided to look into it once again."We could not legally just run into the house based on what people said. We had to get our own information. So, days of surveillance out here, days of trying to negotiate with Paige… but she agreed last week to surrender one of the dogs to us," Budensiek said.The sheriff said that dog appeared to be malnourished, giving them the probable cause to execute a warrant Monday.Investigators on Monday were busy sweeping the house to make sure no dogs were hiding inside or dead.O'Donnell, a former AKC Border Collie breeder, had been living in this house and was taking a bath when they arrived to serve the warrant. Budensiek said she didn't come to the door, prompting them to bust it open.Budensiek applauded WPTV's efforts reporting the story, which kept the case on their radar."You keeping the story alive in your newsroom kept us engaged, kept us back out here and looking. It’s a collective effort," Budensiek said. Meanwhile, the 36 dogs rescued on Monday will be taken to the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast for care.

One person is in custody as Martin County sheriff’s deputies investigate what authorities describe as a serious animal hoarding case involving Border Collies at a Palm City home. The Martin County Sheriff’s Office said deputies were serving a search warrant Monday at a home at 1245 SW Alligator Street. The search follows an ongoing investigation by Martin County Animal Services officers and sheriff’s detectives, who have been working to determine the scope of the situation and the animals' condition. "The animals themselves, the dogs, which are supposed to be Border Collies, beautiful dogs, are covered in feces. They're supposed to be white and black dogs, and they're solid black from the feces," said John Budensiek, Martin Co. Authorities said 36 Border Collies had been removed from the home so far, while deputies and animal services officers continued working to safely remove the remaining dogs. Investigators said it was unclear exactly how many animals remained inside because some of the dogs were skittish and hiding in the home. The woman who was arrested was identified as Paige O'Donnell, 62. She is being charged with felony animal cruelty and improper confinement. "She, on purpose, kept these dogs trapped in this jail that she has behind us and abused them for lack of a better word," Sheriff Budensiek said. The conditions inside the home were described as extremely concerning. Deputies and animal services officers were required to wear Tyvek protective clothing because of extensive accumulations of feces, urine-soaked materials, boxes and other debris throughout the residence. Authorities said those conditions were making it difficult and time-consuming to locate and safely remove the animals; they also said it was extremely hot and that she may not have had A/C. "It's just stacked with garbage. There's feces over every square inch of the house," Sheriff Budensiek said. "It's really sad to see them in such rough shape. But also I'm very happy to see them finally getting out," said Kelsey Weidenheimer, a neighbor. Investigators and animal services personnel are continuing to assess the condition of the dogs and determine the full scope of the case. WARNING: DISTURBING IMAGES IN VIDEO BELOW Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek provided an update on the investigation. He said the dogs were running loose in the house and conditions in the house were very bad. "The house is so deteriorated that about a foot and a half of drywall is gone. The furniture is destroyed and the animals are in deplorable condition. The food bowls, the water bowls in there are covered in feces," Sheriff Budensiek explained. Budenseik says O'Donnell will face at least 40 charges. She is expected to make her first appearance before a judge on Tuesday. She's supposed to be an animal breeder and she's gonna let the animals live like that? That's just, there's something wrong with her," said Kimberly Todd, another neighbor who lives on SW Alligator Street.

As Murray Middle School students head back to class this week in Stuart, they're returning to a campus that looks much different than when they left. Nearly two years after a tornado spawned by Hurricane Milton tore through the school, damaged buildings are now gone, and a major rebuild is taking shape. Students are seeing plenty of construction that’ll continue throughout the school year. But district leaders say the work zone is completely separated from the rest of campus, so students can learn safely while crews rebuild. See also: Palm Beach County schools continue layered approach to campus safety as school year begins The October 2024 tornado destroyed two buildings and left a third with major roof damage. Those spaces housed the school's band, chorus, and agriculture programs. Superintendent Michael Maine says those programs never stopped. Over the summer, crews demolished two buildings. It'll make way for a new administration building and media center, plus modern spaces for band, chorus, and agriculture science. Crews will also renovate the gym. Be excited for the new year. Yes, it's going to take a little bit of time to get there, but it's well deserved. And when those students arrive on campus, there's nothing like seeing the bright smiles of the students to say, Wow, this is ours.’ It's incredible when you walk into a classroom environment that's clean, and new and fresh, and teachers are able to do so much more when we're able to provide the very best, said Superintendent Maine. The gym is expected to be finished by next August. The new administration building, media center, and specialized classrooms are expected to follow in December 2027. The project is being paid for through state support, insurance reimbursements, and district capital funds.

A 48-year-old Vero Beach man riding an electric bicycle was killed after being struck by a pickup truck that fled the scene Sunday night in unincorporated Indian River County. According to the Florida Highway Patrol , the crash happened around 8:57 p.m. Sunday at the intersection of 8th Street and 14th Avenue. FHP said the bicyclist was traveling west in the westbound lane of 8th Street and approaching 14th Avenue. A light-colored Ford F-150, believed to be a 2015 to 2020 model, was traveling behind him in the same lane, investigators said. See also: 19-year-old identified as victim in deadly Boynton Beach shooting s the pickup approached the bicyclist, the driver took evasive action, traveling southwest and partially entering the eastbound lane. However, troopers said the truck was unable to avoid the bicyclist and the right side of the pickup struck him. The bicyclist tumbled onto the roadway and came to rest in the eastbound lane of 8th Street. FHP said the driver fled the scene without rendering aid or contacting law enforcement. Investigators said the Ford F-150 is believed to be missing its right-side rearview mirror as a result of the crash. The bicyclist was taken to Lawnwood Hospital, where he was pronounced dead. His identity has not been released pending notification of next of kin. Both eastbound and westbound lanes of 8th Street were blocked while troopers investigated the crash. Anyone with information about the vehicle or driver is asked to contact the Florida Highway Patrol.

Senate race is attracting millions of dollars, but before Democrats can challenge Republican Sen. Ashley Moody, they must settle a primary between two candidates offering very different arguments.Retired Army Lt. Alex Vindman enters the Democratic primary with the national profile and fundraising advantage. By: Samantha Roesler Posted and last updated PALM BEACH COUNTY, Fla. — Firefighters worked through the night to contain a large fire at a tire recycling lot in the Palms West Industrial Park off Belvedere Road, according to Palm Beach County Fire Rescue. The blaze began at approximately 10:35 p.m. and prompted emergency response from both Palm Beach County Fire Rescue and the West Palm Beach Fire Department. A total of 19 units and 40 firefighters responded to the scene. Fire crews brought the flames under control by midnight, successfully containing the fire to the area of origin within the tire recycling lot. No buildings were damaged in the incident, and no injuries were reported. Firefighters will remain on scene for an extended overhaul due to smoldering typical of tire fires, given the dense, combustible nature of rubber. No roadways were affected by the incident, and traffic flow in the area remains normal.

Keeping track of your child’s school bus is about to get easier for families in Indian River County. The School District of Indian River County is rolling out a new feature in its free app this school year that allows parents to track their child’s bus in real time. Parents can tap the bus icon in the district’s app to see where the bus is and get an estimated arrival time. The app will also send push notifications when a bus is running late. See also: Palm Beach County students return to school Monday with changes to free meal program Superintendent David K. Moore says the new feature is designed to give parents more peace of mind. You feel good as a parent, speaking as a parent, when your kid’s in school. But when they are on the bus, there’s just a little bit of angst until they get off that bus and walk in that front door, Moore told CBS12 News. Now parents have greater access when they are walking in that front door. The district is also adding another layer of security for students. Students will scan their school ID when they board the bus, allowing the district to keep better track of who is riding each bus. Moore says every school bus driver position is filled, meaning the district is fully staffed. The new tracking feature is expected to give parents another way to stay informed about their child’s ride to and from school especially on days when buses are delayed.

Tradition Lakes K-8 in St. Lucie County has delayed its opening by a week. Construction is still underway at the school. Some parents are now concerned about safety and scrambling for childcare options. The school, originally scheduled to welcome 1,600 students on Monday, will now open on Aug. 17, according to district officials. Prince released a statement explaining that after inspecting the school, he did not feel staff had enough time to "adequately prepare it for parents and children," leading to the decision to push the opening. Parents and residents expressed concerns about the delay and the state of the school. "The kids' safety needs to come first. I don’t know how they’re going to do it," one grandmother said. "I’m concerned that they’re going to bring 1,600 kids with it looking like construction. There are signs all over that say hard hat area." Parent Robyn Johnson questioned whether the school would be ready in time. "It doesn’t look at all done, especially towards the back there," she said. Tradition Lakes K-8 is expected to provide much-needed classroom space for one of the county’s fastest-growing communities. However, some parents feel the process has been mishandled. "It’s a nice idea, absolutely wonderful that they have a new school coming, but they haven’t run this, in my opinion, the right way. But hopefully, they get it done," a grandmother said. The district said it will share community childcare options for families during the delay. An open house is scheduled for next Friday. FORT PIERCE — From locally made gifts to Fort Pierce-themed keepsakes, Sunshine State of Mind Boutique gives residents a place to celebrate home and visitors a way to take a little of it with them. Sunshine State of Mind opened in early June on Second Street, offering Fort Pierce souvenirs, locally made works of art and Florida-inspired apparel and gifts. The boutique is a passion project for Kim Brant, who has worked in downtown Fort Pierce for many years. She spent 10 years at the Original Tiki Bar and has worked at Cobbs Landing for the past five years. Brant said she saw the need for a shop dedicated to showcasing the city’s charm and character. “Every town around us has something like that,” she said, mentioning the Shell Bazaar in Port St. “I just wanted to share how amazing Fort Pierce is. It seems that there’s always been a bit of a cloud over the town, but I think it’s really a paradise!,” Brant added. Sunshine State of Mind offers a unique collection of Fort Pierce souvenirs, ranging from T-shirts and sweatshirts to locally made jewelry and woodwork, reflecting the city and Florida lifestyle. One wall features a shelf labeled “Locals Only,” showcasing work by local artists and crafters. Brant said she keeps all the vendors as local as possible. She even designs most of the shirts and sweatshirts herself. While this is her first endeavor as a business owner, she said “everything is figure-outable.” The shop is a family affair. Her husband, Chris, and their children help so Brant can continue working at Cobbs Landing. Brant said customer feedback has been positive since the store opened. Local resident Miranda Talley discovered Sunshine Boutique on TikTok “I thought it looked super cute, so I had to come check it out,” she said, looking over the display of refrigerator magnets for something to add to her collection. Just a few weeks after opening, Sunshine State of Mind Boutique is attracting residents and visitors looking for keepsakes that capture the spirit of Fort Pierce. For Brant, the shop is an opportunity to highlight the city she loves while giving local artists and makers a place to showcase their work. As downtown Fort Pierce continues to grow, she said she hopes Sunshine Boutique will become another stop that encourages people to discover and appreciate what this unique community has to offer. An act of bravery and compassion is bringing two strangers together on the Treasure Coast. A young man rescued a woman whose car got stuck on a railroad crossing in Hobe Sound, saving her from near disaster. Stay up-to-date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25 Just a few days ago, Josiah Baur and Debbie Spoelstra didn’t know each other, but now, they share a special connection. “Friday, I was leaving work, and I was heading back home. I was trying to get home for a tire appointment, funny enough, and running late for it. Train crossing went down, and I looked down on my phone, and I glimpsed up, and I saw the car stuck behind the railroad crossing,” Baur said. Spoelstra was still inside that car, stuck on the train tracks at Bridge Road and Dixie Highway in Hobe Sound. What I did is, I put my car in reverse, and apparently the gate got stuck on top of my car on the antenna. So, when I tried to reverse, it would not let me reverse. I sat there, I saw the train,” Spoelstra said. Baur, realizing she was still in the car, didn’t hesitate and jumped out of his car to help. “I threw it in park and just took off running. Try to see what side the train was on to see if it would clear her or not. But it was on her side and didn't really want to take a chance. So, I ran across and tried to push up on the thingy to release her,” Baur said. That split-second decision helped to avoid what could have been a devastating crash from a freight train. “He came just like a hero. And lifted the gate up off of my car. And I was able to reverse and get off the tracks. And as soon as he did that, within seconds, the train passed by me. So it was very scary, you know, life-changing experience for me,” Spoelstra said. “We think of heroes, I think police officers and military, not what I did. It was just a good, good thing to do,” Baur said. The two said they’ve now bonded over this unique experience, attributing it to their shared faith. “He was put in one place, I was put in one place, and it was just fate. And it was a God thing, you know, and then once I told him my grandson was Josiah, and then he was just like, ‘Oh, wow. It's definitely a God thing.’ So, I don't know. I would just say, like I said, I'm so grateful for him,” Spoelstra said. He puts us exactly where we need to be. If you're running late for something, it's probably for a reason. Just trust his plan,” Baur said. Spoelstra said she wasn’t texting or distracted while driving and was simply just taken off guard by the railroad crossing arms lowering. She wants to pass this message on to other drivers: always be careful and look both ways before crossing train tracks. Get the latest news updates with the WPBF 25 News app.

The weeklong event will feature performances, professional dance training, public classes, artist talkbacks and community experiences designed to strengthen South Florida’s dance community.Festival founders Ericka Squire of Natural Movers Foundation and Branndi Lewis of Grounded WPB said the event was created to expand opportunities for dancers and choreographers while positioning Palm Beach County as a destination for dance.“At its core, Banyan is about creating opportunities for artists,” Squire said in a statement. “Palm Beach County is Florida’s Cultural Capital®, and we wanted to create an opportunity for audiences to experience high-quality dance performances while also creating real pathways for dancers and choreographers to train, work, create, and be seen right here in Palm Beach County.”Festival organizers said the event will bring together professional artists, students and community members through performances, creative development and educational programming hosted at venues throughout the city.Featured artists include internationally recognized choreographers and educators Sean Aaron Carmon, Babatunji and Loni Landon, along with local, national and international performers participating throughout the week.Carmon, a former dancer with Alvin Ailey American Dance Theater, will create an original work for the Banyan Dance Company. Babatunji, a former member of Alonzo King LINES Ballet, will choreograph a new piece for the Banyan Dance Ensemble.Landon, a Princess Grace Choreography Fellowship Award winner and Guggenheim fellow, will teach during the festival and create a featured solo work for a dancer participating in the Banyan Dance Intensive.The festival’s inaugural Banyan Choreography Fellowship was awarded to Betty Garcia Diaz, a Cuban-born dancer and choreographer who has performed with companies including Northwest Dance Project, Malpaso Dance Company and Boston Dance Theater. Organizers said Garcia Diaz will create a newly commissioned work during the festival.Programming throughout the week includes:Youth Artist Program classes for dancers ages 9-15A pre-professional dance intensive for dancers ages 16-25Community dance classes sponsored by the Downtown Development AuthorityA Banyan Silent Disco at Nora DistrictRehearsal observations and artist talkbacks at Ballet FloridaThe Banyan Gala at the Community Foundation for Palm Beach and Martin CountiesThe Banyan Dance Festival Concert at the Norton Museum of ArtLewis said the festival is designed to create opportunities for dancers who previously may have needed to leave South Florida to pursue professional growth.“Banyan Dance Festival is building something that doesn’t currently exist in South Florida,” Lewis said in a statement. “Together, Grounded WPB and Natural Movers Foundation have created a platform that expands the local dance ecosystem while investing in artists through paid opportunities, professional training, and a full creative pipeline.”More information and a full schedule can be found at banyandancefestival.com or on Instagram at @banyandancefestival.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. The Soup Kitchen in Boynton Beach is celebrating 10 years of its Meals on Wheels program, a service that has delivered more than 520,000 meals to homebound seniors across Palm Beach County, according to organization leaders.The nonprofit, located at 8655 Boynton Beach Blvd., serves thousands of hot meals each day and has become a critical resource for seniors who are unable to leave their homes.Leaders with The Soup Kitchen said volunteers now deliver meals to between 90 and 120 seniors on a typical day. According to the organization, The Soup Kitchen now provides more than 300 meals each week to seniors who rely on the center for food and community connection.Dimitry Viarenich, chief operating officer of The Soup Kitchen, said the partnership has helped stabilize services for seniors during a difficult time.Regina Fay, who leads the Meals on Wheels program, said volunteers are essential to keeping deliveries running each day. Palm Beach County’s growing culinary scene is earning international recognition after several local restaurants received honors from the MICHELIN Guide Florida, including one West Palm Beach restaurant making history.Monday, 10 restaurants were awarded 2026 MICHELIN plaques by Discover The Palm Beaches.Emelina, a 16-seat tasting-menu restaurant in West Palm Beach’s Flamingo Park neighborhood, earned Palm Beach County’s only MICHELIN Star this year. According to Discover The Palm Beaches, Emelina also became the first Cuban restaurant in the world to receive a MICHELIN Star.Several other Palm Beach County restaurants received MICHELIN recognition through recommendations and Bib Gourmand honors, which recognize quality food at a good value.MICHELIN inspectors evaluate restaurants based on ingredient quality, flavor harmony, cooking techniques, consistency and the chef’s personality reflected in the cuisine.In Palm Beach County kitchens, chefs are chasing perfection and now, MICHELIN is noticing.Chef Pushkar Marathe said MICHELIN inspectors visit anonymously.“They never really shared that they’re going to be in your restaurant,” Marathe said.Marathe’s Palm Beach Gardens restaurants, Stage Kitchen & Bar and Ela Curry & Cocktails, both earned MICHELIN recommendations this year. His first reaction after learning about the recognition focused on improvement.“First thought was, how could we do better to get a star?” Marathe said.Marathe explained that MICHELIN recommendations place restaurants within reach of earning a future star.“When you’re recommended, you’ve been considered for the star, but there’s still some things you need to work on,” he said.Chef Tim Lipman’s Coolinary and the Parched Pig also received a MICHELIN recommendation.“You don’t necessarily strive for the award, but you strive for excellence,” Lipman said.Lipman said the recognition has helped local restaurants stand out in a competitive dining market.“Definitely needle in a haystack, right? There’s so many great restaurants out there,” he said.Aioli in West Palm Beach earned a Bib Gourmand designation for the second consecutive year. Owners Michael and Melanie Hackman said the recognition validates their commitment to scratch-made baking and consistency.“We are a scratch sourdough bakery,” Michael Hackman said. “It’s definitely why MICHELIN noticed us. We’re doing stuff the right way. We’re not cutting corners."Aioli’s sourdough takes more than three days to ferment. Hackman said even pop culture trends have influenced customer interest.“They said, ‘I’m only here, because Taylor Swift makes sourdough. I want to learn how to make sourdough,’” Hackman said.Melanie Hackman said maintaining MICHELIN recognition can be even more challenging than earning it initially.“Earning it the first time was huge, but retaining it was even bigger for us,” she said.Restaurant owners also said the recognition is helping business during the slower summer months.“We are in the dead of summer and grateful that our restaurant is full every day,” Melanie Hackman said.Milton Segarra, president and CEO of Discover The Palm Beaches, said culinary tourism is becoming increasingly important to Palm Beach County’s economy.“Normally visitors come here for the beaches and the experiences we can offer. Now they are returning, because we became this powerhouse in the culinary scene,” Segarra said.Segarra said tourism investment tied to culinary marketing efforts has generated measurable returns for the county.“For every dollar that we invest on behalf of the county, we have a return of $3.55 in TDTs,” he said, referring to tourist development tax revenue.Why this matters now: MICHELIN recognition continues to reshape Palm Beach County’s reputation beyond beaches and luxury resorts. As more nationally recognized chefs and restaurants open across the region, local leaders see fine dining and culinary tourism becoming a growing economic driver for South Florida.From scratch bakeries to chef-driven tasting menus, Palm Beach County’s restaurant scene is earning attention from diners around the world — and local chefs say they are still striving for more.2026 Palm Beach County restaurants recognized by Michelin Guide FloridaMICHELIN Star • Emelina — West Palm BeachBib Gourmand • aioli — West Palm BeachMICHELIN Recommended• Stage Kitchen & Bar — Palm Beach Gardens• Ela Curry & Cocktails — Palm Beach Gardens• Coolinary — Palm Beach Gardens• būccan — Palm Beach• Moody Tongue Sushi — West Palm Beach• Nicholson Muir — Boynton Beach• The Butcher’s Club — Palm Beach GardensWhat do MICHELIN distinctions mean?• MICHELIN Star: Awarded for exceptional cooking and culinary excellence.• Bib Gourmand: Recognizes high-quality food at a good value.• Recommended: Honors restaurants serving standout meals with quality ingredients and strong execution.What do you want me to Shine A Light on? United Way of Palm Beach County is encouraging more adults to become volunteer mentors as nearly 1,000 local students remain on a waiting list for support through mentoring programs across the county.The organization’s Mentor Center oversees 24 local mentor programs and also serves as the anchor for the Palm Beach County Mentor Network, a coalition of 60 formal mentoring programs that collectively oversee nearly 6,000 mentor matches each year.During an interview with WPTV’s T.A. Walker, United Way of Palm Beach County President and CEO Laurie George explained how the mentoring process works and why consistent adult support can make a difference for children navigating school and life challenges.“So what we do is we match mentors, adult caring mentors, with a sixth grade child, and it basically you’re their support system for the year,” George said.According to United Way, volunteer mentors meet with students about one hour each week in a supervised setting. Organizers say the role is less about expertise and more about being present and listening.“You just listen to them more than anything,” George said. “They need a caring adult.”George said mentorship often gives children a safe place to talk openly about their feelings, struggles and experiences.“What happens is that people feel safe,” George said. They come to school more often. Their grades are better, and they make wise choices.”United Way said formal mentor experience is not required. LUCIE – The Daytona Tortugas scored 11 unanswered runs over the final three innings on Thursday to pull away for a 17-3 win over the St. Lucie Mets at Clover Park. The Mets hit three doubles in the fifth inning, including back-to-back RBI doubles by John Smith III and Julio Zayas to cut the Daytona lead to 6-3. But the Tortugas took advantage of six walks issued by Mets relievers Jean Brito and Luis Sotillo in the seventh inning. They scored six runs in the frame to go up 12-3 and break the game open. The Mets relied the DH Zayas to finish the game on the mound for the final two innings. The Tortugas scored five runs off Zayas in the eighth inning to stretch the lead to 17-3, but Zayas pitched a scoreless ninth. He induced a double play in the inning. The Mets scored first in the game on a RBI single by Reed Stallman in the second inning. Then with the bases loaded and one out, Tortugas started Mason Morris started a 1-2-3 double play off the broken bat of Kooper Schulte to escape further damage. The Tortugas used that momentum in the top of the third. They scored five runs on five hits off Mets starter Jose Lopez to go up 5-1. Bernard Moon hit a two-run double in the inning which was his FSL-leading 28th double. Lopez pitched well outside of the third inning. Overall he pitched 5.1 innings and gave up six runs on seven hits. He walked one and struck out six. It was the longest outing by a Mets pitcher since the first game of the second half on June 19th. Elian Peña went 2 for 5 with a double. It was the third straight two-hit game for Peña. Smith III was 2 for 4 with a double and RBI. He allowed three runs over 5.0 innings. The Mets (14-23, 47-56) and Tortugas (24-13, 45-58) continue their series at Clover Park on Friday. All veterans and active duty military receive free admission courtesy of LYNQ Real Estate. Italy defeated Pakistan to claim the 2026 Amerigol LATAM Cup ice hockey championship on Sunday, with goalkeeper Rocco Bruno earning MVP honors in a game that highlighted hockey's expanding global footprint.The tournament, held in Florida, featured two countries not traditionally associated with the sport. Pakistan scored first, but Italy responded with two unanswered goals — including a decisive shot that sealed the championship.Bruno was a standout throughout the tournament."It means the world to me to be able to come out here and represent these colors. It's a once-in-a-lifetime experience; I'm just so thankful to be able to be a part of this team here," Bruno said.When asked about the MVP award, Bruno kept his focus on the bigger prize."I wasn't expecting it whatsoever. I go out there and play a game, and sometimes I get rewarded for it, but I like the big trophy; that one is more important to me," Bruno said.Italian team captain John Schiavo described the energy inside the arena."It was amazing; the atmosphere all tournament was awesome. Obviously, with this being the biggest game, the crowd was rocking, and there's no better feeling than to play in front of an awesome crowd," Schiavo said.For Pakistan's players, the experience carried meaning far beyond the scoreboard. Tariq Khan reflected on what competing on this stage represents."It's a huge honor to be able to show kids around the world that we have an ice hockey team; it shows that anything is possible no matter where you're from," Tariq Khan said.Zaakir Khan echoed that sentiment."It's nothing I've ever experienced. I'm not good enough to play for the United States, but just to be able to play for your country is something I wish everyone could feel; it's god's gift," Zaakir Khan said.Florida's hockey culture, fueled in part by the recent Stanley Cup championships of the Florida Panthers and Tampa Bay Lightning, has helped create a platform for the sport's international growth.

A Martin County woman is facing felony and misdemeanor animal cruelty charges after deputies discovered 36 dogs living in unsanitary conditions inside her Palm City home. The Martin County Sheriff’s Office executed a search warrant earlier today and spent much of the afternoon removing the animals, which ranged from puppies to adult border collies. Investigators wore hazmat suits as they worked to retrieve the dogs. “The animals are in deplorable conditions,” Sheriff John Budensiek said. Budensiek described the state of the home, saying, “The food bowls, the water bowls in there are covered in feces. The animals themselves, the dogs, which are supposed to be border collies, beautiful dogs, are covered in feces. They're supposed to be white and black dogs, and they're solid black from the feces.” He added that some of the dogs were skittish and hiding, making it difficult for investigators to remove them. “Currently right now, there's more dogs in there than what they've been able to get out because they're skittish, they're hiding,” Budensiek said. According to Budensiek, the homeowner, Paige O'Donnell, was previously an AKC breeder. He said the last time officials were allowed inside the home was in 2020, when the animals were in acceptable condition. However, between 2020 and 2022, O'Donnell reportedly underwent treatment for alcohol abuse and began “playing the legal game” to block officials from accessing her home. A neighbor, Tessa Nabors, expressed hope that the situation would lead to change. “Hopefully she gets the help that she also needs, but she shouldn't be subjecting animals to that type of situation because they're being forced to live in that, and that's disgusting on her part,” Nabors said. The sheriff confirmed that all 36 dogs removed from the home will be taken to the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast. To donate to the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast, click here. O'Donnell is expected to appear in court Tuesday. Keeping track of your child’s school bus is about to get easier for families in Indian River County. The School District of Indian River County is rolling out a new feature in its free app this school year that allows parents to track their child’s bus in real time. Parents can tap the bus icon in the district’s app to see where the bus is and get an estimated arrival time. The app will also send push notifications when a bus is running late. See also: Palm Beach County students return to school Monday with changes to free meal program Superintendent David K. Moore says the new feature is designed to give parents more peace of mind. You feel good as a parent, speaking as a parent, when your kid’s in school. But when they are on the bus, there’s just a little bit of angst until they get off that bus and walk in that front door, Moore told CBS12 News. Now parents have greater access when they are walking in that front door. The district is also adding another layer of security for students. Students will scan their school ID when they board the bus, allowing the district to keep better track of who is riding each bus. Moore says every school bus driver position is filled, meaning the district is fully staffed. The new tracking feature is expected to give parents another way to stay informed about their child’s ride to and from school especially on days when buses are delayed.

The Martin County Sheriff's Office conducted a search warrant Monday at a Palm City home in connection with an alleged animal hoarding case.Sheriff’s deputies rescued 36 dogs from a home in the 1245 block of Southwest Alligator Street following a WPTV investigation. WPTV was told that the hoarding case involves Border Collies.WATCH BELOW: Dogs rescued after WPTV investigation into suspected animal hoardingMartin County Sheriff John Budensiek said the owner of the home, Paige O'Donnell, will face charges of felony animal cruelty and misdemeanor improper confinement. The latter charge comes after investigators said she never let the dogs outside — something that neighbors previously told WPTV had been occurring."The house is so deteriorated that about a foot and a half of drywall is gone. The furniture is destroyed, and the animals are in deplorable condition. The food bowls, the water bowls in there are covered in feces. The animals themselves, the dogs, which are supposed to be border collies, beautiful dogs, are covered in feces," Budensiek said.Monday's search warrant comes after WPTV's investigation revealed that Martin County Animal Control officers and sheriff's deputies had visited homes in the area at least 11 times since 2020 — all related to concerns about dogs and their owners.As law enforcement continued to respond, the homeowner built a fence and stopped letting deputies in — making it hard to find probable cause for a warrant.But after WPTV started asking the sheriff’s office about the house, they decided to look into it once again."We could not legally just run into the house based on what people said. We had to get our own information. So, days of surveillance out here, days of trying to negotiate with Paige… but she agreed last week to surrender one of the dogs to us," Budensiek said.The sheriff said that dog appeared to be malnourished, giving them the probable cause to execute a warrant Monday.Investigators on Monday were busy sweeping the house to make sure no dogs were hiding inside or dead.O'Donnell, a former AKC Border Collie breeder, had been living in this house and was taking a bath when they arrived to serve the warrant. Budensiek said she didn't come to the door, prompting them to bust it open.Budensiek applauded WPTV's efforts reporting the story, which kept the case on their radar."You keeping the story alive in your newsroom kept us engaged, kept us back out here and looking. It’s a collective effort," Budensiek said. Meanwhile, the 36 dogs rescued on Monday will be taken to the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast for care.

What started as a routine drive home from work turned into a terrifying race against time for Debbie Spoelstra. Spoelstra says she was turning onto Bridge Road from Dixie Highway in Hobe Sound Friday evening when a railroad crossing arm suddenly came down on her car, leaving her trapped on the tracks. Dash-cam video captured the tense moments that followed. A train's horn can be heard as it quickly moved closer and closer to Spoelstra's red car as it sat between the crossing gates. Then, a young man runs toward her. I was pretty much frozen, Spoelstra said. Then I thought about getting out of the car, and then at that moment I saw Josiah running across the railroad tracks. That man was 23-year-old Josiah Baur. Baur said he left work late that evening and was on his way home to Port Saint Lucie when he stopped at the crossing. He was on the other side of the tracks when he saw what was happening. You only get a couple seconds to react, Baur said. He immediately ran toward the crossing. I just took off running, he said. Baur reached the crossing and lifted the gate with both arms, giving Spoelstra enough time to back her car away from the tracks before the train came through. He said he first looked to see where the train was. It was on her side, so I ran up and pushed up on it and released it just in time for her to back up, Baur said. Another witness, Lizzy Dominguez, was behind Baur's car when she saw what was happening. She and the others in her car could only watch. We were just saying, Please, God, please, God, please, God,’ Dominguez said. We were frozen in the car. After the rescue, Dominguez took a photo of Baur and posted it on social media , hoping to find him and thank him for what he had done. It was very emotional, Dominguez said. We thought, oh, we just witnessed a miracle. Spoelstra and Baur met again at the railroad crossing Sunday. When they saw each other, they hugged. Spoelstra said she's grateful to Baur and believes things could have turned out very differently if he hadn't been there. You know, first of all, that a total stranger, would help another person, she said. I won't ever forget what he's done for me. He is a true American hero. Baur, however, doesn't describe himself that way. I’m just very fortunate that God put me right where I was, he said. "He's got a plan and we just got to follow it sometimes. We don't understand why." Witnesses say the crossing arm malfunctioned during the incident. See also: Foodborne illnesses are rising. What not to eat right now. Spoelstra says she reported the problem to Florida East Coast (FEC) Railway line and was told someone would come out to inspect the gate. The incident remains a powerful reminder of how quickly a dangerous situation at a railroad crossing can unfold and how one person's decision to act can make all the difference. For Spoelstra, there is also a personal connection that makes the story feel even more remarkable. She says her baby grandson shares the same name as the man who came to her rescue: Josiah.

A Palm City woman is facing dozens of animal cruelty charges after Martin County deputies say they found more than three dozen Border Collies living in deplorable conditions inside her home. But animal welfare experts say cases like this are often more complex than simply owning too many pets. According to investigators, 62-year-old Paige O'Donnell was arrested Monday after deputies executed a search warrant at her Palm City home. Authorities said at least 36 Border Collies were removed from the property, where deputies described conditions as unsanitary and dangerous for both the animals and anyone entering the residence. "The animals themselves, the dogs, which are supposed to be Border Collies, beautiful dogs, are covered in feces," Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek said. "They're supposed to be white and black dogs, and they're solid black from the feces." See also: Homeowner in custody after 20+ Border Collies found in Palm City hoarding case For many people, cases like this prompt a difficult question: How do conditions become so severe? Experts at the ASPCA say animal hoarding is often much more complicated than a love of animals. While some people intentionally neglect animals, others begin with good intentions and eventually become overwhelmed by the number of pets in their care. "We do see a few different subtypes of hoarding," said Dr. Maya Gupta, Vice President of Research at the ASPCA. "One is the person who is caring for animals, maybe caring for other people and just gets overwhelmed." Another common type involves what experts call a "rescuer hoarder" someone who believes they are helping animals but gradually loses the ability to care for them or place them in new homes properly. The latest Palm City case may fit into that discussion. Investigators said O'Donnell previously operated as a Border Collie breeder, and all of the dogs recovered from the home appear to be Border Collies. Gupta says one of the most powerful factors in animal hoarding is what she describes as a rescue mentality. "When somebody starts to believe that they are the only one who can provide care for the animals, that's where it can get dangerous," Gupta said. Researchers say mental health can sometimes play a role in animal hoarding cases. The Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders identifies animal hoarding as a feature that can be associated with hoarding disorder. However, experts caution that not every person who hoards animals has a diagnosable mental health condition. Instead, hoarding often involves a combination of factors, including social isolation, emotional attachment to animals, and a diminished awareness of how serious conditions have become. "Something has gone wrong in the relationships that that person has with others around them," Gupta said. "That's not something we can definitely apply to every case, but it's something we see more often than not." Experts say another challenge is that many animal hoarding cases remain hidden for years. Individuals often avoid allowing visitors into their homes, and neighbors may only become aware of a problem after noticing strong odors, excessive numbers of animals, or concerns about the animals' welfare. The latest case comes just weeks after another major animal hoarding investigation in Martin County, where more than 100 dogs and cats were rescued from a different Palm City home. Authorities said that the owner claimed she was rescuing animals she encountered along her mail route. While the rescued Border Collies are now receiving care, Gupta says it's important to remember these situations impact more than animals. "This is not 'just' an animal problem," she said. "The welfare of the people living in these homes is often really compromised." Animal welfare experts say recognizing warning signs early and reporting concerns to local authorities can help prevent situations from escalating before animals and people are put at risk. O'Donnell is expected to make her first court appearance Tuesday. Deputies said the investigation remains ongoing.

Senate race is attracting millions of dollars, but before Democrats can challenge Republican Sen. Ashley Moody, they must settle a primary between two candidates offering very different arguments.Retired Army Lt. Alex Vindman enters the Democratic primary with the national profile and fundraising advantage. He raised roughly $14.5 million through June, according to the latest campaign-finance totals, outpacing Moody.Watch report from Forrest SaundersVindman is highlighting his military service and presenting himself as a candidate capable of reaching voters beyond the Democratic base. He has largely focused his campaign on the November election and the need to place a congressional check on President Donald Trump.“Getting a Democratic House and a Democratic Senate is absolutely essential in this environment because I think the Republicans in office have absolutely abrogated, abandoned their responsibilities to be any kind of check on power,” Vindman said.First, however, Vindman must defeat state Rep. Angie Nixon, a Jacksonville Democrat whom he has so far declined to debate.Nixon is countering Vindman’s national profile with her Florida roots, a more progressive platform and a working-class message centered on wages and affordability.Her campaign’s social-media posts have highlighted everyday challenges on the trail, including car trouble and a flat tire. Nixon has portrayed those moments as evidence that she deals with many of the same problems confronting the voters she hopes to represent.At the Florida Capitol, Nixon has also developed a reputation as an outspoken protester. She used a bullhorn during the fight over Florida’s new congressional maps and was later charged following a sit-in demonstration at the governor’s office.“I shouldn’t have been the one that got locked up,” Nixon said afterward. “They should have been the ones that got locked up.”While Democrats decide between Vindman and Nixon, Moody faces three lower-profile candidates in the Republican primary. None is expected to seriously threaten the appointed senator, allowing Moody to concentrate much of her attention on November.Moody is framing the general election as a choice between Republicans and Democrats whom she argues are moving the country toward socialism and greater government control.“There’s a very big difference right now — Republicans that are pushing for this great country, and another side of the aisle that is pushing for a completely different kind of America,” Moody said.The latest Decision Desk HQ polling average gives Moody a seven-point advantage over Vindman, 47% to 40%. That places the race within competitive territory, though it has not yet emerged as a top-tier national toss-up.Florida’s primary is Aug. 18.The ultimate winner in November will complete the final two years of former Sen. The new senator will then have to run again in 2028 to secure a full six-year term.

Roger Craig revealed during his induction speech into the Pro Football Hall of Fame that he has vascular dementia.The former San Francisco 49ers star running back spoke in a prerecorded video message while he sat on stage wearing his gold jacket at Tom Benson Stadium on Saturday. Presented by former teammate Jamie Williams, he received a standing ovation from the crowd and hugs from the many Hall of Famers on stage.Nearly eight minutes into a nine-minute speech, Craig announced his diagnosis, saying his doctors believe “it may be related, at least in part, to the concussions” he experienced during his playing career.“The changes were gradual,” Craig said. “At first, they were easy to dismiss as normal aging. Over time, my family noticed, too.”Symptoms of vascular dementia, according to the Mayo Clinic, include: confusion; trouble finding the right words; difficulty paying attention; trouble organizing thoughts or actions; difficulty planning and following through with plans; slowed thinking; uncertainty about what to do next; and memory issues.RELATED STORY | College sideline collisions contributed to one death and other serious injuries“Two things could be true,” Craig said. “Football gave me opportunities beyond anything I can imagine. It helped shape the man I became. At the same time, we know more today about brain health than when I played. I hope sharing my story encourages people to pay attention to their health and seek help when something doesn’t feel right.“I want people to know that this diagnosis doesn’t define me. I am still a father, still a husband, a teammate, a friend and someone who loves this game and the people who brought it to my life. If sharing my story helps even one family or one former player, then it’s worth it. Football gave me everything: opportunity, discipline, lifelong friends and the platform to grow as a man. This honor belongs to my parents who started it all.”Selected by the 49ers in the second round of the 1983 draft as a fullback out of Nebraska, Craig become one of the most versatile players in league history.He excelled as a runner, receiver and blocker, helping the 49ers win three of their five Super Bowls.In 1985, Craig became the first player in NFL history to have 1,000 yards rushing and 1,000 yards receiving in a season. He was the AP NFL Offensive Player of the Year in 1988.“When I learned that Bill Walsh wanted me, that meant something because he saw something in me that others didn’t,” Craig said. “He didn’t just want a running back, he wanted a complete football player. He trusted me to do whatever the team needed. That’s why a 1,000-yard rushing, 1,000-yard receiving season means so much to me. We weren’t chasing numbers. I didn’t realize I was making history. It just felt like we were doing something special as a team. Looking back, I can appreciate how difficult it is and how few players have done it since.RELATED STORY | How the NFL is working to prevent concussions and protect players“What means the most is knowing we helped expand what people thought a running back could be. None of that happens without great teammates. What made those 49ers teams special: We weren’t selfish. We didn’t care who got the credit. We cared about winning.”Craig was selected from the seniors category and entered the Pro Football Hall of Fame Class of 2026 with Drew Brees, Larry Fitzgerald, Luke Kuechly and Adam Vinatieri.

Miami Dolphins head coach Jeff Hafley is not easing into the preseason. With Friday's game against the Washington Commanders just days away, Hafley made clear that every player on the roster should be prepared to take the field."Everyone who is on our team right now should be ready to play. That's how I see it, truthfully," Hafley said.WATCH BELOW: Dolphins ready to play starters in preseason openerThe message landed well in the locker room. You're going against new competition, and these aren't your teammates; these are people you're about to play. You need to go out there and compete," Paul said.The stakes are real for much of the roster. The Dolphins carry an NFL-leading 40-plus players on one-year deals, giving nearly everyone on the team added motivation to perform on every snap.New wide receiver Tutu Atwell, a South Florida native, is among those eager to make his mark."I'm ready. There's nothing like playing football, and we've been getting some good work with the defense, a lot of big plays, a lot of good plays going on on both sides," Atwell said.Atwell, who is looking to become an integral piece of the offense, said returning to the field carries personal meaning."The season's back. I've been waiting the whole offseason to get back to it. It's a new team, and I'm home, and I'm just very excited to play with these guys," Atwell said.Running back De'Von Achane is also using the preseason as a foundation heading into the regular season."I always like to play and get in and get tackled; it's always nice to go in and go against someone other than our defense. For me, get a couple touches and get tackled, fall on the ground just to get it going before we get into Week One when it actually matters," Achane said.Friday's game carries an added personal dimension for Paul. His older brother, Chris Paul, is an offensive guard for the Commanders."It's definitely a blessing to have two brothers in the NFL. It's going to be great to see him working at his craft and his space and how he is in his environment where he works and how it looks," Paul said.The Dolphins and Commanders are also scheduled to hold joint practices this week before Friday's preseason opener, which kicks off at 7 p.m. on WPTV.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI.
