What started as a routine drive home from work turned into a terrifying race against time for Debbie Spoelstra. Spoelstra says she was turning onto Bridge Road from Dixie Highway in Hobe Sound Friday evening when a railroad crossing arm suddenly came down on her car, leaving her trapped on the tracks. Dash-cam video captured the tense moments that followed. A train's horn can be heard as it quickly moved closer and closer to Spoelstra's red car as it sat between the crossing gates. Then, a young man runs toward her. I was pretty much frozen, Spoelstra said. Then I thought about getting out of the car, and then at that moment I saw Josiah running across the railroad tracks. That man was 23-year-old Josiah Baur. Baur said he left work late that evening and was on his way home to Port Saint Lucie when he stopped at the crossing. He was on the other side of the tracks when he saw what was happening. You only get a couple seconds to react, Baur said. He immediately ran toward the crossing. I just took off running, he said. Baur reached the crossing and lifted the gate with both arms, giving Spoelstra enough time to back her car away from the tracks before the train came through. He said he first looked to see where the train was. It was on her side, so I ran up and pushed up on it and released it just in time for her to back up, Baur said. Another witness, Lizzy Dominguez, was behind Baur's car when she saw what was happening. She and the others in her car could only watch. We were just saying, Please, God, please, God, please, God,’ Dominguez said. We were frozen in the car. After the rescue, Dominguez took a photo of Baur and posted it on social media , hoping to find him and thank him for what he had done. It was very emotional, Dominguez said. We thought, oh, we just witnessed a miracle. Spoelstra and Baur met again at the railroad crossing Sunday. When they saw each other, they hugged. Spoelstra said she's grateful to Baur and believes things could have turned out very differently if he hadn't been there. You know, first of all, that a total stranger, would help another person, she said. I won't ever forget what he's done for me. He is a true American hero. Baur, however, doesn't describe himself that way. I’m just very fortunate that God put me right where I was, he said. "He's got a plan and we just got to follow it sometimes. We don't understand why." Witnesses say the crossing arm malfunctioned during the incident. See also: Foodborne illnesses are rising. What not to eat right now. Spoelstra says she reported the problem to Florida East Coast (FEC) Railway line and was told someone would come out to inspect the gate. The incident remains a powerful reminder of how quickly a dangerous situation at a railroad crossing can unfold and how one person's decision to act can make all the difference. For Spoelstra, there is also a personal connection that makes the story feel even more remarkable. She says her baby grandson shares the same name as the man who came to her rescue: Josiah.

The first day of the new school year at Okeechobee High School have been marked by significant traffic delays, prompting the sheriff's office to address both mechanical failures and driver behavior contributing to the congestion.According to the sheriff's office, two separate issues caused this morning's traffic problems. The primary culprit was a traffic signal that became locked in the red position due to a circuit board failure. Officials say the mechanical issue was identified and corrected, but not before contributing significantly to the initial backup of vehicles."That issue was obviously outside anyone's control," the sheriff's office stated in their traffic update.However, authorities also pointed to a controllable factor that made the situation worse: drivers cutting in line by moving from the outside lane to the inside lane as they approached the school. "We observed vehicles moving from the outside lane into the inside lane and cutting in front of other vehicles," officials noted. "This caused additional stopping, merging, and backups during what was already an unfamiliar and frustrating traffic situation."The sheriff's office emphasized their message with a pointed reminder: "PLEASE STAY IN YOUR RESPECTIVE LANE."The congestion comes as the school implements a new traffic pattern that parents, students, and bus drivers are still learning to navigate. For the first time, all of Okeechobee's high school students are learning from the same campus — the new building houses grades 9-12 together, with capacity for up to 1,700 students. Previously, freshmen attended a separate campus.For parent drop-off and pick-up, the established rules include parents entering through the north gate for both drop-off and pick-up, with afternoon pick-up stacking allowed beginning at 1:30 p.m. No stacking is allowed on U.S. 441.The sheriff's office plans to meet later today to review the morning's traffic flow and discuss ways to improve response and efficiency going forward. "We understand everyone has somewhere to be," officials acknowledged. "Parents are trying to get children to school, students are learning a new traffic pattern, buses are moving, and deputies and school personnel are working to keep everything flowing safely."This story has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Today is the day parents and students have been waiting all summer for -- it's back to school day! And this year, Martin County students will have fewer bus routes this school year. The school board voted to cut three routes -- a move expected to save the district $255,000 a year. The district is reducing its bus routes from 58 to 55. But some employees are raising concerns about what that could mean for already-crowded buses. Superintendent Michael Maine says they aren't eliminating any stops and every bus will continue to operate within its legal capacity. Maine says the district is "right-sizing" its transportation system, combining underused routes serving the same areas. He says it doesn't make sense to have 16 or 20 students on a 77-passenger bus. According to Maine, some routes may take a little longer, but drivers will be paid for any additional time they work. None of the buses are going to be over capacity. We have laws that we have to follow. All of our buses have seatbelts, so, depending on the age, students have to be buckled up. We're never going to run a transportation route or a bus that's over capacity, said Superintedent Maine. While bus stops aren't changing, some students may see a different bus number this year. Maine says families should expect the usual first-week delays as drivers settle into their new routes. Parents can check your child's bus assignment in the focus parent portal or track their bus in real time using the MyReaxium app .

After two years of construction and renovations, West Riviera Beach Elementary is ready to welcome students back this week. The 60-year-old school has been completely transformed with a brand-new cafeteria, media center and updated play areas."With all the new technology and improvements at the school, it's going to be amazing and make my job so much easier," said Crystal Watson, a second-grade teacher at the school.WATCH: But the biggest change isn't just the shiny new facilities—it's how the school will operate. Unlike traditional elementary schools that serve students from kindergarten through fifth grade, West Riviera will focus exclusively on younger learners: pre-K through second grade.Principal Alicia Taylor believes this specialized approach will give students a stronger foundation in reading and math during these crucial early years."It allows my leadership team to really focus on those foundational skills that we need to make sure are rock-solid," Taylor explained.To fill the renovated campus, the Palm Beach County School District has realigned enrollment, moving pre-K, first, and second-graders from Dr. Mary McLeod Bethune and Lincoln Elementary schools. The district expects about 600 students to attend West Riviera this year.For Dr. Camille Long, the school's reopening holds special meaning. Long was once a student at West Riviera Elementary herself, and now serves as the North Regional Superintendent for the School District."I think it's a game-changer to have a state-of-the-art campus, and it's really exciting for the community," Long said.The school will officially welcome students and families when classes begin on Aug.

Buses will be picking students sometimes in the dark as Indian River County public schools begin the 2026-2027 year. At multi-lane paved roads without a raised median or physical barrier, vehicles traveling in both directions must stop when a school bus is stopped to pick up or discharge children. At two-lane paved roads, vehicles traveling in both directions must stop when a school bus is stopped to pick up or discharge children. INDIAN RIVER COUNTY – Public school for all students in Indian River County begins on Monday, Aug. High schools open their doors to students at 7:20 a.m.; middle school K-8 schools at 8:10 a.m.; and elementary schools at 9 a.m. That means many students could be walking to bus stops sometimes in the dark on a on a daily basis as the days grow shorter. That is especially true for students who meet the bus at the stop near State Road 60 and Rollins Ranch Road, scheduled for 5:51 a.m., according to Dr. Kyra Schafte, executive director of the school district’s strategic communications and marketing. “Parents who drive their children to bus stops should park a safe distance away from buses during both morning pickup and afternoon drop off to help maintain clear visibility and safe loading areas,” she said in a statement. “We also encourage families to remind students to wait until the school bus has come to a complete stop and the stop arm is fully extended before approaching or crossing the street.” Transportation details are available on the Indian River County schools webpage at www.indianriverschools.org/o/sdirc/page/transportation , as well as the district s Facebook and Instagram accounts. The School District and Indian River County Sheriff’s Office urge all parents/students/motorists to be cautious and observe rules and laws pertaining to school bus safety throughout the 2026-27 school year. “There will be new challenges with drop offs, pickups, buses,” Sheriff Eric Flowers said in a video posted on the sheriff’s office’s Facebook page. “All the schools are changing and we want to make sure your kids are safe. We’ve got measures in place to make sure that it is a smooth beginning to the school year.” “Please be patient as during drop off periods as new students entering the schools are entering through metal detectors,” he said. “All of the safety measures we have in place will take some time for everyone to get used to.” School district officials offer these tips that parents are encouraged to review with their children regarding bus safety: * Have the child arrive at the bus stop at least 10 minutes early. * Supervise younger children while they wait for the bus. * Teach children to stay well off the roadway until the bus comes to a complete stop. * Remind children to wait for the driver’s signal before crossing the street. * Ensure backpacks, clothing, and drawstrings cannot get caught in bus handrails or doors. When walking to a bus stop, children should: * Make eye contact with the driver before crossing the street * Cross at least 10 feet in front of the bus. * Never cross behind a school bus. At bus stops, students should: * Stand at least 10 feet away from the roadway while waiting. * Never play or run near traffic. * Stay out of the bus’s ‘danger zone’—the area around the front sides, and rear where the driver may not see anyone. * If something is dropped near the bus, tell the driver instead of reaching under the bus. When on the bus, students should: * Stay seated in assigned seats and wear seat belts (when equipped) while the bus is moving. * Keep hands, arms, and head inside the bus. * Keep aisles clear of backpacks and personal items. * Speak quietly so the driver can focus on driving safely. * Do not eat, drink or throw objects on the bus. * Follow the driver’s instructions at all times. “Motorists also play an important role by slowing down, remaining alert in school zones and neighborhoods, and always stopping when required by (state) law for a school bus displaying its stop arm and flashing red lights,” Schafte said. Drivers also must stop on two-lane roads and on multi-lane roads without a raised median or physical barrier, according to the state Department of Transportation’s web site As of May 1, Florida began issuing citations for illegal passing of a stopped school bus with stop arm extended and red lights flashing, with a $225 fine for the offense. For a second or subsequent offense within five years, the Department of Highway Safety and Motor Vehicles may suspend a driver’s license for 90 days up to 6 months A driver does not have to stop when traveling in the opposite direction only if the roadway is divided by a raised median, a physical barrier or an unpaved median at least five feet wide, according to the DOT web site. In addition, the driver’s cell phone must be “hands-free” in a school zone. Using a wireless communications device in a handheld manner while driving in a designated school crossing, school zone, or active work zone area is against the law, according to the DOT web site. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office wants the public’s help locating a missing American Paint Horse believed to have been stolen from its owner’s pasture in Port St. "Every detail could help bring Strait from Above home safely," the agency posted Saturday on Facebook. The 2-year-old stallion was last seen at approximately 3 p.m. Sunday at 2801 Williams Road near St. Lucie West and west of Interstate 95 in a rural area. Distinctive features include a white forelock and mane with a black and white tail, pinto coat with distinctive black and white spots. "We are asking residents, property owners, horse enthusiasts, agricultural communities, and anyone who may have seen or been offered a horse matching this description to take a close look at the identifying information and report any potential sightings or information to the St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office at (772) 462-7300 or submit a tip by email at PatrolTips@stluciesheriff.com," the agency said. Lucie Wednesday released the emotional 911 call from a neighbor after a weekend murder-suicide at a home on Southeast Oxmoor Terrace. I think my neighbor was shot," the caller said during the 911 call. Authorities identified the victim as 50-year-old Elizabeth Ortega, a communications officer for the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office. Investigators believe Ortega was shot and killed by her longtime boyfriend, 50-year-old Ralph Varela Sr., who then shot and killed himself. According to police, Ortega had recently ended their 30-year relationship, but the two were still living together while Varela searched for a new place to live. The neighbor who called 911 said she had been in her backyard with her children when they heard the gunshots. "You heard the gunshot?" the dispatcher asked. There was, like, six of them. And I thought it was maybe on the other side of the street because we do have people that shoot off fireworks all the time. But this one made my house rattle," the caller said. When asked if she saw the gun, the caller responded, "No. We heard it a couple of minutes ago, and I made my kids come inside because it sounded really, really close." The caller said she did not know her neighbors' names but mentioned she often heard them yelling. "Her and her husband were fighting?" the dispatcher asked. "I don't know if they're fighting. They're just always cursing at each other," the caller said. Police arrived at the scene and began their investigation, which they are calling a murder-suicide. Big Brothers Big Sisters of Palm Beach and Martin Counties is preparing for the return of Big Taste of Martin County, a food and spirits event scheduled for Oct. 6 at Atlantic Aviation in Stuart.Organizers say the annual fundraiser brings together local restaurants, chefs and community partners to support mentoring programs for children across the Treasure Coast. Guests can sample food, wine and beer from area businesses while participating restaurants compete for Big Taste awards and local bragging rights.According to Big Brothers Big Sisters of Palm Beach and Martin Counties, the event helps fund mentorship opportunities for children who are currently waiting to be matched with a mentor, known as a “Big.”The nonprofit said community members can support the mission by purchasing tickets, attending the event or volunteering to become a mentor.Spritz Stuart plans to feature several menu items during the event promotion, including a Tuscan salmon dish, a smash burger and a specialty cocktail called the “Fig & Flame.”Big Brothers Big Sisters of Palm Beach and Martin Counties serves children and families throughout Palm Beach and Martin counties through one-on-one mentoring relationships designed to support academic achievement, confidence and personal growth.Community events like Big Taste of Martin County continue to grow in popularity across South Florida as nonprofits look for new ways to connect residents with local causes while supporting area businesses and restaurants.More information about the event and mentorship opportunities is available through Big Brothers Big Sisters of Palm Beach and Martin Counties.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. The energy was contagious at the annual Glades Teacher Appreciation Breakfast, where educators gathered to celebrate their dedication before welcoming students back to school Monday."This event is fantastic," said Jamie Wyatt, Deputy Superintendent for Palm Beach County Schools. "The Glades Teacher Appreciation Breakfast is one of the most exciting, fun events of the year."WATCH:The celebration highlighted the commitment of local educators, including one remarkable teacher who received a standing ovation for her extraordinary milestone— Rita Schoenfeld, celebrating 51 years in the profession, 50 of those at Glades Day School. For Schoenfeld, teaching has been more than a career—it's been a calling driven by desire to make a difference. You know, knowing that you want to do something for kids and work with the kids," Schoenfeld said.When the room erupted in applause for her milestone achievement, Schoenfeld was both grateful and humble. "It was very cool, but it was embarrassing also," Schoenfeld said and laughed. "You look around and you think, holy mackerel, there's a whole bunch of people that are doing the same thing that I've done, and hopefully they'll keep at it."Schoenfeld's five decades at Glades Day School have created something truly special, as she's now teaching children whose parents, and sometimes grandparents, were once her students. "In teaching as long as I have, I have students that I taught their parents and even sometimes it's sad to say I taught their grandparents," she said. "So it's family, is really what it comes down to."School Board member Marcia Andrews, who brings her own 51 years of education experience including 16 years on the school board, emphasized the importance of recognizing teachers before the school year begins."Teachers work every day, morning, noon, and night, 24/7, to make sure children are successful," Andrews said. "It's certainly not for money. It's about your heart, your desire to see every child succeed."For educators just starting their careers, Schoenfeld offers both practical and heartfelt guidance. That's really the first thing," she said. "And then know that you have a possibility of making a difference in a student's life. Treat them like your own kid. You know, when they need to be corrected, you correct them. When they need the love, you love them."The event showcased the unique spirit that defines education in the Glades area, where teachers and community members work together as partners in student success. "There's greatness out here, and the teachers and the community they rally because they are excited about what they're doing," Wyatt explained. "They believe in what they're doing. They believe in the students. The community wraps their arms around, and we partner together for education."Schoenfeld echoed this sentiment about the teacher appreciation event, noting how it brings together educators who might not otherwise see each other during the school year. "It's awesome because a lot of times we don't get to see each other in the different schools," Schoenfeld said. "As teachers, you don't get a lot of recognition. Sometimes you get all the blame, and now with the (Hand Foundation) giving the kudos to the teachers from the individual schools—it's awesome."District leadership expressed confidence in the year ahead for Palm Beach County's A-rated school district. "We want to let our families and our students know that we're ready for them on Monday," Wyatt said. "We're excited to see them. The teachers have been preparing all week, getting their classrooms set up, and just looking forward to another fantastic school year."This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

The Florida Department of Financial Services is holding a Treasure Hunt auction Saturday, Aug. 8, in West Palm Beach, featuring 512 lots with a combined opening bid of just under $1.3 million.WATCH WPTV'S COVERAGE BELOW:Items up for bid include collector coins, fine jewelry and golden chickens — all recovered from forgotten or neglected safe deposit boxes, organizers said.The auction is in-person only and begins at 9 a.m. Saturday, at the Embassy Suites at 1601 Belvedere Rd. in West Palm Beach.The items were turned over to the state by financial institutions after three years of non-payment of rent on the safe deposit boxes, organizers said. The state then waits at least two years to attempt to contact the owners before setting items up for auction.Any proceeds from sold items are still set aside for the rightful owners.For more information about the Florida Unclaimed Property Auction, click here.

The woman made it safely to the hospital for treatment.Local resident Macario Lopez told WPTV he felt compelled to walk around the area to see what was happening."You feel safe here in this area, but when you hear about things like this, you feel a little uncomfortable because you don't know what kind of people you have around you," Lopez said.Investigators believe this was a targeted attack and emphasize there's no ongoing threat to the public.Police are asking anyone who witnessed the shooting or has information about the incident to contact them immediately.This story is developing and will be updated as more information becomes available.

The aerial and location map for the 6.89-acre property home to the current Westside Racquet Club whose new owner had requested a conditional use permit and Phase 1 site plan approval for a significant remodeling and expansion project. The aerial and location map for the 6.89-acre property home to the current Westside Racquet Club whose new owner had requested a conditional use permit and Phase 1 site plan approval for a significant remodeling and expansion project. VERO BEACH – The Indian River County Commission approved the special exception use and Phase 1 site plan Aug. 4 for the renovation and expansion of the existing Westside Racquet Club, a 1970s-era facility that in recent years has fallen into disrepair. The Planning Zoning Commission previously heard the same requests on June 11, voting unanimously to recommend approval but adding a special condition of approval due to concerns about potential noise pollution and light infiltration onto adjacent property owners. Senior Planner Kelly McKinley introduced the agenda item during the latest meeting. “Before you today is the Westside Racquet Club’s special exception use and site plan approval request to expand the existing facility with the intent of restoring it, as well as providing additional enhancements,” she said. “The subject parcel is 6.89 acres located east of 43rd Avenue Southwest, north of 6th Lane Southwest and south of Fifth Place Southwest. The special exception use will cover all four phases, [but] only Phase 1 is before you for site plan approval at this time. The additional phases will subsequently be approved.” McKinley proceeded to provide further details on the color-coded phasing plan for the property, which currently houses a small, existing racquet court building and eight tennis courts. “The white [Phase 1] is going to restore the existing eight tennis courts, construct four new padel courts and construct associated site improvements like utilities, stormwater, parking and landscaping,” she continued. “The green will restore the existing 2,400-square-foot clubhouse and construct two additional padel courts. Phase 3, the pink, will include the pool house as a clubhouse amenity and construct four pickleball courts. Phase 4, the blue, will consist of two additional tennis courts.” McKinley also described the proposed stormwater improvements and landscaping plan, which will include a stormwater pond along the southern part of the project and a swale. Additional landscaping will include a 20-foot buffer along 43rd Avenue Southwest and a 30-foot-Type B landscape buffer around the other three perimeters. Foundation plantings will be installed around the pool and the existing clubhouse building. After she recommended approval and described the P Z Commission’s additional condition of approval, Vice-Chairwoman Laura Moss posed her first question and initial concerns to staff. “I’m just confirming what they’re adding,” she said. “So, it’s four padel courts, a pool and four pickleball courts. Is that reason why this is a special exception?” “The site is zoned RS-3,” McKinley replied. “Within that zoning district, the use itself is the special exception.” Chairman Deryl Loar chimed in with another important fact. “I think it’s also because you’re going over a threshold and you’re expanding the existing use by more than 10 percent,” he said. Vice-Chairwoman Moss then addressed the heart of her concern, the fact that all subsequent phases would be administratively approved and not require any further public hearings. “I think to vote on this, we’re in effect being asked operationally to vote in the blind because I don’t know what it’s going to be in totality,” she continued. “Once we grant the special exception, basically anything goes [and] we lose control of it. On top of that, if we change it, that land maintains the special exception designation no matter who owns it.” Vice-Chairwoman Moss acknowledged that she’d viewed the June Planning Zoning Commission hearing and lamented what she viewed as a lack of technical expertise for the concerned neighboring residents. She also bemoaned the fact the applicant’s representative was not present that day. “Pickleball is very loud, [and] somebody made a really good point,” she said of the earlier hearing. “The noise ordinance only applies when it’s a sustained level of sound. Pickleball’s not a sustained level of sound, so they really don’t have protection in terms of the noise. It was mentioned that the lighting would end up in peoples’ backyards. A privacy fence was suggested. I’m not comfortable that this was thoroughly addressed and will not adversely affect the public interest.” While Chairman Loar responded by insisting her comment about losing control was “not an exact description of our professional staff,” Deputy County Attorney Susan Prado provided a legal opinion of the exact task before commissioners that morning. She also attempted to alleviate some of the vice-chairwoman’s concerns about the lack of technical expertise during the P Z Commission hearing. “As was stated, none of the other phases will come back,” Prado said. “If you’re wanting to place conditions on the other phases, that will need to be placed today as well as for all phases. As far as evidence presented, affected persons can come forward and present their evidence as to issues. If there is that [pickleball noise] concern, there is case law that says both sides have to bring their own professionals and that will also include the people impacted.” For his part, District 3 Commissioner Joseph Earman pointed out the continuity of use on the parcel and local community support for the planned improvements. “Commissioners understand this has always been what it’s always been – it’s nothing different,” he said. “It just went silent because it had no ownership. I’ve heard from a few of the residents out there that think it’s great because it’ll add value to their property and everything as a whole because it is run down right now.” Vice-Chairwoman Moss’ final concern was related to potential traffic impacts, which were addressed by Planning Development Services Director John Stoll, who also touched on her noise and lighting concerns. “The traffic studies will be cumulative,” he explained. “As soon as they have a use that kicks them over the 400 average daily trips, we’ll require a traffic study. We have a number of noise-mitigation measures that we’ve found, including a new noise study specifically to pickleball. We can limit nighttime lighting and operational hours, require special paddles and balls and increase the separation from the neighbors if we need to.” There was only public speaker that evening, 4th Lane Southwest resident Mark Jaffe. “I travel on 5th Street Southwest every single day since 1996 and pass this neighborhood many times a day,” he said. “When I moved here, Westside Neighborhood was there. I drive past that dilapidated racquet club almost every single day. I would like to see this move forward.” The County Commission then voted unanimously to approve the requests. An act of bravery and compassion is bringing two strangers together on the Treasure Coast. A young man rescued a woman whose car got stuck on a railroad crossing in Hobe Sound, saving her from near disaster. Stay up-to-date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25 Just a few days ago, Josiah Baur and Debbie Spoelstra didn’t know each other, but now, they share a special connection. “Friday, I was leaving work, and I was heading back home. I was trying to get home for a tire appointment, funny enough, and running late for it. Train crossing went down, and I looked down on my phone, and I glimpsed up, and I saw the car stuck behind the railroad crossing,” Baur said. Spoelstra was still inside that car, stuck on the train tracks at Bridge Road and Dixie Highway in Hobe Sound. What I did is, I put my car in reverse, and apparently the gate got stuck on top of my car on the antenna. So, when I tried to reverse, it would not let me reverse. I sat there, I saw the train,” Spoelstra said. Baur, realizing she was still in the car, didn’t hesitate and jumped out of his car to help. “I threw it in park and just took off running. Try to see what side the train was on to see if it would clear her or not. But it was on her side and didn't really want to take a chance. So, I ran across and tried to push up on the thingy to release her,” Baur said. That split-second decision helped to avoid what could have been a devastating crash. “He came just like a hero. And lifted the gate up off of my car. And I was able to reverse and get off the tracks. And as soon as he did that, within seconds, the train passed by me. So it was very scary, you know, life-changing experience for me,” Spoelstra said. “We think of heroes, I think police officers and military, not what I did. It was just a good, good thing to do,” Baur said. The two said they’ve now bonded over this unique experience, attributing it to their shared faith. “He was put in one place, I was put in one place, and it was just fate. And it was a God thing, you know, and then once I told him my grandson was Josiah, and then he was just like, ‘Oh, wow. It's definitely a God thing.’ So, I don't know. I would just say, like I said, I'm so grateful for him,” Spoelstra said. He puts us exactly where we need to be. If you're running late for something, it's probably for a reason. Just trust his plan,” Baur said. Spoelstra said she wasn’t texting or distracted while driving and was simply just taken off guard by the railroad crossing arms lowering. She wants to pass this message on to other drivers: always be careful and look both ways before crossing train tracks. Get the latest news updates with the WPBF 25 News app.

Jacob Craig will perform MacDowell s Piano Concerto No. 2 with the Space Coast Symphony Orchestra during Landscapes Legends. For tickets,visit SpaceCoastSymphony.org or call toll-free (855) 252-7276. VERO BEACH – The Space Coast Symphony Orchestra explores magic and myth during Landscapes Legends on Sunday, Aug. The concert at the Community Church of Vero Beach, 1901 23rd Street, opens with Dukas’ The Sorcerer’s Apprentice, famously depicted in Disney’s Fantasia. Guest conducted by Brevard music educator Patrick Phillips, the vivid, 11-minute orchestral tone poem musically narrates a tale of magic gone wrong. The world premiere performance of Kenneth Fuchs’ Cloud Slant shifts the focus inward, capturing light, motion and atmosphere. A Fuchs album recorded with the London Symphony Orchestra for Naxos won the 2018 GRAMMY Award for Best Classical Compendium. Landscapes Legends continues when Vero Beach music and arts leader, Dr. Jacob Craig joins the orchestra for Edward MacDowell’s Piano Concerto No. 2, a deeply romantic and expressive work in three-movements. Composed in 1885, the work has the distinction of being the first major piano concerto written by an American. Renowned pianist, Van Cliburn chose MacDowell’s Piano Concerto No. 2 at age 18 for his professional orchestral debut. Landscapes Legends concludes with Pines of Rome, the world famous 1924 orchestral tone poem by Italian composer, Ottorino Respighi. Lasting about 22 minutes, it dramatically depicts four different locations around Rome framed by iconic pine trees. Ancient streets, distant echoes, and the sound of a nightingale are sculpted into one of the greatest works of the orchestral repertoire. $35 tickets for Landscapes Legends are available through the orchestra website at www.SpaceCoastSymphony.org or at Marine Bank Trust branches. Tickets at the door are $40. Concertgoers aged 18 and under or with a college ID are admitted free to every SCSO concert. For more information about Landscapes Legends, call 855-252-7276 or visit www.SpaceCoastSymphony.org . Collins, Conductor and Artistic Director for the Space Coast Symphony Orchestra, describes what makes the Landscapes Legends concert special. “A good orchestral concert can make the invisible feel real,” said Collins. “The works on this program aren’t just pretty melodies with dramatic flourishes – they create places, characters, atmospheres, and emotional landscapes for a truly one-of-a-kind musical experience.” Concertgoers aged 18 and under or with a college ID are admitted free to every SCSO concert. For more information about the Space Coast Symphony s 2026-27 season or the Symphony for Everyone discounted ticket program, visit SpaceCoastSymphony.org or call (855) 252-7276. The Florida Supreme Court is poised to decide whether Citizens Property Insurance's controversial arbitration system is constitutional, a ruling that could have major implications for homeowners across the state.WATCH BELOW: 'Big ramifications if the Supreme Court decides in favor of Citizens,' Aaron Bass tells Investigative Reporter Kate HusseyThe development comes after months of WPTV investigative reporting into the state-backed insurer’s mandatory arbitration process, which requires certain policyholders to resolve insurance disputes outside traditional court and before a single administrative law judge.Documents WPTV obtained show those judges are paid through contracts funded by Citizens.Attorneys challenging the system argue that arrangement creates an inherent conflict and strips homeowners of their constitutional right to a jury trial.“This is the textbook legal example of a thumb on the scale of the outcome here,” insurance attorney Aaron Bass told WPTV.WPTV has interviewed at least five attorneys who have raised concerns about the program.Emails WPTV obtained in a public records request show State Senator Erin Grall wrote to the state-run insurer, questioning its constitutionality, and Citizens' authority to enforce it, before the arbitration requirement took effect.A WPTV review of one year of Citizens final hearing decisions also found judges ruled in Citizens’ favor in 99% of the cases examined.“It’s unprecedented,” Bass said. “I’m not aware of anything anywhere else in the country where this occurs.”The constitutional fight escalated in May, when Miami-Dade Circuit Judge Milton Hirsch refused to force a Citizens policyholder into arbitration.“Citizens policyholders — and Floridians generally — are entitled to ask — indeed, cannot help but ask — why they must be stripped of their right to trial by jury — as a condition of insuring their homes,” Hirsch wrote.Citizens appealed.The Florida Supreme Court has now agreed to take up the case."Big ramifications if the Supreme Court decides in favor of Citizens," said Bass, who added the implications could extend well beyond Citizens policyholders.Last year, Florida lawmakers considered legislation that would have allowed other property insurers to require similar arbitration.If the Supreme Court ultimately sides with Citizens, Bass believes the decision could open the A school crossing guard in Martin County waits at an intersection for youngsters to ensure they cross streets safely. The 2026-2027 school session for students begins in Martin County on Monday, Aug. At two-lane paved roads, vehicles traveling in both directions must stop when a school bus is stopped to pick up or discharge children. At multi-lane paved roads without a raised median or physical barrier, vehicles traveling in both directions must stop when a school bus is stopped to pick up or discharge children. MARTIN COUNTY – Public school for all students in Martin County begins on Monday, Aug. The 12 elementary schools for 2026-27 will open at 7:40 a.m.; all four high schools, including Indiantown High School charter school, start at 8:30 a.m.; and five middle schools begin at 9:20 a.m. With the elementary schools, that means many students would be walking to bus stops sometimes in the dark on a daily basis as the days grow shorter. That is especially true for Jensen Beach Elementary students who meet the bus at the stop at Southeast Aster Lane and Southeast Astorwood Terrace at 6:10 a.m., according to Martin School District’s bus transportation schedules. As a result, the School District urges all parents/students/motorists to be extra cautious and to observe rules and laws pertaining to school bus safety throughout the 2026-27 school year. “As we prepare to welcome students back on Aug. 10, Martin County School District encourages families to take a few moments to review school bus safety with their children,” Kirstie Germaine, coordinator of public information community relations, said in a statement. “Students should arrive at their bus stop 5-10 minutes before their scheduled pickup time, remain off the roadway while waiting, and follow the bus driver’s instructions when boarding, exiting, or crossing the street,” she said. “We also encourage families to review their child’s bus stop location and schedule before the first day of school and ensure younger students have appropriate supervision at the bus stop. We are grateful for the partnership of families, our transportation staff, and local law enforcement agencies as we work together to keep students safe throughout the school year. The Martin County School District’s transportation page (www.martinschools.org/page/transportation) gives information including links to download bus routes, bus stop rules, and safety guidance. The page also has instructions on downloading MyReaXium app, which gives parents details on the location of the school bus which will pick up and drop off their children. School district officials offer these tips that parents are encouraged to review with their children regarding bus safety: • Supervise younger children while they wait for the bus. • Remind children to wait for the driver’s signal before crossing the street. • Ensure that backpacks, clothing, and drawstrings cannot get caught in bus handrails or doors. When walking to a bus stop, children should: • Make eye contact with the driver before crossing the street • Cross at least 10 feet in front of the bus. • Never cross behind a school bus. At bus stops, students should: • Stand at least 10 feet away from the roadway while waiting. • Never play or run near traffic. • Stay out of the bus’s ‘danger zone’—the area around the front sides, and rear where the driver may not see anyone. • If something is dropped near the bus, tell the driver instead of reaching under the bus. When on the bus, students should: • Stay seated in assigned seats and wear seat belts (when equipped) while the bus is moving. • Keep hands, arms, and head inside the bus. • Keep aisles clear of backpacks and personal items. • Speak quietly so the driver can focus on driving safely. • Do not eat, drink or throw objects on the bus. • Follow the driver’s instructions at all times. Drivers are required by Florida law to stop for a school bus displaying flashing red lights and an extended stop arm, according to the state Department of Transportation’s web site. Drivers also must stop on two-lane roads and on multi-lane roads without a raised median or physical barrier, according to the web site. As of May 1, Florida began issuing citations for illegal passing of a stopped school bus with stop arm extended and red lights flashing, with a $225 fine for the offense. For a second or subsequent offense within five years, the Department of Highway Safety and Motor Vehicles may suspend your driver’s license for 90 days up to 6 months A driver does not have to stop when traveling in the opposite direction only if the roadway is divided by a raised median, a physical barrier or an unpaved median at least five feet wide, according to the DOT web site. In addition, the driver’s cell phone must be “hands-free” in a school zone. Using a wireless communications device in a handheld manner while driving in a designated school crossing, school zone, or active work zone area is against the law, according to the DOT web site. A tree-trimming job turned into a rescue Saturday afternoon in Stuart after a man became trapped about 40 feet in the air on a broken lift. Martin County Fire Rescue says crews were dispatched around 1 p.m. When rescuers arrived, they found the man stuck on the lift after it stopped moving up and down. He had been trimming trees in the area when the equipment stopped working. Because access for a ladder was limited, firefighters used a specialized rescue approach. Crews first removed nearby tree limbs. They then used a series of high-angle rescue maneuvers to secure the man, transfer his weight and carefully bring him to safety. Martin County Fire Rescue credited the C-Shift crews from Heavy Rescue 23, Battalion 2, EMS 2 and EMS 22 for the rescue.

A petition with nearly 800 signatures is mounting against a proposal that could transform Fort Pierce's Museum Pointe — a public waterfront park along the Indian River Lagoon — into a mega-yacht marina.WATCH BELOW: 'We have been talking for years about better locations for that history center,' Erick Gill tells WPTV's Kate HusseyThe proposal is part of the Port of Fort Pierce's updated 2026 Master Plan. It calls for redeveloping Museum Pointe, which is currently home to a history center, public waterfront access, fishing piers, and green space, into a facility featuring floating docks, a multi-story marina, an event center, a waterfront restaurant, and a clubhouse.Opponents fear the plan could privatize one of the city's most treasured public spaces."Giving public land to private folks," said Terry Howard, a volunteer at the History Center at Museum Pointe Park. Howard contacted WPTV's Kate Hussey after learning about the master plan. "Development is just rampant in Florida, and at least we can fight for this one particular area and keep it green," Howard said.He said the loss of public waterfront access is a concern — but his biggest worry is the fate of the museum itself."This is the place where this museum should be, right here on this Museum Pointe," said Howard. For more than 50 years, the museum has preserved artifacts from Florida's Native American tribes, Spanish shipwrecks, and more. The master plan's renderings place the proposed marina clubhouse exactly where the museum stands today."Basically taking away a gem — a public gem that belongs to the people and replacing it with a facility for mega yachts," Howard said. "We're trying to keep this area as it is." St. Lucie County spokesperson Erick Gill said the museum's future is not in jeopardy if the project moves forward."Staff's intent was never to close the museum," Gill said. "We have been talking for years about better locations for that history center; it is on a barrier island, in a flood zone, so it may not be the best place to store artifacts."Gill said the museum and its collection would be preserved and relocated if the project proceeds. He added that the master plan is designed to expand economic development, create jobs, and generate county revenue."I think all local governments are looking for a way to generate revenue, so we can continue to lower the taxes for St. Lucie County residents and generate revenue from economic development, and we already have dock space there," Gill said."Anything that's going to be a positive economic driver for the City of Fort Pierce, I'm going to embrace completely," Fort Pierce City Commissioner Michael Broderick added. Broderick said the city will have the final say on whether the project moves forward, and that commissioners will have to weigh economic benefits against preserving waterfront access.When asked which priority — economic development or waterfront access — would take precedence, Broderick said the answer is not simple."That's the challenging question right there. I believe that we can strike a balance," Broderick said. "We always have to be careful not to eliminate public access to the waterway. Period." For Howard, the stakes go beyond the present."This is a gem that once we develop around it, it'll never be replaced again," Howard said. "The museum has been here since the 1970s. If they want to boat docks for mega yachts, they can do it someplace else." St. Lucie County leaders are scheduled to discuss the proposal and its current status at a 9 a.m. Lucie County Commission Chambers.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Lucie County Jail on $1.5 million bond each, according to the jail web site. 20, 2025, deputies, detectives, and crime scene investigators with the St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office responded to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital in Fort Pierce after a 3-month-old child was brought to the emergency room by the child’s grandfather, according to a St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office Facebook posting. A Martin County community is restoring a mangrove island next to their marina that erosion has slowly destroyed. Residents at Piper's Landing Yacht and Country Club spent two years cultivating 6,000 mangroves in an on-site nursery. Now, they are planting them in the waterway to bring the island back to life. WATCH BELOW: "The mangroves were so thick and lush and we've watched them deteriorate and in some areas the island is dead now," Lisa Standing, a resident at Piper's Landing Yacht and Country Club, said. Standing rallied her neighbors to take action. The community built 10 planter pools to grow red and white mangroves. "We were able to collect just white and red seeds from our mangrove island," Standing said. The effort required extensive research and permitting before a single plant could go into the water. They say it was an elaborate operation that turned into a labor of love "We tried to match the habitat of all of our plants to the river habitat," Standing said. Italy defeated Pakistan to claim the 2026 Amerigol LATAM Cup championship on Sunday, with goalkeeper Rocco Bruno earning MVP honors in a game that highlighted hockey's expanding global footprint.The tournament, held in Florida, featured two countries not traditionally associated with the sport. Pakistan scored first, but Italy responded with two unanswered goals — including a decisive shot that sealed the championship.Bruno was a standout throughout the tournament."It means the world to me to be able to come out here and represent these colors. It's a once-in-a-lifetime experience; I'm just so thankful to be able to be a part of this team here," Bruno said.When asked about the MVP award, Bruno kept his focus on the bigger prize."I wasn't expecting it whatsoever. I go out there and play a game, and sometimes I get rewarded for it, but I like the big trophy; that one is more important to me," Bruno said.Italian team captain John Schiavo described the energy inside the arena."It was amazing; the atmosphere all tournament was awesome. Obviously, with this being the biggest game, the crowd was rocking, and there's no better feeling than to play in front of an awesome crowd," Schiavo said.For Pakistan's players, the experience carried meaning far beyond the scoreboard. Tariq Khan reflected on what competing on this stage represents."It's a huge honor to be able to show kids around the world that we have an ice hockey team; it shows that anything is possible no matter where you're from," Tariq Khan said.Zaakir Khan echoed that sentiment."It's nothing I've ever experienced. LUCIE – The Daytona Tortugas held off the St. Lucie Mets for a 5-4 victory in the series finale between the teams on Sunday at Clover Park. Daytona won the series 4-3. The Tortugas scored five runs across the fourth and fifth innings to take a 5-0 lead. The Mets scored three in the sixth and another run in the eighth to close the gap to one. But Daytona pitchers Lisnerkin Lantigua and Jesus Colina retired the last six Mets in a row to finish the game. Mets starter Joel Lara cruised through the first three innings, allowing just one base runner on a walk. However, Lara struggled with his command in the third, walking the first three batters. Lara threw a wild pitch that brought home Ichiro Cano for the first run. Then with two outs Anielson Buten hit a two-run single to make it 3-0. Jean Brito replaced Lara with one on and out in the fifth inning. Cano hit the first pitch from Brito for a two-run homer that made it 5-0. Meanwhile Daytona starter Justin Henschel was cruising. Henschel shut out the Mets over 5.0 innings on 75 pitches. He scattered three hits, walked one and struck out four. Elian Peña started the Mets comeback bid in the sixth inning with a leadoff double against Lantigua. The double extended Peña’s hitting streak to 11 games. Later in the inning with two outs Kuhio Aloy ripped a two-run double to get the Mets on the board. Simon Juan followed with a RBI single to make it 5-3. The first two Mets reached base to start the eighth inning vs. Lantigua but the Mets only got a sac fly by Juan to make it 5-4. Colina retired the side in order in the ninth with a fly out and back-to-back strikeouts to notch his first save. The first seven batters in the Mets order recorded a hit. Reed Stallman went 2 for 4. Julio Zayas went 1 for 3 win a single, walk and run to add to his bid for FSL Player of the Week. Austin Brown (undrafted 2025 – Chipola JC) made his team debut by pitching two scoreless innings in the seventh and eighth. The Mets (16-25, 49-58) are off on Monday. Lucie police are investigating the death of 77-year-old Michael Joseph Kramer, who was found unresponsive in a pond near his home on Friday afternoon after being reported missing earlier that day. At approximately 1:18 p.m. today, officers responded to a residence on the 1400 block of SW Mockingbird Drive regarding a missing adult. Kramer was last seen by his wife inside their home at approximately 10 p.m. the following morning, Kramer was no longer inside the residence. Kramer’s personal belongings, including his shoes, wallet, and cellphone, were still inside the home. His wife searched for him and contacted local hospitals before reporting him missing to law enforcement at approximately 1:18 p.m. Officers began searching the neighborhood and, during the canvass, located an unresponsive person in a pond directly across the street from Kramer’s residence at approximately 2 p.m. The individual and clothing matched Kramer’s description. Lucie Police Department Dive Team recovered Kramer from the water near the shoreline of the pond, where he was confirmed deceased. The circumstances surrounding Kramer’s death remain under investigation. Police said there are no known indications of foul play at this preliminary stage of the investigation. Authorities encourage the public to promptly contact law enforcement when a person is believed to be missing, emphasizing that timely reporting allows officers to begin investigative and search efforts as quickly as possible.

Lucie Police Department on Sunday identified the victim and suspect involved in the domestic-related murder-suicide that occurred the night before at a residence. The victim has been identified as Elizabeth Ortega and the shooter as Ralph Varela Sr., both 50. "The investigation has revealed that Varela and Ortega had been involved in a long-term cohabitation domestic relationship and resided together with their adult son," the agency said in a news release. "Through the investigation, it was learned Varela and Ortega were in the process of separating." At approximately 7:40 p.m., officers responded to the 2000 block of Southeast Oxmoor Terrace, west of U.S. 1 and near HCA Florida St. Lucie Hospital, after receiving multiple 911 calls reporting possible gunshots and a domestic disturbance. Officers found a woman suffering from a gunshot wound. She was airlifted to a local hospital, where she was pronounced deceased, police said. Police also located a man who was deceased from an apparent self-inflicted gunshot wound. Investigators learned the unnamed adult son left the residence to pick up dinner from a local restaurant. Investigators have determined there was no known argument or disturbance inside the home before his departure. At some point after the son left, investigators believe Varela utilized an AR-style .223 caliber rifle and began shooting Ortega inside the residence. Ortega fled the home in an attempt to escape, while Varela continued firing. Investigators recovered home surveillance video that shows Ortega attempting to flee into the front yard while Varela continued to fire at her before she collapsed. After the shooting, Varela returned inside the residence. Responding officers located Ortega with multiple gunshot wounds. She was airlifted to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital, where she was later pronounced deceased. Varela was later observed inside the home, where he appeared to have died from an apparent self-inflicted gunshot wound. "It is shocking," a neighbor who didn't want to go on camera told WPBF's Rachel Williams. "You never know who has problems. I never heard arguing or any kind of domestic violence ever." The investigation remains active as detectives continue are processing evidence and they are awaiting the final results from the Medical Examiner's Office. On April 23, 2014, he was convicted of discharging a firearm in public, and was later sentenced to 192 days in jail with all time served credited, according to Palm Beach Clerk records. On June 12, 2017, he was convicted of possession of cocaine, reckless driving reduced from DUI, driving while license wasn't active and refusal to submit to chemical or physical test. He was sentenced to 20 days in jail, which was served. Lucie Police Department extends its deepest condolences to the family and loved ones affected by this tragic incident," the agency said. An investigation was launched after one campaign sign was found on the ground while another had been placed in the yard. Investigators reviewed surveillance footage that showed Giordano and the woman approaching campaign signs displayed in the yard. PSLPD said the video then showed the woman removing a campaign sign supporting Mayor Shannon Martin before another sign was placed in the yard. PSLPD said officers and detectives are working to determine the circumstances surrounding the placement, movement and authorization of the campaign signs. Giordano said he saw a man remove a sign from the ground and throw it. Giordano then grabbed his cellphone and began recording the encounter. The man appears to be Shannon Martin's husband, Aaron Martin, a lieutenant with the Port St. Video shows a profanity-laced confrontation between Giordano and Martin. The two can be heard shouting at each other and making accusations about campaign signs being placed in the community without property owners' permission. Investigators said the language barrier contributed to the confrontation over the campaign signs and whether the previously placed sign could be moved or removed. PSLPD said investigators are reviewing the video. At this time, police said there is no indication that any campaign signs involved in the incident were stolen or intentionally damaged. Lucie Police Department acknowledges that Aaron Martin is employed by the department. Martin is a department employee will not influence the investigative process. As with every investigation, the facts and evidence will determine the outcome, and this investigation will be conducted fairly, impartially, and in accordance with department policy," PSLPD said in a news release. Following the incident, Mayor Shannon Martin said in a statement: My campaign is aware of recent incidents involving the unauthorized removal of my campaign signs at different locations over several days. Signs were taken down without permission and replaced with Mr. In response, my husband simply restored the signs that had been removed. At no time were my opponent's signs stolen or damaged, one small sign was temporarily moved and put back in the ground. Lucie Police Department is investigating reports related to political campaign signs that occurred this week. We fully support a thorough, impartial review of the facts. I remain focused on the issues that matter to the city and will continue running a positive, transparent campaign. According to police, officers responded to the reported incidents, documented the scenes, collected available evidence and began interviewing those involved. The Humane Society of the Treasure Coast is asking for donations, foster homes, adopters, and help from rescue organizations after taking in more than 100 animals from what the Martin County sheriff described as the worst animal hoarding case in the county’s history. "We need adopters and fosters. Anyone that's willing to adopt and has been thinking about getting a pet, the time is now," said Sarah Fisher, spokesperson, Humane Society of the Treasure Coast. Employees and volunteers have been working around the clock to care for the animals while the Palm City shelter continues its regular operations. A total of 108 animals were brought to the humane society for medical treatment and care after 77-year-old Gail Giustino was arrested July 20. Since then, 10 cats and 17 dogs from the case have been adopted, while five microchipped cats have been reunited with their owners. "I think she thought she was doing a good thing. She thought she was rescuing cats from the outdoors and unfortunately, she was way in over her head, couldn't care for it and ended up in a terrible situation," Fisher said. The shelter’s workload has continued to grow. Following the initial case, the Martin County Sheriff’s Office reportedly received an influx of requests for animal welfare checks. Last week, the humane society took in 26 cats from another situation and five dogs from a separate case. We expect more animals in the coming weeks due to the calls that have come in requesting animal welfare checks and the initial information we are receiving from Animal Services, which is following up on these calls, Humane Society Director of Operations Lori Tucker said. Many calls have been cleared, but there are cases that are requiring further follow-up. The organization said monetary donations are its greatest immediate need because of the continuing costs of medical care, food and housing while the animals await placement. Donations may be made through the shelter’s emergency medical fund. The humane society is also urging residents to adopt or foster animals already in its care. Officials said the influx doubled the shelter’s animal population even as normal admissions and services continued. Adopting or fostering a dog, cat, rabbit or guinea pig would free space for rescued animals still receiving treatment and preparing for adoption. See also: Road rage ends in violent 4-vehicle crash on U.S. Lucie man arrested We are still in need of people to adopt working cats, that is, cats that are suitable for safe outdoor living, Tucker said. We also are in desperate need of adopters and rescue groups willing to help take some of our animals. The shelter is offering a Name Your Price adoption special until further notice. Short- and long-term foster opportunities are also available. Information about adoptable animals is available at hstc1.org/Adopt , and foster information is available at hstc1.org/foster . Prospective adopters may call 772-223-8822 . Foster inquiries may be sent to catfoster@hstc1.org or dogfoster@hstc1.org , or made by calling 772-600-3220 . The victim in a weekend murder-suicide in Port St. Lucie has been identified as a communications officer with the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office. Fifty-year-old Elizabeth Ortega had been employed at PBSO for the last 10 years. The shooting happened Saturday night both inside and outside a home in the 2000 block of Southeast Oxmoor Terrace. In a video statement released Monday, police said a man began shooting at the woman inside their home, chased her outside, and continued firing, hitting her multiple times. "One of the neighbors actually located that victim after they observed her lying in the front yard unresponsive," Officer Brittany McNally of the Port St. Lucie Police Department said. On Monday afternoon, PBSO posted about Ortega on social media, saying, in part, "She was a respected and cherished part of our PBSO family, known for her kindness, compassion, and a warm smile that could brighten any room." Police said the shooter was Ortega’s longtime boyfriend, 50-year-old Ralph Varela Sr. After killing Ortega, Varela went back inside the home and killed himself. McNally said Ortega and Varela had been together for about 30 years, but Ortega had recently ended the relationship. "Although the relationship had ended, it appears the two had agreed to live together until Ralph could find other living arrangements," McNally said. Investigators are working to determine what led to the violence. The couple’s son, Varela Jr., had left the home just minutes before the shooting and told police everything seemed fine. "There’s no evidence to suggest that there was a disagreement, a disturbance or an argument that occurred directly prior to the shooting," McNally said. Varela Jr., is a firefighter with Palm Beach County Fire Rescue. The Palm Beach County Sheriff’s Office has provided therapy dogs to help Ortega’s co-workers cope with the loss. Lucie Police Department is investigating the death of a 77-year-old man who was found in a pond, according to a press release from the PSLPD . PSLPD says that on Friday, around 1:18 p.m., officers were called to a residence on SW Mockingbird Drive in reference to a missing adult who was later identified as Michael Joseph Kramer, 77. The investigation revealed that Kramer was last seen by his wife inside of their residence at around 10:00 p.m. However, when Kramer’s wife woke up at approximately 7:00 a.m. on Friday, Kramer was nowhere to be found despite all of his personal belongings remaining in the residence. See also: Delray Beach body shop owner accused of insurance fraud stemming from 2024 claims After an extensive search of the area, PSLPD says that they located an unresponsive man that matched Kramer’s description in a pond directly across the street from the residence at around 2:00 p.m. The PSLPD Dive Team recovered Kramer from the water, and he was pronounced deceased. PSLPD says that currently, the circumstances surrounding his death remain unclear, but no indications of foul play seem apparent.

Homes wants to rezone in order to build a 135,000-square-foot indoor and outdoor recreation area known as the Riverland-West Sports Recreation complex. Because so many residents both emailed the city and spoke out in protest during the July 27 quasi-judicial rezoning hearing, the City Council voted unanimously that day to table the request until Aug. 24 to give the applicant time to hold a neighborhood meeting. LUCIE – City Council members found themselves defending their actions to frustrated Tradition-area residents July 27, prompting them to table a quasi-judicial rezoning request from the developer of the Riverland/Kennedy Development of Regional Impact. The delay will give the developer’s representatives time to meet with area homeowners and address their concerns. Planner Francis Forman introduced the controversial agenda item that evening to a packed Chambers. “The item before you is the Riverland-West Sports Recreation Master Planned Unit Development rezoning,” he said. “The applicant is Azlina Goldstein with Riverland/Kennedy II LLC. This site is located south of Southwest Discovery Way and east of Southwest Sundance Vista Boulevard. The request is to rezone approximately 33.23 acres from St. Lucie County Agricultural to Riverland-West Sports Recreation MPUD.” Forman proceeded to provide more details on the GL Homes request to develop the site in a manner that many Riverland homeowners claim is different than what was planned when they purchased their properties years ago. “This site is designated Neighborhood Village Commercial, which allows a mixture of residential and non-residential uses such as commercial and offices, personal and household services, institutional, public facilities, parks, playgrounds and similar services,” he explained. “Any Neighborhood Village Commercial area must contain at least two of those uses. Currently the Riverland-West Sports Recreation MPUD is proposing to provide about 135,000 square feet of indoor recreation with some commercial as well as some outdoor RV/boat storage areas.” Because the city had received numerous emails from nearby residents in opposition, Vice-Mayor Jolien Caraballo immediately asked City Attorney Richard Berrios to describe the formalities of the quasi-judicial process. “This is a rezoning, which is limited to what Mr. Forman presented,” Berrios said. “Not part of it are things like landscaping, indoor and outdoor features and specifics of what it will ultimately be. Those things are better suited for the site-plan process. As far as the process here, the legislators take off their legislative hats and put on their judge robes, and it’s limited to taking sworn testimony and the facts presented and applying them to a specific problem.” Councilman Anthony Bonna, however, believed more information was needed for the area residents. “Can you go into more detail about what evidence is allowed to be weighed [and] is a rezoning discretionary?” he asked. While Berrios admitted the Council’s hands were tied as far as any pre-existing DRI entitlements, he deferred Councilman Bonna’s question to Planning Zoning Director Mary Savage-Dunham. The latter emphasized the legal framework of controlling agreements and city codes. A pre-existing Development of Regional Impact (DRI) is a large-scale project approved under older Florida growth laws that retains vested development rights despite later changes to local plans or the elimination of the state’s formal DRI program. “The DRI document talks about what’s going to be built there,” Savage-Dunam said. “We also have the comprehensive plan. As staff testified, this rezoning was found to be consistent with the comprehensive plan, [which] follows the DRI. Those are the road maps that guide development in that section of the city. So, you would be looking at the totality of what the applicant submitted showing their intended uses there and how that aligns with the comp plan and the DRI.” Vice-Mayor Caraballo then chimed back in with her own perspective. “If you’re confused, I understand,” she said. “It’s not our process – it’s the way it’s legally required by the state. It’s definitely not the simplest thing for anybody to understand.” After the applicant’s contracted Land Use Attorney Goldstein provided her own presentation, 10 nearby homeowners aired their complaints, beginning with Southwest River Rock Road resident Jim Riordan. “My property is located at the southern end of the proposed Riverland-West Sports Recreation Center,” he said. “I spoke at the July 7 Planning Board meeting, and the chairman encouraged me to meet with Ms. At that time, I gave her our primary concerns with the project. On Friday, she did contact me, but none of those concerns were addressed. What she did say was exactly what she said right now: This is not the time – the time is later – but we feel this is the time before we move forward.” Riordan pointed out that GL Homes had “1,300 other acres where they could build this complex.” “GL has already sold parcels in the new section advertising the fitness center,” he continued. “So, I guess it’s a done deal based on this picture and what they’re advertising. We purchased our property, as well as every citizen here, from The Grove with the understanding that this parcel will be a city park. Now they’re basically trying to make this something different.” Both Harriet Gallas and her husband Lawrence agreed. “We chose to move here for quality of life,” the former said. “When we bought our house, we were told there was going to be a park over the berm next to us. They’re [now] talking 72 pickleball courts, bocci courts, tennis courts, a dog park and RV park, and that’s going to destroy my quality of life. Noise pollution’s a real thing: It causes stress, and pickleball is loud, stabbing and sharp. I respectfully beg you to not pass this rezoning.” The other residents echoed similar fears, resulting in more staff explanations and Council debate until Mayor Shannon Martin asked Goldstein a pivotal question. “Has their been a public meeting with the neighbors with regard to this issue?” she asked. Riordan regarding the issue of the buffer,” Goldstein responded. That response gave Mayor Martin the impetus she needed. “Being that there are so many concerns from the residents, is GL willing to have a meeting with the residents in order to address the issues?” she prodded. Goldstein, however, resisted the delay at first. “This is a straight-forward rezoning,” she insisted. “We don’t have all those details yet for the site plan because that’s not this process. When we’re ready to get there and we have those details, we’d be more than happy to meet with everybody to discuss what’s planned.” That response brought a loud uproar of protest from the audience and a plea from the vice-mayor. “I would really appreciate very much if you’d be willing to just table this,” Caraballo said. “I’m sorry to slow it down, but even this part of the process I don’t think they comprehend.” The City Council then voted unanimously to table the request until the Aug. This week I'm at Vero Beach High School where students are getting ready to go back to school, and I decided to do something I've never done before – I joined the marching band! I crashed band camp at Vero Beach High School just a few days before school started, and let me tell you, it was an incredible experience.WATCH: The first time I stepped onto that practice field, I could feel the history before I even picked up my instrument. This wasn't just another high school band – this was a tradition stretching back to 1934, when the Fighting Indians Band was founded as part of the Federal Music Project during the Great Depression. Every student who had ever worn that uniform had helped build an incredible legacy.I got to meet some amazing students who are keeping that tradition alive, like Annabel Robbins who plays flute piccolo and is a drum major. Brady, an incoming senior, is the woodwind captain and section leader."It's kind of scary, you know," Brady said. "You're in charge of a lot of kids, so you got to make sure they're all doing good.The band director, Sean Srigley, has a special connection to this program that goes way back. "I'm actually alumni of Vero Beach High School. I was in the band myself," Srigley explained. "The cool thing about Vero is we've got awesome academics, awesome athletics. Our band is right there with them. We've marched in pretty much every big parade you could have in America."And he's not exaggerating! This band has an absolutely incredible resume. They performed in the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade in 1988, marching through the streets of New York City and playing "Alexander's Ragtime Band" for millions of television viewers. That single performance became one of the defining moments in the program's history and remains a source of pride for every new generation of members.But that's not all – they've also performed in the Tournament of Roses Parade, the Fiesta Bowl Parade, the Orange Bowl and even Carnegie Hall! The program has earned decades of Superior ratings and national recognition while representing our Treasure Coast with pride.After learning about all this amazing history, it was time for me to get to work. But honestly, that wasn't really my thing, so I tried the drums next.But joining the marching band for practice meant more than just learning music and drill. It meant discipline and the ability to stand for a long time in that Florida heat – something these kids do with incredible dedication.As I marched onto the football field, I couldn't help but imagine all the students who had stood in that same place before me. Some had gone on to march through Manhattan in the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade. Others had performed in famous bowl games or international parades.As I left Vero Beach High School that day, I was thankful for the opportunity to be part of something so special, even for just one practice. These students aren't just making music – they're carrying on a legacy that's been building for nearly 90 years.

MARTIN COUNTY – Public school for all students in Martin County begins on Monday, Aug. The 12 elementary schools for 2026-27 will open at 7:40 a.m.; all four high schools, including Indiantown High School charter school, start at 8:30 a.m.; and five middle schools begin at 9:20 a.m. With the elementary schools, that means many students would be walking to bus stops sometimes in the dark on a daily basis as the days grow shorter. The Martin County School District’s transportation page (www.martinschools.org/page/transportation) gives information including links to download bus routes, bus stop rules, and safety guidance. The page also has instructions on downloading MyReaXium app, which gives parents details on the location of the school bus which will pick up and drop off their children. School district officials offer these tips that parents are encouraged to review with their children regarding bus safety: • Supervise younger children while they wait for the bus. • Remind children to wait for the driver’s signal before crossing the street. • Ensure that backpacks, clothing, and drawstrings cannot get caught in bus handrails or doors. When walking to a bus stop, children should: • Make eye contact with the driver before crossing the street • Cross at least 10 feet in front of the bus. • Never cross behind a school bus. At bus stops, students should: • Stand at least 10 feet away from the roadway while waiting. • Never play or run near traffic. • Stay out of the bus’s ‘danger zone’—the area around the front sides, and rear where the driver may not see anyone. • If something is dropped near the bus, tell the driver instead of reaching under the bus. When on the bus, students should: • Stay seated in assigned seats and wear seat belts (when equipped) while the bus is moving. • Keep hands, arms, and head inside the bus. • Keep aisles clear of backpacks and personal items. • Speak quietly so the driver can focus on driving safely. • Do not eat, drink or throw objects on the bus. • Follow the driver’s instructions at all times. Drivers are required by Florida law to stop for a school bus displaying flashing red lights and an extended stop arm, according to the state Department of Transportation’s web site. Drivers also must stop on two-lane roads and on multi-lane roads without a raised median or physical barrier, according to the web site. As of May 1, Florida began issuing citations for illegal passing of a stopped school bus with stop arm extended and red lights flashing, with a $225 fine for the offense. For a second or subsequent offense within five years, the Department of Highway Safety and Motor Vehicles may suspend your driver’s license for 90 days up to 6 months A driver does not have to stop when traveling in the opposite direction only if the roadway is divided by a raised median, a physical barrier or an unpaved median at least five feet wide, according to the DOT web site. In addition, the driver’s cell phone must be “hands-free” in a school zone. Using a wireless communications device in a handheld manner while driving in a designated school crossing, school zone, or active work zone area is against the law, according to the DOT web site.
