European soccer's governing body UEFA said Thursday it is maintaining its demand for FIFA President Gianni Infantino to resign and is not ruling out a boycott of FIFA events, including the next men's and women's World Cups.The threat comes after Infantino faced criticism over his failed plan to bring in private investors to buy into some of FIFA's competitions. FIFA admitted to mistakes in the plan, but the UEFA said its demands have not been met, leaving FIFA's leadership and the stability of international soccer in question.RELATED STORY | Senior FIFA official resigns over Infantino's World Cup sell-off plan"UEFA's associations were very clear about the conditions attached to the non participation in FIFA competitions," it said in a statement obtained by the Associated Press. "First, the proposals to sell off the major competitions had to be withdrawn and secondly, assurances have to be made that such attempts to disfigure the game in this way will never be made again.""These conditions have not been met. In addition, UEFA made it abundantly clear in it's statement on Saturday that it has lost confidence in Gianni Infantino's presidency. That position holds."IN CASE YOU MISSED IT | The 2026 World Cup is officially the most attended ever, according to FIFAIn response to the recent international backlash, FIFA called an emergency meeting this week in attempt to present a united front as concerns grow over finances and tensions with international associations. Following the meeting, FIFA announced that Infantino had the full support of those in attendance.Nonetheless, the feud could have major implications for the future of international soccer and billions of dollars in revenue tied to the world's most popular sport.

A road rage confrontation erupted into a violent four-vehicle crash on U.S. 1 Wednesday, leaving four injured and a Port St. Officers with the Port St. Lucie Police Department say they responded around 6:45 p.m. to the intersection of South U.S. Highway 1 and SE Lyngate Drive/SE Tiffany Avenue, where investigators determined that a red Harley-Davidson motorcycle and a black Ford Super Duty pickup truck were involved in an ongoing road-rage incident. "These two vehicles were involved in an active road rage incident just prior to the crash, and this is based off the dash camera and witness statements that we've collected," said Officer Brittany McNally with the Port St. Detectives say the pickup, driven by 54-year-old Kevin Lonergan, was pursuing the motorcycle as both vehicles traveled northbound on U.S. 1 and approached the intersection. According to witness statements and dash-camera video, the motorcycle entered the intersection against a red light and collided with a black Chevrolet Silverado, throwing the 31-year-old rider from the bike. See also: Miami man faces prison after pleading guilty to online threats against Rubio, Noem Police say Lonergan then entered the intersection against the red signal, struck the ejected motorcyclist, and crashed head-on into a blue Toyota RAV4. The motorcyclist and two people inside the RAV4 were taken to Lawnwood Medical Center , per PSLPD. The Silverado driver was transported to St. Investigators say the motorcyclist suffered serious injuries, including a brain bleed and facial fractures, and lost consciousness after the crash. He remains hospitalized in stable condition.\ Based on witness statements, dash-camera video and the investigation, police arrested Lonergan for two counts of reckless driving causing serious bodily injury and one count of reckless driving causing injury. The investigative findings indicate that the pickup truck was actively pursuing that motorcyclist just moments prior to that crash, said McNally. After being medically cleared, Lonergan was booked into the St. The intersection remained closed for hours while investigators processed the scene before all lanes reopened around 2 a.m. This case does, though, serve as hopefully a powerful reminder that allowing your anger to dictate your actions behind the wheel can put multiple innocent lives at risk, McNally said.

Distributing donated backpacks to Pinewood Elementary School in Stuart are, from left, Costco Membership Manager Ray Perry, Pinewood Elementary Principal Amy Porter, Education Foundation of Martin County Executive Director Lisa Rhodes, Pinewood Elementary Assistant Principal Dana Carroll, and Costco Administrative Manager Mike Fabis. Education Foundation of Martin County Executive Director Lisa Rhodes joins Murray Middle School Principal Tiffany Roth and Assistant Principal Robert Beasley unloading backpacks donated by Costco. STUART — Thanks to the partnership-building efforts of the Education Foundation of Martin County and the generosity of Costco, approximately 750 students will head into the 2026-27 school year with a new backpack in hand. On Thursday morning, Stuart Costco Administrative Manager Mike Fabis and Membership Manager Ray Perry arrived at Pinewood Elementary School with pickup trucks loaded with hundreds of backpacks. The donation marked the second consecutive year Costco has provided backpacks for local students, but this year’s contribution was significantly larger. “We received backpacks last year, but this year we had almost 400 coming in, which is incredible,” said Pinewood Elementary Principal Amy Porter. “Our kids were so excited when they got them last year, so I can’t wait to see their faces this year.” The deliveries continued across Stuart, where Fabis and Perry unloaded another truckload of backpacks at Murray Middle School, ensuring hundreds more students will be prepared for the first day of classes. “Anytime we have an opportunity to help our families, making sure that they have access to new resources for back to school to relieve that financial burden is always so appreciated,” said Murray Middle School Principal Tiffany Roth. In addition to the backpacks, Costco donated a $500 gift card to each school to help meet additional student needs. School leaders say the donation is an example of the Education Foundation of Martin County’s unique role in connecting community partners with schools to provide meaningful support for students and families. “The Education Foundation of Martin County is really the powerhouse of our school district and our schools,” Roth said. “They really act as a liaison, helping to connect us with all of our community partners.” Porter echoed that sentiment. “We want to thank Costco and the Education Foundation, who does so much for our students,” she said. The Foundation coordinated the partnership between Costco and both schools, helping transform a corporate donation into direct assistance for local families. By fostering relationships with businesses and community organizations, the Education Foundation continues to expand opportunities that benefit students throughout Martin County. When students arrive at Pinewood Elementary and Murray Middle School next month, they will be able to choose from patterned, solid-color, or clear backpacks. For many families facing the rising costs of back-to-school shopping, the new backpacks represent more than just school supplies—they provide financial relief and help ensure every child begins the school year with confidence. For the Education Foundation of Martin County, the backpack giveaway reflects its broader mission: bringing together community partners and schools to remove barriers to learning and create opportunities for every student to succeed. Trump asked him to serve in the ambassadorial role. He said he will take the oath of office later this month, and his resignation from the Florida House takes effect Friday, Aug. 21.Under House Rule 2.5(d), Speaker pro tempore Wyman Duggan will assume the duties, powers, and prerogatives of the Speaker, Perez stated in his resignation letter. "We have been on a sometimes thrilling and sometimes tumultuous journey together. The energy was contagious at the annual Glades Teacher Appreciation Breakfast, where educators gathered to celebrate their dedication before welcoming students back to school Monday."This event is fantastic," said Jamie Wyatt, Deputy Superintendent for Palm Beach County Schools. "The Glades Teacher Appreciation Breakfast is one of the most exciting, fun events of the year."The celebration highlighted the commitment of local educators, including one remarkable teacher who received a standing ovation for her extraordinary milestone— Rita Schoenfeld, celebrating 51 years in the profession, 50 of those at Glades Day School. For Schoenfeld, teaching has been more than a career—it's been a calling driven by desire to make a difference. You know, knowing that you want to do something for kids and work with the kids," Schoenfeld said.When the room erupted in applause for her milestone achievement, Schoenfeld was both grateful and humble. "It was very cool, but it was embarrassing also," Schoenfeld said and laughed. "You look around and you think, holy mackerel, there's a whole bunch of people that are doing the same thing that I've done, and hopefully they'll keep at it."Schoenfeld's five decades at Glades Day School have created something truly special, as she's now teaching children whose parents, and sometimes grandparents, were once her students. "In teaching as long as I have, I have students that I taught their parents and even sometimes it's sad to say I taught their grandparents," she said. "So it's family, is really what it comes down to."School Board member Marcia Andrews, who brings her own 51 years of education experience including 16 years on the school board, emphasized the importance of recognizing teachers before the school year begins."Teachers work every day, morning, noon, and night, 24/7, to make sure children are successful," Andrews said. "It's certainly not for money. It's about your heart, your desire to see every child succeed."For educators just starting their careers, Schoenfeld offers both practical and heartfelt guidance. That's really the first thing," she said. "And then know that you have a possibility of making a difference in a student's life. Treat them like your own kid. You know, when they need to be corrected, you correct them. When they need the love, you love them."The event showcased the unique spirit that defines education in the Glades area, where teachers and community members work together as partners in student success. "There's greatness out here, and the teachers and the community they rally because they are excited about what they're doing," Wyatt explained. "They believe in what they're doing. They believe in the students. The community wraps their arms around, and we partner together for education."Schoenfeld echoed this sentiment about the teacher appreciation event, noting how it brings together educators who might not otherwise see each other during the school year. "It's awesome because a lot of times we don't get to see each other in the different schools," Schoenfeld said. "As teachers, you don't get a lot of recognition. Sometimes you get all the blame, and now with the (Hand Foundation) giving the kudos to the teachers from the individual schools—it's awesome."District leadership expressed confidence in the year ahead for Palm Beach County's A-rated school district. "We want to let our families and our students know that we're ready for them on Monday," Wyatt said. "We're excited to see them. The teachers have been preparing all week, getting their classrooms set up, and just looking forward to another fantastic school year."This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Boynton Beach city staff said the New Public Safety Training Center was requested by police to meet growing training demands in the area.The proposed complex is set to include a 12-lane, 50-yard shooting range, dedicated equipment storage, a defense tactics room, a virtual reality training room and more. The plans also called for a staged apartment to simulate real-world law enforcement scenarios.'Leave Us Alone': Residents Voice ConcernsFor residents whose homes are directly across from the proposed site, the news of the development was alarming.“My stomach turned inside out,” said Stacey Deloye, a resident who told WPTV she had just completed a major home renovation to take advantage of the view. “I just sit at my computer and have my coffee and watch the birds and its beautiful view.”Others echoed her concerns, focusing on environmental and financial impacts.“I completely support our police department but I want them to build their gun range somewhere else and not to tear down one of the few remaining blocks of woods that we have left in east Boynton,” said Tony Cenk, who has lived in the Golfview neighborhood for over 20 years. The Martin County Sheriff’s Office is reporting a rise in DUI arrests, including an increase in incidents occurring during the day. Body camera footage from Wednesday shows deputies responding to a single-vehicle crash on I-95 near Martin Highway. Deputies said an intoxicated driver collided with a guardrail, abandoned the wrecked car in the center lane of the interstate, and fled the scene. The driver was taken into custody and faces several charges, including DUI, possession of heroin, and driving without a license. Sheriff John Budensiek said the county recorded five DUI arrests as of Thursday morning. Among the incidents was a wrong-way driver on Kanner Highway, a driver on A1A who hit a railroad crossing at high speed and rolled her car, and another driver with no license or insurance. "And then while we are getting ready to talk to you today yet again, we had another DUI in Hobe Sound: a driver slumped over the wheel, so our DUI units went down there, and he's sitting in our jail right now," Budensiek said. According to the sheriff’s office, DUI charges have increased every year since 2022, and this year is currently on pace to continue the trend. The sheriff’s office reported the following DUI arrest numbers: 2022 -- 506 DUI charges 2023 -- 532 DUI charges 2024 -- 537 DUI charges 2025 -- 540 DUI charges 2026 -- 349 (year-to-date) "All the information we're putting out there, you would think that DUI is becoming a thing of the past, but they're not — we're seeing more and more of them, and lately we're seeing more daytime DUIs, which is extremely concerning," Budensiek said. He said the aggressive driving unit will continue monitoring roadways day and night to combat impaired and dangerous drivers. "So, I would suggest, as sheriff, if you intend to drink at all, catch you a rideshare to wherever you are going to go drinking and catch it back home," Budensiek said. He also credited members of the public who call and report suspicious activity. Lucie Police Department has released an update on 2 separate investigations involving political campaign signs, both occurring this week in the area of SW Airoso Boulevard.Although both incidents involve political campaign signs in the same area, police say they are being investigated as separate cases, with each evaluated independently based on their own facts, evidence, and applicable law.The first incident occurred on August 5, 2026, near the intersection of SW Airoso Boulevard and SW Thanksgiving Avenue.A Port St. Lucie Police sergeant observed Steven Giordano and an unidentified adult female near political campaign signs at a residence and initiated an investigation after one campaign sign was found on the ground while another had been placed in the yard.Detectives reviewed surveillance video from the area, which appears to show Giordano and the unidentified adult female arrive at the residence, approach campaign signs displayed in the yard, and interact with the signage. The video further appears to show the unidentified female remove a campaign sign supporting Mayor Shannon Martin before a different campaign sign was placed in the yard.Detectives collected the video evidence and are evaluating it alongside statements, physical evidence, and all other information gathered during the investigation.Officers and detectives are working to determine the circumstances surrounding the placement, movement, and authorization of the campaign signs, including whether the movement or replacement of the signs was authorized by the property owner at the time the incident occurred.The second incident occurred on August 7, 2026, near SW Airoso Boulevard and SW Thornhill Drive, where officers responded to a disturbance involving political campaign signs.During the investigation, officers learned that Aaron Martin and Steven Giordano were involved in a verbal confrontation regarding the placement and movement of campaign signs at a nearby residence.Officers reviewed video recordings provided by the involved parties, which depict Martin and Giordano engaged in a verbal confrontation regarding the placement and movement of political campaign signs at the residence.Investigators interviewed the homeowners and learned that both residents believed they had separately granted permission for campaign signs to be placed on the property. Officers determined that one homeowner communicated permission for one campaign's sign, while another resident of the home, who has limited English proficiency, separately conveyed permission to individuals associated with the opposing campaign.Investigators believe the language barrier contributed to a misunderstanding regarding which campaign signs were authorized to be displayed and whether previously placed signs could be moved or replaced.The preliminary investigation indicates that both individuals believed they had permission from residents of the property to place campaign signs. At this time, there is no indication that any campaign signs associated with this incident were stolen or intentionally damaged.Information related to the placement of the campaign signs has been forwarded to the City of Port St. Lucie Code Compliance for review.Many residents were taken back after learning of the incidents.“I think it’s childish and if they’re going to be childish with their personalities and who they are then they probably shouldn't be in that position,” said resident Trumaine Pearson.The Port St. Lucie Police Department acknowledged that Aaron Martin is employed by the department."The fact that Mr. Martin is a department employee will not influence the investigative process," the department said. "As with every investigation, the facts and evidence will determine the outcome, and this investigation will be conducted fairly, impartially, and in accordance with department policy."The department said that should the investigation identify any potential policy violations involving a department employee, the matter will be handled in accordance with established department procedures. Consistent with Florida law, department employees are afforded the rights and protections provided under the Florida Law Enforcement Officers' Bill of Rights. Any related administrative review will proceed following the completion of the ongoing criminal investigation.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. A school crossing guard in Martin County waits at an intersection for youngsters to ensure they cross streets safely. The 2026-2027 school session for students begins in Martin County on Monday, Aug. At two-lane paved roads, vehicles traveling in both directions must stop when a school bus is stopped to pick up or discharge children. At multi-lane paved roads without a raised median or physical barrier, vehicles traveling in both directions must stop when a school bus is stopped to pick up or discharge children. MARTIN COUNTY – Public school for all students in Martin County begins on Monday, Aug. The 12 elementary schools for 2026-27 will open at 7:40 a.m.; all four high schools, including Indiantown High School charter school, start at 8:30 a.m.; and five middle schools begin at 9:20 a.m. With the elementary schools, that means many students would be walking to bus stops sometimes in the dark on a daily basis as the days grow shorter. That is especially true for Jensen Beach Elementary students who meet the bus at the stop at Southeast Aster Lane and Southeast Astorwood Terrace at 6:10 a.m., according to Martin School District’s bus transportation schedules. As a result, the School District urges all parents/students/motorists to be extra cautious and to observe rules and laws pertaining to school bus safety throughout the 2026-27 school year. “As we prepare to welcome students back on Aug. 10, Martin County School District encourages families to take a few moments to review school bus safety with their children,” Kirstie Germaine, coordinator of public information community relations, said in a statement. “Students should arrive at their bus stop 5-10 minutes before their scheduled pickup time, remain off the roadway while waiting, and follow the bus driver’s instructions when boarding, exiting, or crossing the street,” she said. “We also encourage families to review their child’s bus stop location and schedule before the first day of school and ensure younger students have appropriate supervision at the bus stop. We are grateful for the partnership of families, our transportation staff, and local law enforcement agencies as we work together to keep students safe throughout the school year. The Martin County School District’s transportation page (www.martinschools.org/page/transportation) gives information including links to download bus routes, bus stop rules, and safety guidance. The page also has instructions on downloading MyReaXium app, which gives parents details on the location of the school bus which will pick up and drop off their children. School district officials offer these tips that parents are encouraged to review with their children regarding bus safety: • Supervise younger children while they wait for the bus. • Remind children to wait for the driver’s signal before crossing the street. • Ensure that backpacks, clothing, and drawstrings cannot get caught in bus handrails or doors. When walking to a bus stop, children should: • Make eye contact with the driver before crossing the street • Cross at least 10 feet in front of the bus. • Never cross behind a school bus. At bus stops, students should: • Stand at least 10 feet away from the roadway while waiting. • Never play or run near traffic. • Stay out of the bus’s ‘danger zone’—the area around the front sides, and rear where the driver may not see anyone. • If something is dropped near the bus, tell the driver instead of reaching under the bus. When on the bus, students should: • Stay seated in assigned seats and wear seat belts (when equipped) while the bus is moving. • Keep hands, arms, and head inside the bus. • Keep aisles clear of backpacks and personal items. • Speak quietly so the driver can focus on driving safely. • Do not eat, drink or throw objects on the bus. • Follow the driver’s instructions at all times. Drivers are required by Florida law to stop for a school bus displaying flashing red lights and an extended stop arm, according to the state Department of Transportation’s web site. Drivers also must stop on two-lane roads and on multi-lane roads without a raised median or physical barrier, according to the web site. As of May 1, Florida began issuing citations for illegal passing of a stopped school bus with stop arm extended and red lights flashing, with a $225 fine for the offense. For a second or subsequent offense within five years, the Department of Highway Safety and Motor Vehicles may suspend your driver’s license for 90 days up to 6 months A driver does not have to stop when traveling in the opposite direction only if the roadway is divided by a raised median, a physical barrier or an unpaved median at least five feet wide, according to the DOT web site. In addition, the driver’s cell phone must be “hands-free” in a school zone. Using a wireless communications device in a handheld manner while driving in a designated school crossing, school zone, or active work zone area is against the law, according to the DOT web site. A tree-trimming job turned into a rescue Saturday afternoon in Stuart after a man became trapped about 40 feet in the air on a broken lift. Martin County Fire Rescue says crews were dispatched around 1 p.m. When rescuers arrived, they found the man stuck on the lift after it stopped moving up and down. He had been trimming trees in the area when the equipment stopped working. Because access for a ladder was limited, firefighters used a specialized rescue approach. Crews first removed nearby tree limbs. They then used a series of high-angle rescue maneuvers to secure the man, transfer his weight and carefully bring him to safety. Once he was back on the ground, paramedics evaluated him and determined he had minor injuries. The man declined transportation to the hospital. Martin County Fire Rescue credited the C-Shift crews from Heavy Rescue 23, Battalion 2, EMS 2 and EMS 22 for the rescue.

STUART – After months of debate, the Stuart City Commission unanimously approved draft language July 28 for a referendum that would prohibit the sale or long-term lease of the city’s ballfields without voter approval. Commissioners also agreed to hold special hearings to ensure the measure qualifies for the November ballot. The proposal follows years of discussion over the future of the ballfields at Guy Davis and Sailfish parks. A first reading stalled in May after the resignation of Commissioner Christopher Collins left the commission deadlocked. Commissioner Laura Giobbi later persuaded the board to revisit the issue and requested additional information on the parks’ history, use and redevelopment efforts. Community Services Director Jim Chrulski presented that overview, describing Sailfish Park as a historic community asset that has served local baseball since the 1950s. He also reviewed past improvement projects and the city’s unsuccessful effort to secure state funding for a tournament complex at Guy Davis Park. Chrulski said the fields remain heavily used. In 2025, Guy Davis hosted 24 user groups with 227 field reservations, while Sailfish Park accommodated 25 groups with 673 field uses. The city generated about $31,000 in combined facility revenue from the two parks. He also revisited a 2018 unsolicited proposal to redevelop Sailfish Park, which sparked public opposition and ultimately led to the current referendum effort. City Attorney Lee Baggett said the proposed ballot language mirrors protections already in the city charter for certain waterfront properties, requiring voter approval before the city could sell, convey or enter into long-term leases for the ballfield properties. Commissioner Campbell Rich voiced concerns that language allowing leases for sports, recreation or concession uses could create an unintended loophole and argued for stricter limits while also noting the city’s annual ballfield maintenance costs exceed $300,000. After further discussion, Baggett revised the language to address commissioners’ concerns, and the measure passed 4-0. The commission held the referendum’s first reading Aug. A second reading is scheduled for Aug. 17 to meet the Supervisor of Elections deadline for the November ballot. Your comment has been submitted. Reported There was a problem reporting this. A road rage confrontation erupted into a violent four-vehicle crash on U.S. 1 Wednesday, leaving four injured and a Port St. Officers with the Port St. Lucie Police Department say they responded around 6:45 p.m. to the intersection of South U.S. Highway 1 and SE Lyngate Drive/SE Tiffany Avenue, where investigators determined that a red Harley-Davidson motorcycle and a black Ford Super Duty pickup truck were involved in an ongoing road-rage incident. "These two vehicles were involved in an active road rage incident just prior to the crash, and this is based off the dash camera and witness statements that we've collected," said Officer Brittany McNally with the Port St. Detectives say the pickup, driven by 54-year-old Kevin Lonergan, was pursuing the motorcycle as both vehicles traveled northbound on U.S. 1 and approached the intersection. According to witness statements and dash-camera video, the motorcycle entered the intersection against a red light and collided with a black Chevrolet Silverado, throwing the 31-year-old rider from the bike. Lucie City Council voted unanimously on July 27 to postpone a rezoning request for a 135,000-square-foot indoor and outdoor sports recreation complex in the Riverland area after dozens of Tradition-area homeowners packed City Chambers in protest. The council tabled the request from Riverland/Kennedy II LLC until August 24 to give the developer time to hold a neighborhood meeting with concerned residents. The developer GL Homes is seeking to rezone approximately 33.23 acres south of Southwest Discovery Way and east of Southwest Sundance Vista Boulevard from St. Lucie County Agricultural to Riverland-West Sports Recreation Master Planned Unit Development. Residents who spoke at the hearing said they purchased their homes with the understanding that the parcel would be a city park, not a commercial recreation facility. Southwest River Rock Road resident Jim Riordan told the council GL Homes has 1,300 other acres where they could build the complex and that the company is already advertising the fitness center in sales materials for new parcels. Harriet Gallas said she was told when she bought her house there would be a park over the berm next to her property. She told the council the planned 72 pickleball courts, bocci courts, tennis courts, dog park and RV park would destroy her quality of life through noise pollution. Planning Zoning Director Mary Savage-Dunham told the council the rezoning is consistent with the city comprehensive plan and a pre-existing Development of Regional Impact for the area. The site is designated Neighborhood Village Commercial, which allows a mixture of residential and non-residential uses including commercial offices, personal and household services, institutional facilities, public facilities, parks, playgrounds and similar services. Land Use Attorney Azlina Goldstein, representing the applicant, initially resisted postponing the request and said details about landscaping, buffers and specific indoor and outdoor features would be addressed during the site-plan process, not the rezoning. Mayor Shannon Martin asked Goldstein if GL Homes would be willing to meet with residents to address their concerns. Vice-Mayor Jolien Caraballo urged Goldstein to table the request, saying residents did not comprehend the quasi-judicial rezoning process. After loud protest from the audience, the council voted to postpone the hearing until August 24. City Attorney Richard Berrios explained that the rezoning is a quasi-judicial process limited to sworn testimony and facts applied to the specific rezoning request, with details about landscaping and specific features reserved for the site-plan process. The Kings Landing development in Fort Pierce is facing another delay. WATCH BELOW: 'It's taking so long,' Funky Cuda owner Jon Nolli tells WPTV's St. Lucie County reporter Tyler Hatfield Live Oak Development, the secondary developer on the project, told commissioners they’re short said they are $15 million short of the $60 million needed to complete the Marriott hotel and restaurant portion of the project — and city commissioners are divided on what to do next. Live Oak Development, the secondary developer on the project, told commissioners the $15 million shortfall is due in part to rising construction costs. “We have seen construction costs continue to balloon, “ said CEO Paul Bertozzi. “We've had those challenges across multiple industries but that is a portion of the cause of the delta that is being created." City leaders said developers initially asked the city to cover the gap through a loan or grant. Commissioner Michael Broderick said that request was denied. "Unfortunately, the city does not have $15 million. Nor would I advocate the city investing $15 million into a private enterprise,” said Broderick. Live Oak Development is now asking for 180 days to find the money through private sources. Bertozzi told commissioners the outreach has already begun. "We're already in the process of reaching out to participating parties,” said Bertozzi. "We're looking at friends and families and investment and private equity verses institutional investors." But commissioners are debating about the city reclaiming the property. Broderick said he believes trying to reclaim the property through legal action would be expensive and time-consuming. "Clawing the property back through reverter clauses is going to be litigation for years and a ton of money,” said Broderick. He said he would rather give developers the time they are asking for. "What are we going to lose by 180 days? That's the question I would ask,” said Broderick. “What are we going to lose? It's just time." Commissioner Chris Dzadovsky said he does not want to wait. "I think it's time to as they say, cut bait and move on," he said. Jon Nolli, owner of Funky Cuda in Fort Pierce, said he has been waiting on the development and is ready for it to be finished. "It's been taking some time,” said Nolli. Nolli said the completed project would benefit the surrounding area. He said he even has plans to open businesses inside Kings Landing — but the delays are wearing on him. "I've got a couple deposits on the commercial side. I was looking to a beer garden, and a deli, and I mean it's taking so long that I don't even know the trends have changed,” said Nolli WPTV reached out to Live Oak Development and still working on a response. The city commission has scheduled a special meeting on September 14 to discuss next steps.

STUART — Thanks to the partnership-building efforts of the Education Foundation of Martin County and the generosity of Costco, approximately 750 students will head into the 2026-27 school year with a new backpack in hand. On Thursday morning, Stuart Costco Administrative Manager Mike Fabis and Membership Manager Ray Perry arrived at Pinewood Elementary School with pickup trucks loaded with hundreds of backpacks. The donation marked the second consecutive year Costco has provided backpacks for local students, but this year’s contribution was significantly larger. “We received backpacks last year, but this year we had almost 400 coming in, which is incredible,” said Pinewood Elementary Principal Amy Porter. “Our kids were so excited when they got them last year, so I can’t wait to see their faces this year.” The deliveries continued across Stuart, where Fabis and Perry unloaded another truckload of backpacks at Murray Middle School, ensuring hundreds more students will be prepared for the first day of classes. “Anytime we have an opportunity to help our families, making sure that they have access to new resources for back to school to relieve that financial burden is always so appreciated,” said Murray Middle School Principal Tiffany Roth. In addition to the backpacks, Costco donated a $500 gift card to each school to help meet additional student needs. School leaders say the donation is an example of the Education Foundation of Martin County’s unique role in connecting community partners with schools to provide meaningful support for students and families. “The Education Foundation of Martin County is really the powerhouse of our school district and our schools,” Roth said. “They really act as a liaison, helping to connect us with all of our community partners.” Porter echoed that sentiment. “We want to thank Costco and the Education Foundation, who does so much for our students,” she said. Lucie Police is investigating two separate incidents regarding campaign signs for the city’s mayoral seat. 5, near the intersection of Southwest Airoso Boulevard and Southwest Thanksgiving Avenue, Port St. Lucie, a sergeant saw Steven Giordano, one of three candidates for the office of mayor, and an unidentified woman near political campaign signs at a home, according to police reports. The sergeant started an investigation after discovering one campaign sign on the ground, while another was placed in the yard. As part of the investigation, detectives reviewed surveillance video, which appears to show Giordano and the woman arrive at the residence and go to the campaign signs displayed in the yard, according to police reports. The video also shows the woman removing a campaign sign supporting Mayor Shannon Martin and putting a different campaign sign in the yard, according to police reports. Detectives have collected the video evidence and are evaluating it in conjunction with statements, physical evidence, and all other information gathered during the investigation, according to police reports. Officers and detectives are working to determine whether the movement or replacement of the campaign signs was authorized by the property owner at the time the incident occurred. In a separate incident on Aug. 7, near Southwest Airoso Boulevard and Southwest Thornhill Drive, officers responded to a disturbance involving placement of political campaign signs. Upon investigating, officers learned through video surveillance that Aaron Martin — a lieutenant in the city’s police force and husband of the current mayor — and Giordano were arguing over placement and movement of signs at a nearby home. Investigators also interviewed the homeowners and learned that both residents believed they had separately granted permission for campaign signs to be placed on the property, according to police reports. During the investigation, officers determined that one homeowner gave permission for one campaign’s sign, while another resident of the home, who has limited English proficiency, separately gave permission to individuals associated with the opposing campaign. Investigators believe this language barrier contributed to a misunderstanding as to which campaign signs were authorized to be displayed and whether previously placed signs could be moved or replaced, according to police reports. At this time, there is no indication that any campaign signs associated with this incident were stolen or intentionally damaged, according to police reports. Information related to the placement of the campaign signs also was forwarded to the City of Port St. Lucie Code Compliance for review, as appropriate. A Martin County community is restoring a mangrove island next to their marina that erosion has slowly destroyed.Residents at Piper's Landing Yacht and Country Club spent two years cultivating 6,000 mangroves in an on-site nursery. Now, they are planting them in the waterway to bring the island back to life.WATCH BELOW:"The mangroves were so thick and lush and we've watched them deteriorate and in some areas the island is dead now," Lisa Standing, a resident at Piper's Landing Yacht and Country Club, said.Standing rallied her neighbors to take action. The community built 10 planter pools to grow red and white mangroves."We were able to collect just white and red seeds from our mangrove island," Standing said.The effort required extensive research and permitting before a single plant could go into the water. They say it was an elaborate operation that turned into a labor of love"We tried to match the habitat of all of our plants to the river habitat," Standing said. "We were here almost every day in the nursery and we inspected the plants, watered them if needed, monitored their health, matched salinity to the river."With the nursery phase complete, residents brought in Keith Rossin, CEO of Mang Consulting Services, to do the planting."These are dredge filled little management areas and so they take that dredge fill and they actually bring it up to the right level for the elevation for the mangroves and that allows for us to plant these mangroves in here so this very unique way I've never actually seen this done before of how we can actually create mangrove habitat," Rossin said.What are now thousands of small trees are expected to grow into the foundation of a new ecosystem."We will be able to go down to the mangrove island and enjoy beautiful lush island," Standing said. "It's just wonderful."This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Lucie police are investigating the death of 77-year-old Michael Joseph Kramer, who was found unresponsive in a pond near his home on Friday afternoon after being reported missing earlier that day. At approximately 1:18 p.m. today, officers responded to a residence on the 1400 block of SW Mockingbird Drive regarding a missing adult. Kramer was last seen by his wife inside their home at approximately 10 p.m. the following morning, Kramer was no longer inside the residence. Kramer’s personal belongings, including his shoes, wallet, and cellphone, were still inside the home. His wife searched for him and contacted local hospitals before reporting him missing to law enforcement at approximately 1:18 p.m. Officers began searching the neighborhood and, during the canvass, located an unresponsive person in a pond directly across the street from Kramer’s residence at approximately 2 p.m. The individual and clothing matched Kramer’s description. Lucie Police Department Dive Team recovered Kramer from the water near the shoreline of the pond, where he was confirmed deceased. The circumstances surrounding Kramer’s death remain under investigation. Police said there are no known indications of foul play at this preliminary stage of the investigation. Authorities encourage the public to promptly contact law enforcement when a person is believed to be missing, emphasizing that timely reporting allows officers to begin investigative and search efforts as quickly as possible.

Two sharks were spotted along the Atlantic Ocean shore — one that washed up dead and another of fishermen struggling with a hooked one. Both incidents occurred Friday, with video sent to WPBF. Jensen Beach resident and avid beach walker Kathy Green was walking along Normandy Beach on Hutchinson Island in St. Lucie County when she filmed a group of fishermen struggling with a 12-foot shark they had hooked. The fishermen unhooked the deadly beast and released it back into the water. Shark expert and conservationist Jim Abernethy believes it was a great white shark by looking at the video. Also Friday, a hammerhead shark was spotted dead just south of the Jupiter Beach Resort. Christopher Ray, a musician, submitted video to WPBF. Later that day, Fish Wildlife removed the shark. Shark Week 2026 ran from July 26 to Saturday on the Discovery Channel. Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission has ordered Martin County, which also includes Hutchinson Island, to follow rules about people fishing for fish or sharks from the beach or shoreline. Shark fishing requires a state saltwater fishing license to fish within 1,000 feet of the guarded beach boundaries at any time. Under the current county ordinance, shark fishing is prohibited within 1,000 yards of the county's four guarded beaches: Jensen, Stuart, Bathtub and Hobe Sound. On Tuesday, commissioners postponed making a decision and asked attorneys to review the law.

Thomas Todd, and his wife, have a neighbor they're worried about — not because of anything they can see, but because of what they can hear and smell. WATCH BELOW: 'She really has legally walled us off from investigating,' Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek tells Chief Investigative Reporter Jamie Ostroff The couple sent video of dogs barking from behind a fence next door at their Martin County home. Todd said he believes there are between 15 and 20 dogs on the property. I visited the Todds' home on a calm, July afternoon. But when the wind picks up, Todd said the smell coming from next door is overwhelming. "It's a combination of garbage and animal feces and urine," Todd said. "I mean, I don't know how somebody could live in that." Todd first raised his concerns at a WPTV Let's Hear It event in Jensen Beach in May. When asked what a solution would look like, his answer was simple: "Save those dogs. Get them out of there." Public records obtained by WPTV show Martin County Animal Control officers and sheriff's deputies have visited the home at least 11 times since 2020 — all related to concerns about the dogs and their owner. The owner is not being named because she has never been charged with a crime. One incident report from 2020 describes accounts of as many as 25 dogs inside the home. On multiple occasions, authorities noted feces on the floor and furniture. Records show the owner did clean up after initial visits and told animal control she had re-homed some of the dogs, but she eventually stopped allowing law enforcement inside. Multiple reports note that deputies were not allowed to see the dogs when they visited the home. A code enforcement officer took photos through the glass front door in 2023, noting "a dog with feces on it." After that visit, the owner put up a fence. Todd said she also stopped letting the dogs outside, but he can still hear them barking in the house. For Todd, what's out of sight is not out of mind — let alone out of sound or smell. And there's nothing anybody can do or will do," Todd said. Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek said the fence has created a legal barrier to further investigation. "You can't even see into the property anymore," Budensiek said. "So, she really has legally walled us off from investigating exactly what's going on inside." When asked whether deputies have a lawful way to enter the property and look for themselves, Budensiek said they do not — unless there is visible evidence of mistreatment. "If there was something that we could see from the outside that -- you know -- dogs are being mistreated, malnourished, not taken care of — we would absolutely get a search warrant and go in there," Budensiek said. Florida statutes require that confined animals be provided "a sufficient quantity of good and wholesome food and water." Budensiek said that standard appears to be met based on what deputies can observe. "We saw recently — as recently as last week — that there's food boxes that are out there, empty food boxes, so we know the animals from the outside look to be being taken care of," Budensiek said. I attempted to reach the owner by phone and left three voicemails. In the most recent incident report — from July 2025 — the owner told deputies she had 7 dogs, then "redacted and said that she only had five dogs," according to the report. Todd said he does not believe that statement. "Seems like from everything I've been told, the law's on her side," Todd said. Since I visited the Todds last month, they say they continue to hear the dogs and have continued to follow up with the sheriff's office. They have also seen animal control in front of the owner's house a few times since this story began — but deputies have not gone in. Budensiek acknowledged the neighbors' frustration but said there is little more his office can do. "I know the neighbors are worried and, and we'll still respond out there for complaints. But again, it's not illegal to be a bad neighbor," Budensiek said. We want to be your voice and help you find solutions. A road rage confrontation erupted into a violent four-vehicle crash on U.S. 1 Wednesday, leaving four injured and a Port St. Officers with the Port St. Lucie Police Department say they responded around 6:45 p.m. to the intersection of South U.S. Highway 1 and SE Lyngate Drive/SE Tiffany Avenue, where investigators determined that a red Harley-Davidson motorcycle and a black Ford Super Duty pickup truck were involved in an ongoing road-rage incident. "These two vehicles were involved in an active road rage incident just prior to the crash, and this is based off the dash camera and witness statements that we've collected," said Officer Brittany McNally with the Port St. Detectives say the pickup, driven by 54-year-old Kevin Lonergan, was pursuing the motorcycle as both vehicles traveled northbound on U.S. 1 and approached the intersection. According to witness statements and dash-camera video, the motorcycle entered the intersection against a red light and collided with a black Chevrolet Silverado, throwing the 31-year-old rider from the bike. See also: Miami man faces prison after pleading guilty to online threats against Rubio, Noem Police say Lonergan then entered the intersection against the red signal, struck the ejected motorcyclist, and crashed head-on into a blue Toyota RAV4. The motorcyclist and two people inside the RAV4 were taken to Lawnwood Medical Center , per PSLPD. The Silverado driver was transported to St. Investigators say the motorcyclist suffered serious injuries, including a brain bleed and facial fractures, and lost consciousness after the crash. He remains hospitalized in stable condition.\ Based on witness statements, dash-camera video and the investigation, police arrested Lonergan for two counts of reckless driving causing serious bodily injury and one count of reckless driving causing injury. The investigative findings indicate that the pickup truck was actively pursuing that motorcyclist just moments prior to that crash, said McNally. After being medically cleared, Lonergan was booked into the St. The intersection remained closed for hours while investigators processed the scene before all lanes reopened around 2 a.m. This case does, though, serve as hopefully a powerful reminder that allowing your anger to dictate your actions behind the wheel can put multiple innocent lives at risk, McNally said.

A 76-year-old woman was arrested after police said she used barcode stickers and tags she brought into the store with her to pay deeply reduced prices for merchandise at a Target store in Port St. Officers responded Tuesday, August 4 to the Target at Tradition store, 10720 SW Village Parkway after store loss-prevention employees detained Joan McKeon, according to the Port St. Investigators said McKeon entered the store carrying barcode stickers and barcode tags for lower-priced products. She allegedly placed or scanned those barcodes at self-checkout instead of using the barcodes attached to the merchandise she selected. During the most recent incident, police said an item priced at $32.99 was scanned as a $1.29 purchase. Officers searching McKeon’s purse found 28 barcode stickers, some bearing the names of other retailers, including TJ Maxx, Publix and Burlington, police said. Investigators planned to contact those businesses as part of the continuing investigation. "Listen, times clearly are hard for people in America. Healthcare is high, food is high so people are doing anything that they can to make ends meet," said Noesha Jennings, a shopper from Port St. "Me personally I think it's pretty clever but we are a growing city and we can't be having those things going on around here, man," said Stephon Jennings, a shopper from Port St. See also: No Powerball jackpot winner; prize climbs to estimated $856 Million Target loss-prevention employees told officers the incident was not isolated. According to the arrest report, a Target Loss Prevention Manager at that store told police this was the twelfth retail theft McKeon committed at that store, dating back to September 2025. McKeon is charged with fraud-swindle-obtain property under $20,000. "You don't rip anybody off like that. I'm very shocked how the world's turning out. So it's very disappointing to hear," said Kimise Volpe, a shopper from Palm Beach Gardens. We reached McKeon by phone Friday. She said she did commit the crime and she did not know why she did it. She also said she was not thinking clearly and she said I know I was wrong. Target's media relations office did not respond to an e-mail seeking comment.

The Humane Society of the Treasure Coast is asking for donations, foster homes, adopters, and help from rescue organizations after taking in more than 100 animals from what the Martin County sheriff described as the worst animal hoarding case in the county’s history. "We need adopters and fosters. Anyone that's willing to adopt and has been thinking about getting a pet, the time is now," said Sarah Fisher, spokesperson, Humane Society of the Treasure Coast. Employees and volunteers have been working around the clock to care for the animals while the Palm City shelter continues its regular operations. A total of 108 animals were brought to the humane society for medical treatment and care after 77-year-old Gail Giustino was arrested July 20. Since then, 10 cats and 17 dogs from the case have been adopted, while five microchipped cats have been reunited with their owners. "I think she thought she was doing a good thing. She thought she was rescuing cats from the outdoors and unfortunately, she was way in over her head, couldn't care for it and ended up in a terrible situation," Fisher said. The shelter’s workload has continued to grow. Following the initial case, the Martin County Sheriff’s Office reportedly received an influx of requests for animal welfare checks. Last week, the humane society took in 26 cats from another situation and five dogs from a separate case. We expect more animals in the coming weeks due to the calls that have come in requesting animal welfare checks and the initial information we are receiving from Animal Services, which is following up on these calls, Humane Society Director of Operations Lori Tucker said. Many calls have been cleared, but there are cases that are requiring further follow-up. The organization said monetary donations are its greatest immediate need because of the continuing costs of medical care, food and housing while the animals await placement. Donations may be made through the shelter’s emergency medical fund. The humane society is also urging residents to adopt or foster animals already in its care. Officials said the influx doubled the shelter’s animal population even as normal admissions and services continued. Adopting or fostering a dog, cat, rabbit or guinea pig would free space for rescued animals still receiving treatment and preparing for adoption. See also: Road rage ends in violent 4-vehicle crash on U.S. Lucie man arrested We are still in need of people to adopt working cats, that is, cats that are suitable for safe outdoor living, Tucker said. We also are in desperate need of adopters and rescue groups willing to help take some of our animals. The shelter is offering a Name Your Price adoption special until further notice. Short- and long-term foster opportunities are also available. Information about adoptable animals is available at hstc1.org/Adopt , and foster information is available at hstc1.org/foster . Prospective adopters may call 772-223-8822 . Foster inquiries may be sent to catfoster@hstc1.org or dogfoster@hstc1.org , or made by calling 772-600-3220 . The Humane Society will also offer public microchipping services from 10 a.m. Registration is available at hstc1.org/Clinic . The Humane Society of the Treasure Coast is a private, locally operated nonprofit at 4100 SW Leighton Farm Ave. The no-kill animal welfare organization has served the Martin County area since 1955 and relies on donations to support its programs and services.

After a unanimous vote, the redevelopment of the old Sears space at Gardens Mall is moving forward, with a second vote expected in September.WATCH: Gardens Mall shoppers hear about the possible changesA new Dick's House of Sports and outdoor athletic field are one step closer to replacing the old Sears at the Palm Beach Gardens Mall, following a unanimous vote by local officials.The redevelopment has been years in the making, with plans dating back to 2011. Progress stalled multiple times along the way, including in 2017 when controversy over whether the retailer would sell guns brought negotiations to a halt. Dick's Sporting Goods has since stopped selling guns in its stores, clearing a major point of contention and helping move the project forward.Dick's House of Sports is a larger, experience-focused concept that goes beyond traditional retail. The location would feature rock-climbing walls, HitTrax batting cages, VR sports, and more, alongside an outdoor field for community events, recreational leagues, camps, and other programming. The development would also bring more retail space to the mall.Shoppers in Palm Beach Gardens said the project sounds like an exciting addition to one of the most popular shopping destinations in the city.Suzanne Schoen said:"It's a welcome change."John Schoen said:"I think that's an interesting concept."Amy Smith said:"I think it's a good idea. I mean, I want to try start playing pickleball. That'd probably be a good way to try it."Susan Sands said:"It's convenient, and then it's one-stop shopping. You roam the mall, and it sounds wonderful. So when will they begin it?"The project still requires a second vote in September before receiving final approval. But that vote seems like all but a formality at this point.

As the August election approaches, tensions are rising between the two political camps as incumbent Port St. Lucie Mayor Shannon Martin faces challenger Steve Giordano in the race for mayor. So far, tensions have escalated beyond the polls, with campaign signs being removed or moved. The incidents prompted the Port St. Lucie Police Department to launch investigations into two separate cases involving campaign signs, one of which led to a confrontation. The first incident occurred Wednesday, Aug. 5, near the intersection of Airoso Boulevard and Southwest Thanksgiving Avenue. PSLPD said one of its sergeants noticed mayoral candidate Steve Giordano and an unidentified woman near political campaign signs. An investigation was launched after one campaign sign was found on the ground while another had been placed in the yard. Investigators reviewed surveillance footage that showed Giordano and the woman approaching campaign signs displayed in the yard. PSLPD said the video then showed the woman removing a campaign sign supporting Mayor Shannon Martin before another sign was placed in the yard. PSLPD said officers and detectives are working to determine the circumstances surrounding the placement, movement and authorization of the campaign signs. The August 7th Incident During the overnight hours Friday, Aug. 7, Giordano told CBS12 News that he and his campaign manager were putting up signs near Southwest Airoso Boulevard and Southwest Thornhill Drive. Giordano said he saw a man remove a sign from the ground and throw it. Giordano then grabbed his cellphone and began recording the encounter. The man appears to be Shannon Martin's husband, Aaron Martin, a lieutenant with the Port St. Video shows a profanity-laced confrontation between Giordano and Martin. The two can be heard shouting at each other and making accusations about campaign signs being placed in the community without property owners' permission. See also: South Florida Wendy's worker's lunch break sparks viral friendship PSLPD said investigators learned that one homeowner had given permission for one campaign sign to be placed on the property, while another resident of the home, who has limited English proficiency, told members of the opposing campaign they could also place a sign there. Investigators said the language barrier contributed to the confrontation over the campaign signs and whether the previously placed sign could be moved or removed. PSLPD said investigators are reviewing the video. At this time, police said there is no indication that any campaign signs involved in the incident were stolen or intentionally damaged. Lucie Police Department acknowledges that Aaron Martin is employed by the department. Martin is a department employee will not influence the investigative process. As with every investigation, the facts and evidence will determine the outcome, and this investigation will be conducted fairly, impartially, and in accordance with department policy," PSLPD said in a news release. Following the incident, Mayor Shannon Martin said in a statement: My campaign is aware of recent incidents involving the unauthorized removal of my campaign signs at different locations over several days. Signs were taken down without permission and replaced with Mr. In response, my husband simply restored the signs that had been removed. At no time were my opponent's signs stolen or damaged, one small sign was temporarily moved and put back in the ground. Lucie Police Department is investigating reports related to political campaign signs that occurred this week. We fully support a thorough, impartial review of the facts. I remain focused on the issues that matter to the city and will continue running a positive, transparent campaign. According to police, officers responded to the reported incidents, documented the scenes, collected available evidence and began interviewing those involved. Detectives are reviewing physical evidence, speaking with witnesses and verifying statements provided to investigators. The investigations remain active. Police said all available facts and evidence will be reviewed before any determination is made. Lucie Police Department said it remains committed to conducting a fair, impartial and fact-based investigation.

Dana Trabulsy (R-Fort Pierce) FORT PIERCE–State Rep. Dana Trabulsy (R-Fort Pierce) says Fort Pierce needs the tax base generated by new development, but not at the size of a massive, mixed-use project proposed for Causeway Cove on Seaway Drive. Trabulsy told the Fort Pierce City Commission this week that the hotel, condominium, retail and dining development spread over five proposed high-rise buildings is fraught with map errors, environmental and traffic questions and may conflict with the city’s comprehensive land use plan. According to Trabulsy, 62 percent of local residents disapprove of the Causeway Cove plan in its current form. Causeway Cove includes a complex of five buildings, ranging from 14-17 stories tall. The largest proposes 180 condos, a 204-room hotel, a convention center, bar/restaurant, retail and club space. A second building proposes 365 residential condos, ranging from studios, 1- and 2-bedrooms, while a third building shows 40 condos ranging from 1- to 3-bedrooms and a 203-room hotel. Two other buildings each feature 164 condominium units, and nearly 14,000 square feet of retail space. Causeway Cove is set on an $8 million land parcel at 601 Seaway Dr., currently occupied by a 50-year-old, 1,500-square-foot building with adjacent deck and dock. It’s already appropriately zoned and a city staff report concluded the project “has demonstrated environmental compliance” and is “consistent with the city’s comprehensive plan.” Records show that project is headed by Ashton DePeyster, a Palm Beach philanthropist and real estate developer, under the name G. FLASH General Partners Inc., West Palm Beach. Both Trabulsy and city commissioners also questioned so-called “affordable housing” factors – part of Florida’s Live Local Act – that limit local officials’ say over how the plan is developed if it guarantees that 40 percent of the housing units will qualify as “affordable” for the next 30 years. Commissioner Michael Broderick, who along with Mayor Linda Hudson, have homes on South Hutchinson Island, said he believes Causeway Cove rental rates for designated “affordable housing” will have to average $3,000 a month. “In the City of Fort Pierce, that’s not considered affordable,” Broderick said. “...This is an existential threat to the lives and the lifestyle and the safety of the people who live on South Beach.” Hudson agreed. “This will turn Fort Pierce into something none of us want,” said the mayor. Broderick also questioned the timing of two major development projects being proposed for South Hutchinson Island at a time when the city could be without a permanent city attorney. The commission recently voted against extending the contract of current City Attorney Sara Hedges and the search to hire her successor is expected to take several months. “I find the timing of this to be very unique,” said Broderick. Despite the fact that the state’s Live Local Act removes some of the guardrails that city planners generally can invoke in approving land developments, Trabulsy said she believes issues surrounding state waterways and traffic could tap the brakes. “I’m not against economic development; we do need that tax base,” Commissioner Chris Dzadovsky advocated for the city hiring outside counsel specializing in land development issues. “What you said tonight gives a lot of folks hope,” Dzadovsky told Trabulsy. A second South Beach project, called Boardwalk on the Inlet, is moving on the coattails of Causeway Cove. It’s under development by Woods Family Limited Partnership II, led by Sanford L. Woods Sr., of Tampa, owner of car dealerships in Florida and Michigan, including Treasure Coast Lexus, Fort Pierce. That partnership already owns six land parcels on Seaway Drive it says are currently leased to the city for overflow parking, serving public beach access at the inlet and businesses. Boardwalk on the Inlet proposes construction of two towers. The East Building would include 127 hotel rooms, a cigar lounge, restaurants, rooftop terrace, conference center and ground-level retail space. The West Building is designed for 54 residential condos, 48 hotel rooms, hotel amenities, a fast-casual restaurant, a private club and retail spaces. Your comment has been submitted. This week I'm at Vero Beach High School where students are getting ready to go back to school, and I decided to do something I've never done before – I joined the marching band! I crashed band camp at Vero Beach High School just a few days before school started, and let me tell you, it was an incredible experience.WATCH: The first time I stepped onto that practice field, I could feel the history before I even picked up my instrument. This wasn't just another high school band – this was a tradition stretching back to 1934, when the Fighting Indians Band was founded as part of the Federal Music Project during the Great Depression. Every student who had ever worn that uniform had helped build an incredible legacy.I got to meet some amazing students who are keeping that tradition alive, like Annabel Robbins who plays flute piccolo and is a drum major. Brady, an incoming senior, is the woodwind captain and section leader."It's kind of scary, you know," Brady said. "You're in charge of a lot of kids, so you got to make sure they're all doing good.The band director, Sean Srigley, has a special connection to this program that goes way back. "I'm actually alumni of Vero Beach High School. I was in the band myself," Srigley explained. "The cool thing about Vero is we've got awesome academics, awesome athletics. Our band is right there with them. We've marched in pretty much every big parade you could have in America."And he's not exaggerating! This band has an absolutely incredible resume. They performed in the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade in 1988, marching through the streets of New York City and playing "Alexander's Ragtime Band" for millions of television viewers. That single performance became one of the defining moments in the program's history and remains a source of pride for every new generation of members.But that's not all – they've also performed in the Tournament of Roses Parade, the Fiesta Bowl Parade, the Orange Bowl and even Carnegie Hall! The program has earned decades of Superior ratings and national recognition while representing our Treasure Coast with pride.After learning about all this amazing history, it was time for me to get to work. But honestly, that wasn't really my thing, so I tried the drums next.But joining the marching band for practice meant more than just learning music and drill. It meant discipline and the ability to stand for a long time in that Florida heat – something these kids do with incredible dedication.As I marched onto the football field, I couldn't help but imagine all the students who had stood in that same place before me. Some had gone on to march through Manhattan in the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade. Others had performed in famous bowl games or international parades.As I left Vero Beach High School that day, I was thankful for the opportunity to be part of something so special, even for just one practice. These students aren't just making music – they're carrying on a legacy that's been building for nearly 90 years.

Early voting for Florida's August primary begins Aug. 8 in Palm Beach County and across the Treasure Coast, with dates and hours varying by location. In Palm Beach County, early voting runs through Aug. Voters can cast their ballots at any of the 28 designated early voting sites in the county from 7 a.m. This differs from Election Day, when voters must go to their assigned polling place. Wendy Sartory Link, Palm Beach County supervisor of elections, shared advice for voters preparing for the primary. "Make sure they have a plan. The vote-by-mail deadline to request that we send you a ballot has already passed. If you need to come to our office to pick up a vote by mail ballot, you can do that," Link said. "And if you are waiting until Election Day, just make sure that you know where you're supposed to go." Voters should bring a current, valid photo ID with a signature. If the photo ID does not include a signature, a second form of identification may be required. Election officials recommend checking voter information and reviewing sample ballots before heading to the polls. The county's website also allows voters to check wait times and schedule optional early voting appointments. Early voting in Treasure Coast and Okeechobee counties runs from Aug. 15, with the following hours: Martin County: 8 a.m. Indian River County: 8 a.m. Okeechobee County: 8:30 a.m. Hours and locations vary, so voters should check with their county supervisor of elections before heading to the polls. Florida has closed primaries, meaning party registration determines which primary ballot voters receive. The deadline to change party affiliation has passed. However, all registered voters may still be eligible to vote in nonpartisan or universal-primary contests, depending on their location. Election Day is Tuesday, Aug. Lucie Police Department has released an update on 2 separate investigations involving political campaign signs, both occurring this week in the area of SW Airoso Boulevard.Although both incidents involve political campaign signs in the same area, police say they are being investigated as separate cases, with each evaluated independently based on their own facts, evidence, and applicable law.The first incident occurred on August 5, 2026, near the intersection of SW Airoso Boulevard and SW Thanksgiving Avenue.A Port St. Lucie Police sergeant observed Steven Giordano and an unidentified adult female near political campaign signs at a residence and initiated an investigation after one campaign sign was found on the ground while another had been placed in the yard.Detectives reviewed surveillance video from the area, which appears to show Giordano and the unidentified adult female arrive at the residence, approach campaign signs displayed in the yard, and interact with the signage. The video further appears to show the unidentified female remove a campaign sign supporting Mayor Shannon Martin before a different campaign sign was placed in the yard.Detectives collected the video evidence and are evaluating it alongside statements, physical evidence, and all other information gathered during the investigation.Officers and detectives are working to determine the circumstances surrounding the placement, movement, and authorization of the campaign signs, including whether the movement or replacement of the signs was authorized by the property owner at the time the incident occurred.The second incident occurred on August 7, 2026, near SW Airoso Boulevard and SW Thornhill Drive, where officers responded to a disturbance involving political campaign signs.During the investigation, officers learned that Aaron Martin and Steven Giordano were involved in a verbal confrontation regarding the placement and movement of campaign signs at a nearby residence.Officers reviewed video recordings provided by the involved parties, which depict Martin and Giordano engaged in a verbal confrontation regarding the placement and movement of political campaign signs at the residence.Investigators interviewed the homeowners and learned that both residents believed they had separately granted permission for campaign signs to be placed on the property. Lucie Police Department is investigating the death of a 77-year-old man who was found in a pond, according to a press release from the PSLPD . PSLPD says that on Friday, around 1:18 p.m., officers were called to a residence on SW Mockingbird Drive in reference to a missing adult who was later identified as Michael Joseph Kramer, 77. The investigation revealed that Kramer was last seen by his wife inside of their residence at around 10:00 p.m. However, when Kramer’s wife woke up at approximately 7:00 a.m. on Friday, Kramer was nowhere to be found despite all of his personal belongings remaining in the residence. See also: Delray Beach body shop owner accused of insurance fraud stemming from 2024 claims After an extensive search of the area, PSLPD says that they located an unresponsive man that matched Kramer’s description in a pond directly across the street from the residence at around 2:00 p.m. The PSLPD Dive Team recovered Kramer from the water, and he was pronounced deceased. PSLPD says that currently, the circumstances surrounding his death remain unclear, but no indications of foul play seem apparent.

A Martin County community is restoring a mangrove island next to their marina that erosion has slowly destroyed.Residents at Piper's Landing Yacht and Country Club spent two years cultivating 6,000 mangroves in an on-site nursery. Now, they are planting them in the waterway to bring the island back to life.WATCH BELOW:"The mangroves were so thick and lush and we've watched them deteriorate and in some areas the island is dead now," Lisa Standing, a resident at Piper's Landing Yacht and Country Club, said.Standing rallied her neighbors to take action. The community built 10 planter pools to grow red and white mangroves."We were able to collect just white and red seeds from our mangrove island," Standing said.The effort required extensive research and permitting before a single plant could go into the water. They say it was an elaborate operation that turned into a labor of love"We tried to match the habitat of all of our plants to the river habitat," Standing said. "We were here almost every day in the nursery and we inspected the plants, watered them if needed, monitored their health, matched salinity to the river."With the nursery phase complete, residents brought in Keith Rossin, CEO of Mang Consulting Services, to do the planting."These are dredge filled little management areas and so they take that dredge fill and they actually bring it up to the right level for the elevation for the mangroves and that allows for us to plant these mangroves in here so this very unique way I've never actually seen this done before of how we can actually create mangrove habitat," Rossin said.What are now thousands of small trees are expected to grow into the foundation of a new ecosystem."We will be able to go down to the mangrove island and enjoy beautiful lush island," Standing said. "It's just wonderful."This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. The Kings Landing development in Fort Pierce is facing another delay.WATCH BELOW: 'It's taking so long,' Funky Cuda owner Jon Nolli tells WPTV's St. Lucie County reporter Tyler HatfieldLive Oak Development, the secondary developer on the project, told commissioners they’re short said they are $15 million short of the $60 million needed to complete the Marriott hotel and restaurant portion of the project — and city commissioners are divided on what to do next.Live Oak Development, the secondary developer on the project, told commissioners the $15 million shortfall is due in part to rising construction costs.“We have seen construction costs continue to balloon, “ said CEO Paul Bertozzi. “We've had those challenges across multiple industries but that is a portion of the cause of the delta that is being created."City leaders said developers initially asked the city to cover the gap through a loan or grant.Commissioner Michael Broderick said that request was denied."Unfortunately, the city does not have $15 million. Nor would I advocate the city investing $15 million into a private enterprise,” said Broderick.Live Oak Development is now asking for 180 days to find the money through private sources. Bertozzi told commissioners the outreach has already begun."We're already in the process of reaching out to participating parties,” said Bertozzi. "We're looking at friends and families and investment and private equity verses institutional investors."But commissioners are debating about the city reclaiming the property. Broderick said he believes trying to reclaim the property through legal action would be expensive and time-consuming."Clawing the property back through reverter clauses is going to be litigation for years and a ton of money,” said Broderick.He said he would rather give developers the time they are asking for."What are we going to lose by 180 days? That's the question I would ask,” said Broderick. “What are we going to lose? It's just time."Commissioner Chris Dzadovsky said he does not want to wait."I think it's time to as they say, cut bait and move on," he said.Jon Nolli, owner of Funky Cuda in Fort Pierce, said he has been waiting on the development and is ready for it to be finished."It's been taking some time,” said Nolli.Nolli said the completed project would benefit the surrounding area. He said he even has plans to open businesses inside Kings Landing — but the delays are wearing on him."I've got a couple deposits on the commercial side. I was looking to a beer garden, and a deli, and I mean it's taking so long that I don't even know the trends have changed,” said NolliWPTV reached out to Live Oak Development and still working on a response. The city commission has scheduled a special meeting on September 14 to discuss next steps.
