Lucie police are investigating the death of 77-year-old Michael Joseph Kramer, who was found unresponsive in a pond near his home on Friday afternoon after being reported missing earlier that day. At approximately 1:18 p.m. today, officers responded to a residence on the 1400 block of SW Mockingbird Drive regarding a missing adult. Kramer was last seen by his wife inside their home at approximately 10 p.m. the following morning, Kramer was no longer inside the residence. Kramer’s personal belongings, including his shoes, wallet, and cellphone, were still inside the home. His wife searched for him and contacted local hospitals before reporting him missing to law enforcement at approximately 1:18 p.m. Officers began searching the neighborhood and, during the canvass, located an unresponsive person in a pond directly across the street from Kramer’s residence at approximately 2 p.m. The individual and clothing matched Kramer’s description. Lucie Police Department Dive Team recovered Kramer from the water near the shoreline of the pond, where he was confirmed deceased. The circumstances surrounding Kramer’s death remain under investigation. Police said there are no known indications of foul play at this preliminary stage of the investigation. Authorities encourage the public to promptly contact law enforcement when a person is believed to be missing, emphasizing that timely reporting allows officers to begin investigative and search efforts as quickly as possible.

Lucie Police Department has released an update on 2 separate investigations involving political campaign signs, both occurring this week in the area of SW Airoso Boulevard.Although both incidents involve political campaign signs in the same area, police say they are being investigated as separate cases, with each evaluated independently based on their own facts, evidence, and applicable law.The first incident occurred on August 5, 2026, near the intersection of SW Airoso Boulevard and SW Thanksgiving Avenue.A Port St. Lucie Police sergeant observed Steven Giordano and an unidentified adult female near political campaign signs at a residence and initiated an investigation after one campaign sign was found on the ground while another had been placed in the yard.Detectives reviewed surveillance video from the area, which appears to show Giordano and the unidentified adult female arrive at the residence, approach campaign signs displayed in the yard, and interact with the signage. The video further appears to show the unidentified female remove a campaign sign supporting Mayor Shannon Martin before a different campaign sign was placed in the yard.Detectives collected the video evidence and are evaluating it alongside statements, physical evidence, and all other information gathered during the investigation.Officers and detectives are working to determine the circumstances surrounding the placement, movement, and authorization of the campaign signs, including whether the movement or replacement of the signs was authorized by the property owner at the time the incident occurred.The second incident occurred on August 7, 2026, near SW Airoso Boulevard and SW Thornhill Drive, where officers responded to a disturbance involving political campaign signs.During the investigation, officers learned that Aaron Martin and Steven Giordano were involved in a verbal confrontation regarding the placement and movement of campaign signs at a nearby residence.Officers reviewed video recordings provided by the involved parties, which depict Martin and Giordano engaged in a verbal confrontation regarding the placement and movement of political campaign signs at the residence.Investigators interviewed the homeowners and learned that both residents believed they had separately granted permission for campaign signs to be placed on the property. Officers determined that one homeowner communicated permission for one campaign's sign, while another resident of the home, who has limited English proficiency, separately conveyed permission to individuals associated with the opposing campaign.Investigators believe the language barrier contributed to a misunderstanding regarding which campaign signs were authorized to be displayed and whether previously placed signs could be moved or replaced.The preliminary investigation indicates that both individuals believed they had permission from residents of the property to place campaign signs. At this time, there is no indication that any campaign signs associated with this incident were stolen or intentionally damaged.Information related to the placement of the campaign signs has been forwarded to the City of Port St. Lucie Code Compliance for review.The Port St. Lucie Police Department acknowledged that Aaron Martin is employed by the department."The fact that Mr. Martin is a department employee will not influence the investigative process," the department said. A large law enforcement presence descended on a Fort Pierce neighborhood Tuesday morning as detectives executed a search warrant connected to an alleged fraud scheme that investigators say cost a local business nearly $7 million. Lucie County Sheriff's Office confirmed to CBS12 News that deputies are serving a search warrant as part of the ongoing investigation into the Southern Truss fraud case. Crime scene investigators were seen outside the home of Laura Beth Grasso in the Indian River Estates neighborhood near Sunset Boulevard. Grasso was arrested July 16 along with Sheri Lynn Harrs and Tina Marie Mejia following what the sheriff's office described as a years-long scheme targeting Southern Truss Companies. Grasso has pleaded not guilty to the charges, court records show. Investigators allege Grasso, who worked as the company's bookkeeper and comptroller, used her administrative access to bypass financial controls and funnel millions of dollars out of the business. Detectives say the money was spent on luxury vehicles, vacations, designer goods, jewelry and other personal expenses. Neighbors on Sunset Boulevard told CBS12 News they had long been suspicious of Grasso's lifestyle. They got 4 or 5 brand new trucks. They got food delivery every day, four different food deliveries. I mean, we always wondered what was going on over there," neighbor Greg Longhway said. Grasso faces charges of: First-degree grand theft of $100,000 or more Organized fraud of $50,000 or more Conducting an enterprise through a pattern of racketeering activity (RICO) Money laundering of $100,000 or more Harrs and Mejia each face charges of grand theft, organized fraud and racketeering. Grasso's bond was set at a combined $1.15 million across the four charges. Longhway said he watched deputies storm the house Tuesday morning. "Oh, they came ripping in, and the SWAT gear and everything with the guns pulled and hollering. Come out that search warrant. Come out with your hands up," he said. Prosecutors have asked a judge to hold a hearing on the legitimacy and source of any bail premium or collateral before allowing Grasso to be released from the St. Lucie County Jail, arguing in a court filing that a defendant should not be able to use money obtained through criminal activity to secure her release. Tuesday's search follows an earlier warrant served on a vehicle connected to Grasso. A judge signed that warrant July 24, authorizing detectives to search a blue 2025 Chevrolet Tahoe registered to Grasso that had been towed to the sheriff's office evidence compound the day after her arrest. According to an inventory filed with the court, deputies found roughly $8,500 in cash, a jewelry organizer with jewelry, a Louis Vuitton purse and wallet, and a loaded Smith & Wesson M&P .40 Shield pistol in the glove box. Longhway said the family largely kept to themselves. They've never said a word to anybody. They've been there for a year and a half, two years. They don't talk to anybody, which is fine; we don't care," Longhway said. "We figured something was up over there, though." The alleged scheme started to unravel after a tornado damaged the Southern Truss facility, according to the criminal complaint. With the plant largely shut down, the company's owner noticed operating costs staying suspiciously high, including fuel charges for a company jet that wasn't flying. When he confronted Grasso and told her outside forensic accountants were being brought in, investigators say server logs show she began logging into the company's financial system overnight to alter records. A forensic audit later recovered a secret "shadow ledger" on her computer, according to the complaint, tracking where the missing money had actually gone. Southern Truss also filed a civil lawsuit against the three women, alleging they carried out a coordinated scheme between 2018 and 2025 to divert company funds through unauthorized payroll payments, wire transfers and other transactions. The amended complaint alleges Grasso alone misappropriated at least $5 million, while Mejia and Harrs allegedly received hundreds of thousands more. The criminal case remains pending. Court records show a magistrate in June declined to pause the related civil case because of the criminal proceedings, instead ordering the defendants to respond to discovery by July 30 and complete depositions by Aug. Neighbors say they saw someone arrested by a SWAT team this morning. Lucie County Sheriff's Office has not confirmed any additional arrests or what investigators were searching for on Tuesday.

Thomas Todd, and his wife, have a neighbor they're worried about — not because of anything they can see, but because of what they can hear and smell. WATCH BELOW: 'She really has legally walled us off from investigating,' Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek tells Chief Investigative Reporter Jamie Ostroff The couple sent video of dogs barking from behind a fence next door at their Martin County home. Todd said he believes there are between 15 and 20 dogs on the property. I visited the Todds' home on a calm, July afternoon. But when the wind picks up, Todd said the smell coming from next door is overwhelming. "It's a combination of garbage and animal feces and urine," Todd said. "I mean, I don't know how somebody could live in that." Todd first raised his concerns at a WPTV Let's Hear It event in Jensen Beach in May. When asked what a solution would look like, his answer was simple: "Save those dogs. Get them out of there." Public records obtained by WPTV show Martin County Animal Control officers and sheriff's deputies have visited the home at least 11 times since 2020 — all related to concerns about the dogs and their owner. The owner is not being named because she has never been charged with a crime. One incident report from 2020 describes accounts of as many as 25 dogs inside the home. On multiple occasions, authorities noted feces on the floor and furniture. Records show the owner did clean up after initial visits and told animal control she had re-homed some of the dogs, but she eventually stopped allowing law enforcement inside. Multiple reports note that deputies were not allowed to see the dogs when they visited the home. A code enforcement officer took photos through the glass front door in 2023, noting "a dog with feces on it." After that visit, the owner put up a fence. Todd said she also stopped letting the dogs outside, but he can still hear them barking in the house. For Todd, what's out of sight is not out of mind — let alone out of sound or smell. And there's nothing anybody can do or will do," Todd said. Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek said the fence has created a legal barrier to further investigation. "You can't even see into the property anymore," Budensiek said. "So, she really has legally walled us off from investigating exactly what's going on inside." When asked whether deputies have a lawful way to enter the property and look for themselves, Budensiek said they do not — unless there is visible evidence of mistreatment. "If there was something that we could see from the outside that -- you know -- dogs are being mistreated, malnourished, not taken care of — we would absolutely get a search warrant and go in there," Budensiek said. Florida statutes require that confined animals be provided "a sufficient quantity of good and wholesome food and water." Budensiek said that standard appears to be met based on what deputies can observe. "We saw recently — as recently as last week — that there's food boxes that are out there, empty food boxes, so we know the animals from the outside look to be being taken care of," Budensiek said. I attempted to reach the owner by phone and left three voicemails. In the most recent incident report — from July 2025 — the owner told deputies she had 7 dogs, then "redacted and said that she only had five dogs," according to the report. Todd said he does not believe that statement. "Seems like from everything I've been told, the law's on her side," Todd said. Since I visited the Todds last month, they say they continue to hear the dogs and have continued to follow up with the sheriff's office. They have also seen animal control in front of the owner's house a few times since this story began — but deputies have not gone in. Budensiek acknowledged the neighbors' frustration but said there is little more his office can do. "I know the neighbors are worried and, and we'll still respond out there for complaints. But again, it's not illegal to be a bad neighbor," Budensiek said. We want to be your voice and help you find solutions. Florida's regular spiny lobster season opens Thursday and runs through March.The best spots to find spiny lobster are around coral reefs, rocky ledges, artificial reefs, and near shore patch reefs. Popular locations include Palm Beach, Broward, and Miami-Dade reefs, along with the Florida Keys and the Dry Tortugas.Before heading out, lobster hunters need a valid Florida saltwater fishing license. Divers should bring a lobster gauge and measure every lobster before keeping it. A net or tickle stick should be used to harvest lobsters, and a diver down flag must be displayed at all times for safety.There are also several rules to keep in mind. Egg-bearing or undersized lobsters must not be kept. Harvesting in protected areas and no-take areas is prohibited, and the Florida daily bag limit must not be exceeded.Complete regulations are available on the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission website.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Lucie Mets celebrate their game 2 win against the Daytona Tortugas on August 5. This was the second game of a doubleheader to make up for a rainout on June 20. Lucie Mets split a doubleheader with the Daytona Tortugas on Wednesday at Clover Park, falling 8-4 in the opener before rallying for an 11-10 victory in 10 innings in the nightcap. The twin bill made up a June 20 rainout. Lucie avoided a doubleheader sweep, while Daytona’s seven-game winning streak came to an end. The Mets won the second game when John Smith III delivered a two-run single in the bottom of the 10th inning, scoring Wyatt Vincent and Vladi Gomez after Daytona had taken a 10-9 lead in the top of the inning. Lucie forced extra innings after erasing a three-run deficit in the seventh. Gomez’s two-strike, bases-loaded double tied the game 6-6 with two outs. Both teams scored in the eighth before trading two-run homers in the ninth. Daytona’s Dylan King put the Tortugas ahead 9-7, but Julio Zayas answered with a game-tying two-run homer for the Mets. Gomez finished 4 for 5 with three doubles, two RBIs and two runs. Smith III went 2 for 5 with three RBIs, while Zayas was 3 for 4 with a home run, two RBIs and two runs scored. 5 prospect Aaron Watson earned the win in his Single-A debut, limiting the Mets to two runs over five innings despite allowing eight hits. The Tortugas took control early, capitalizing on two Mets throwing errors in the first inning before scoring four runs in the fourth, highlighted by Adolfo Sanchez’s solo home run. Lucie collected 10 hits in the loss. Elian Peña went 2 for 4 with a double and two RBIs, while Aiden Robbins and Bohan Adderley each had two hits. Kuhio Aloy recorded the first hit of his professional career with a fifth-inning single. The Mets (14-22, 47-55) and Tortugas (23-13, 44-58) continue their series Thursday, August 6 at Clover Park with first pitch scheduled for 6:10 p.m. It’s $2 Night, featuring select $2 beer, hot dogs, fountain drinks and popcorn. The Kings Landing development in Fort Pierce is facing another delay.WATCH BELOW: 'It's taking so long,' Funky Cuda owner Jon Nolli tells WPTV's St. Lucie County reporter Tyler HatfieldLive Oak Development, the secondary developer on the project, told commissioners they’re short said they are $15 million short of the $60 million needed to complete the Marriott hotel and restaurant portion of the project — and city commissioners are divided on what to do next.Live Oak Development, the secondary developer on the project, told commissioners the $15 million shortfall is due in part to rising construction costs.“We have seen construction costs continue to balloon, “ said CEO Paul Bertozzi. “We've had those challenges across multiple industries but that is a portion of the cause of the delta that is being created."City leaders said developers initially asked the city to cover the gap through a loan or grant.Commissioner Michael Broderick said that request was denied."Unfortunately, the city does not have $15 million. Nor would I advocate the city investing $15 million into a private enterprise,” said Broderick.Live Oak Development is now asking for 180 days to find the money through private sources. Bertozzi told commissioners the outreach has already begun."We're already in the process of reaching out to participating parties,” said Bertozzi. "We're looking at friends and families and investment and private equity verses institutional investors."But commissioners are debating about the city reclaiming the property. Broderick said he believes trying to reclaim the property through legal action would be expensive and time-consuming."Clawing the property back through reverter clauses is going to be litigation for years and a ton of money,” said Broderick.He said he would rather give developers the time they are asking for."What are we going to lose by 180 days? That's the question I would ask,” said Broderick. “What are we going to lose? It's just time."Commissioner Chris Dzadovsky said he does not want to wait."I think it's time to as they say, cut bait and move on," he said.Jon Nolli, owner of Funky Cuda in Fort Pierce, said he has been waiting on the development and is ready for it to be finished."It's been taking some time,” said Nolli.Nolli said the completed project would benefit the surrounding area. He said he even has plans to open businesses inside Kings Landing — but the delays are wearing on him."I've got a couple deposits on the commercial side. I was looking to a beer garden, and a deli, and I mean it's taking so long that I don't even know the trends have changed,” said NolliWPTV reached out to Live Oak Development and still working on a response. The city commission has scheduled a special meeting on September 14 to discuss next steps.

WPTV is digging deeper into what the School District’s 1 mill property tax referendum for schools could really mean for the people inside local classroom as Palm Beach County voters get ready for the November election.WATCH BELOW: 'I love the kids so much and that's why I haven't left yet,' Alicia Carr tells WPTV's Joel LopezAfter hearing from Superintendent Mike Burke and the school district’s chief of police about the referendum, WPTV wanted to hear directly from educators whose paychecks, classrooms and futures are tied to the funding.For teachers like Alicia Carr, the conversation is personal.“I love the kids so much and that's why I haven't left yet,” Carr said. “No one goes into teaching for the money but you want to be able to live.”Carr has been an educator for 14 years and has worked at Jupiter Elementary School for the last six.Months after Palm Beach County teachers rallied and secured a 3.5% raise from the district, she says a major piece of her salary still depends on voters renewing the referendum.The School District of Palm Beach County says the 1 mill property tax generates more than $200 million for schools.“How much of your paycheck comes from that referendum,” WPTV’s Joel Lopez asked.“About $454,” Carr responded.That monthly boost has become part of her everyday budgeting.“Without that money what would that mean how would you budget?” Lopez asked.“I don't know I've already cut so much i don't know where to cut,” Carr said.Under the referendum, teachers receive additional money based on experience:$1,000 after their first year$5,000 for teachers with 5-9 years experience$10,000 for teachers with 10 or more years in the classroom“Even with our raise it's still a struggle so losing this $10,000 would be astronomical for many people,” Carr said.Superintendent Mike Burke told WPTV education funding remains lean. According to Burke, Palm Beach County ranks 46th nationally in education funding, but the referendum helps move the district into the mid-30s.The tax has been approved by voters since 2019 and will appear on the ballot again this November.So what does it mean for property owners?One mill means $1 for every $1,000 of taxable property value. For a homeowner with $300,000 in taxable value, that comes out to about $25 per month.The district says:Half of the money goes toward teacher salariesA quarter funds school security and mental health servicesThe remaining funds support choice and career programsDistrict leaders said those programs give students opportunities to attend schools based on the courses and career paths they want to pursue.At Manatee Elementary School, veteran teacher Stacy Tepper told WPTV the referendum affects more than just educators.“They're our future, they're your future doctors, they're your future lawyers,” Tepper said. “Whether you have a child or not, this is a benefit to you as well."This is Tepper’s 40th year as an educator, and she says the funding could also help strengthen her pension as she looks ahead to retirement.“As much as I love my job I have to make sure I'm secure when I'm ready to retire,” said Tepper.For the teachers speaking with WPTV, the referendum is about far more than numbers on a ballot, it's about the support from the community that is in the hands of voters.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. A road rage confrontation erupted into a violent four-vehicle crash on U.S. 1 Wednesday, leaving four injured and a Port St. Officers with the Port St. Lucie Police Department say they responded around 6:45 p.m. to the intersection of South U.S. Highway 1 and SE Lyngate Drive/SE Tiffany Avenue, where investigators determined that a red Harley-Davidson motorcycle and a black Ford Super Duty pickup truck were involved in an ongoing road-rage incident. "These two vehicles were involved in an active road rage incident just prior to the crash, and this is based off the dash camera and witness statements that we've collected," said Officer Brittany McNally with the Port St. Detectives say the pickup, driven by 54-year-old Kevin Lonergan, was pursuing the motorcycle as both vehicles traveled northbound on U.S. 1 and approached the intersection. According to witness statements and dash-camera video, the motorcycle entered the intersection against a red light and collided with a black Chevrolet Silverado, throwing the 31-year-old rider from the bike. See also: Miami man faces prison after pleading guilty to online threats against Rubio, Noem Police say Lonergan then entered the intersection against the red signal, struck the ejected motorcyclist, and crashed head-on into a blue Toyota RAV4. The motorcyclist and two people inside the RAV4 were taken to Lawnwood Medical Center , per PSLPD. The Silverado driver was transported to St. Investigators say the motorcyclist suffered serious injuries, including a brain bleed and facial fractures, and lost consciousness after the crash. He remains hospitalized in stable condition.\ Based on witness statements, dash-camera video and the investigation, police arrested Lonergan for two counts of reckless driving causing serious bodily injury and one count of reckless driving causing injury. The investigative findings indicate that the pickup truck was actively pursuing that motorcyclist just moments prior to that crash, said McNally. After being medically cleared, Lonergan was booked into the St. The intersection remained closed for hours while investigators processed the scene before all lanes reopened around 2 a.m. This case does, though, serve as hopefully a powerful reminder that allowing your anger to dictate your actions behind the wheel can put multiple innocent lives at risk, McNally said.

Lucie man was arrested on Aug 6 on an animal cruelty charge following the circulation of a video on social media that appeared to show the abuse of a small dog. Ricky Lee Schieferstein, 68, of Port St. Lucie County Jail as of Aug. 7 on a $7,500 bond on a charge of cruelty to animals, according to the jail web site. The investigation began after numerous members of the community shared the video and tagged the St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office across its social media platforms, according to the sheriff’s office Facebook posting. The information was then turned over to the sheriff’s office’s criminal investigations division for investigation. Dawn Dale, through her investigation, developed probable cause and obtained an arrest warrant to charge Schieferstein with animal cruelty, according to the Facebook posting. In the 16-second video posted on the sheriff’s office Facebook page with a “viewer discretion” warning, a man can be seen walking behind a dog at a concrete pool and yelling “out, out, out ... in the grass” several times and kicking the dog in its right hip at least once before the dog and the man went out of range. It is not clear about the source of the video. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office appreciates the public’s assistance in bringing this incident to our attention. A road rage incident that escalated into a four-vehicle crash at a major Port St. Lucie intersection has left multiple people hospitalized and one man arrested. The crash occurred Wednesday evening around 6:45 p.m. at the intersection of South U.S. Highway 1 and SE Lyngate Drive/SE Tiffany Avenue, according to Port St. Police say Kevin Lonergan, 54, was driving a black Ford Super Duty pickup truck and pursuing a red Harley-Davidson motorcycle northbound on U.S. Highway 1 during an ongoing road rage incident. Witness statements and dash-camera footage revealed the motorcycle rider entered the intersection against a red traffic signal and collided with a black Chevrolet Silverado, ejecting the rider from the bike. Lonergan's pickup truck then also ran the red light, struck the motorcycle rider who was on the ground, and collided head-on with a blue Toyota RAV4. The 31-year-old motorcycle rider suffered serious injuries, including a brain bleed and facial fractures. He lost consciousness following the crash and remains hospitalized in stable condition at Lawnwood Medical Center. Two occupants of the RAV4 were also transported to Lawnwood Medical Center, while the driver of the Silverado was taken to St. Police arrested Lonergan on two counts of reckless driving causing serious bodily injury and one count of reckless driving causing injury. The intersection was shut down until 2 a.m.

The Kings Landing development in Fort Pierce is facing another delay. WATCH BELOW: 'It's taking so long,' Funky Cuda owner Jon Nolli tells WPTV's St. Lucie County reporter Tyler Hatfield Live Oak Development, the secondary developer on the project, told commissioners they’re short said they are $15 million short of the $60 million needed to complete the Marriott hotel and restaurant portion of the project — and city commissioners are divided on what to do next. Live Oak Development, the secondary developer on the project, told commissioners the $15 million shortfall is due in part to rising construction costs. “We have seen construction costs continue to balloon, “ said CEO Paul Bertozzi. “We've had those challenges across multiple industries but that is a portion of the cause of the delta that is being created." City leaders said developers initially asked the city to cover the gap through a loan or grant. Commissioner Michael Broderick said that request was denied. "Unfortunately, the city does not have $15 million. Nor would I advocate the city investing $15 million into a private enterprise,” said Broderick. Live Oak Development is now asking for 180 days to find the money through private sources. Bertozzi told commissioners the outreach has already begun. "We're already in the process of reaching out to participating parties,” said Bertozzi. "We're looking at friends and families and investment and private equity verses institutional investors." But commissioners are debating about the city reclaiming the property. Broderick said he believes trying to reclaim the property through legal action would be expensive and time-consuming. "Clawing the property back through reverter clauses is going to be litigation for years and a ton of money,” said Broderick. He said he would rather give developers the time they are asking for. "What are we going to lose by 180 days? That's the question I would ask,” said Broderick. “What are we going to lose? It's just time." Commissioner Chris Dzadovsky said he does not want to wait. "I think it's time to as they say, cut bait and move on," he said. Jon Nolli, owner of Funky Cuda in Fort Pierce, said he has been waiting on the development and is ready for it to be finished. "It's been taking some time,” said Nolli. Nolli said the completed project would benefit the surrounding area. He said he even has plans to open businesses inside Kings Landing — but the delays are wearing on him. "I've got a couple deposits on the commercial side. I was looking to a beer garden, and a deli, and I mean it's taking so long that I don't even know the trends have changed,” said Nolli WPTV reached out to Live Oak Development and still working on a response. The city commission has scheduled a special meeting on September 14 to discuss next steps.

A 76-year-old woman was arrested after police said she used barcode stickers and tags she brought into the store with her to pay deeply reduced prices for merchandise at a Target store in Port St. Officers responded Tuesday, August 4 to the Target at Tradition store, 10720 SW Village Parkway after store loss-prevention employees detained Joan McKeon, according to the Port St. Investigators said McKeon entered the store carrying barcode stickers and barcode tags for lower-priced products. She allegedly placed or scanned those barcodes at self-checkout instead of using the barcodes attached to the merchandise she selected. During the most recent incident, police said an item priced at $32.99 was scanned as a $1.29 purchase. Officers searching McKeon’s purse found 28 barcode stickers, some bearing the names of other retailers, including TJ Maxx, Publix and Burlington, police said. Investigators planned to contact those businesses as part of the continuing investigation. "Listen, times clearly are hard for people in America. Healthcare is high, food is high so people are doing anything that they can to make ends meet," said Noesha Jennings, a shopper from Port St. "Me personally I think it's pretty clever but we are a growing city and we can't be having those things going on around here, man," said Stephon Jennings, a shopper from Port St. See also: No Powerball jackpot winner; prize climbs to estimated $856 Million Target loss-prevention employees told officers the incident was not isolated. According to the arrest report, a Target Loss Prevention Manager at that store told police this was the twelfth retail theft McKeon committed at that store, dating back to September 2025. McKeon is charged with fraud-swindle-obtain property under $20,000. "You don't rip anybody off like that. I'm very shocked how the world's turning out. So it's very disappointing to hear," said Kimise Volpe, a shopper from Palm Beach Gardens. We reached McKeon by phone Friday. She said she did commit the crime and she did not know why she did it. She also said she was not thinking clearly and she said I know I was wrong. Target's media relations office did not respond to an e-mail seeking comment.

Former Tennessee Agriculture Commissioner Charlie Hatcher defeated U.S. Andy Ogles in a Republican primary Thursday for a significantly reshaped congressional district — marking a rare rejection of a candidate endorsed by President Donald Trump.Voters also picked a pair of Memphis-area lawmakers to square off in another vastly reconfigured U.S. Brent Taylor will face Democratic state Rep. Justin Pearson, who gained national prominence when he was expelled from the Tennessee House for protesting in support of gun control measures and then reelected by voters.The primaries provided the first test of a new U.S. House map that was redrawn in May by Republican state lawmakers after the U.S. Supreme Court weakened federal Voting Rights Act protections for minorities. Trump cheered along the redistricting as part of a broader national plan to try to hold on to a slim House majority in the midterm elections.RELATED STORY | Abdul El-Sayed defeats Haley Stevens in Michigan's Democratic primary for US SenateRepublicans already hold eight of the state’s nine congressional seats and will be going for a clean sweep of the districts in November.The previously compact 9th Congressional District, based in Memphis, had a majority Black population and is represented by a Democrat. But it was cracked apart by Republicans this year, causing a ripple of changes that also reconfigured Ogles’ 5th District.A Trump-endorsed candidate is defeatedOgles, a member of the conservative Freedom Caucus, had faced controversies related to his campaign finances and his resume, among other things. But Trump gave him an early endorsement last fall — and praised him on Election Day as “a Conservative Warrior” — as Ogles sought a third term.Ogles capitalized on a previous redistricting in the 2022 elections, winning a formerly Democratic-held seat that was reshaped to Republicans’ advantage by splitting the Nashville area among three districts.The new 5th District stretches from Ogles’ base in central Tennessee to the northwest corner of the state before snaking south along the Mississippi River to Memphis — with 82% of its voters new, according to an Associated Press estimate.Although he lacked Trump’s endorsement, Hatcher was backed by Republican Gov. Bill Lee, under whom he served for seven years. Hatcher campaigned as pro-Trump while emphasizing his farming background.“The message resonated, and the message was: Work like a farmer, get things done and serve others,” Hatcher told the AP after winning the primary.Ogles' campaign declined to comment.Ogles' controversies have included the FBI seizing his cellphone in 2024 as part of an investigation into his campaign finance reporting. The Justice Department recently agreed to return the device, signaling that it was abandoning the probe, which began under the Biden administration.RELATED STORY | Troy Jackson wins Democratic nomination in critical Maine Senate raceIn 2023, Ogles acknowledged that he had graduated with a liberal studies degree from Middle Tennessee State University, saying he was “mistaken” for previously describing it as an international relations degree.Columbia Mayor Chaz Molder won the Democratic primary in the 5th District.Pearson and Taylor to face off in revamped Memphis districtThe new 9th District stretches about 200 miles (320 kilometers) east from Memphis across rural areas before reaching north toward Nashville. It previously favored Democrats but now tilts Republican, with 71% of voters new to the district, according to an AP estimate.After the redistricting, longtime Democratic Rep. Steve Cohen announced that he would no longer seek reelection.Pearson noted to supporters Thursday night that it was 61 years ago to the day that the Voting Rights Act was signed. He said the Supreme Court and Tennessee lawmakers have effectively undone portions of it, leading to the redrawing of the formerly majority-Black district.“The political dilution and degradation of our rights is happening,” Pearson said. But he added: “We’re one step closer to Washington, D.C.”Taylor said in a statement to supporters that “Pearson is the face of the extreme left in this race — the same activist who has repeatedly put chaos over order.”While Pearson opposed Trump’s deployment of National Guard troops to address crime in Memphis last year, Taylor joined other Republicans in supporting it, calling it “an investment.”Taylor also sponsored a 2024 law that required law enforcement agencies to communicate with federal immigration authorities if they discover people are in the country illegally.Memphis voters voice dismay over redistrictingFor decades Memphis, the most populous city in Shelby County, formed the base of its own congressional district. Now the county is split among three districts that extend outward like spokes into rural areas.Lonzo Taylor, a retired postal worker and military veteran, said Black voters like himself have had their voices diluted.“We only had one district in the whole state of Tennessee, and you don’t even want that to be fair? It’s just terrible,” said Taylor, 72. “I love this state, but I am very disappointed in our governor,” who called lawmakers into a special session for the redistricting.Terrice Thomas, 45, an educator who votes for Democrats, had to learn a lot more about the candidates when she got switched from District 9 to District 8. She is concerned Memphis constituents could get overlooked.“Is everybody going to have an equal say on what’s happening in their communities or even the people that you’re voting for?” Thomas said. “Are they going to really take into account the different areas and what makes us unique?”Garrett wins Republican primary for open seat in the 6th DistrictRepublican U.S. John Rose opted not to seek reelection in the 6th to run for governor instead. That created a contentious primary for the GOP-leaning district, which stretches east from Nashville.State Rep. Johnny Garrett won a Republican contest that included Rose’s recent chief of staff, former U.S. Mike Croley won a five-way Democratic primary.Republican voters pick Blackburn for governorU.S. Marsha Blackburn defeated Rose in the GOP primary to succeed Gov. Lee, who is barred by term limits from seeking reelection. Memphis City Council member Jerri Green won for the Democrats.Republicans have held the governor's office since 2011 and won every U.S. Senate election since 1994.Sen. Bill Hagerty won the Republican primary without opposition and will face Marquita Bradshaw, who won the Democratic nomination, in November.

Indian River County firefighter-paramedic Geoffrey Lang was honored Tuesday morning at a memorial service held at The Community Church in Vero Beach, following his unexpected death last month. The room was filled with Lang's friends, family, and colleagues, while dozens of community members showed their support through the church’s livestream of the event. Bagpipes led the procession, followed by a prayer, setting the tone for a service focused on remembering Lang's life of service. Speakers described Lang as someone who dedicated himself to his community, sharing stories of his service, compassion, and the lasting difference he made in the lives of many. When there was a need, he met and exceeded, and throughout his career, as having a great honor of served alongside of him, he answered those calls with courage," said Dustin Hawkins, chaplain and firefighter with Indian River County Fire. Firefighters quickly extinguished a boat fire Wednesday afternoon at a home in Stuart, preventing the flames from spreading, officials said. According to Martin County Fire Rescue , crews responded just before 3 p.m. to the 1600 block of Northwest Fork Road after reports of a boat on fire. When firefighters arrived, they found thick black smoke billowing from a small boat sitting on a lift at a residential dock. Crews located the nearest fire hydrant and quickly knocked down the flames before the fire could spread. No injuries were reported, and no one was taken to a hospital. See also: Deputies fatally shoot 18-year-old during violent confrontation with father, PBSO says Firefighters from Stuart Fire Rescue also responded to the scene. The cause of the fire remains under investigation. The State Fire Marshal has been notified and will determine what sparked the blaze.

The Humane Society of the Treasure Coast is asking for donations, foster homes, adopters, and help from rescue organizations after taking in more than 100 animals from what the Martin County sheriff described as the worst animal hoarding case in the county’s history. "We need adopters and fosters. Anyone that's willing to adopt and has been thinking about getting a pet, the time is now," said Sarah Fisher, spokesperson, Humane Society of the Treasure Coast. Employees and volunteers have been working around the clock to care for the animals while the Palm City shelter continues its regular operations. A total of 108 animals were brought to the humane society for medical treatment and care after 77-year-old Gail Giustino was arrested July 20. Since then, 10 cats and 17 dogs from the case have been adopted, while five microchipped cats have been reunited with their owners. "I think she thought she was doing a good thing. She thought she was rescuing cats from the outdoors and unfortunately, she was way in over her head, couldn't care for it and ended up in a terrible situation," Fisher said. The shelter’s workload has continued to grow. Following the initial case, the Martin County Sheriff’s Office reportedly received an influx of requests for animal welfare checks. Last week, the humane society took in 26 cats from another situation and five dogs from a separate case. We expect more animals in the coming weeks due to the calls that have come in requesting animal welfare checks and the initial information we are receiving from Animal Services, which is following up on these calls, Humane Society Director of Operations Lori Tucker said. Many calls have been cleared, but there are cases that are requiring further follow-up. The organization said monetary donations are its greatest immediate need because of the continuing costs of medical care, food and housing while the animals await placement. Donations may be made through the shelter’s emergency medical fund. The humane society is also urging residents to adopt or foster animals already in its care. Officials said the influx doubled the shelter’s animal population even as normal admissions and services continued. Adopting or fostering a dog, cat, rabbit or guinea pig would free space for rescued animals still receiving treatment and preparing for adoption. See also: Road rage ends in violent 4-vehicle crash on U.S. Lucie man arrested We are still in need of people to adopt working cats, that is, cats that are suitable for safe outdoor living, Tucker said. We also are in desperate need of adopters and rescue groups willing to help take some of our animals. The shelter is offering a Name Your Price adoption special until further notice. Short- and long-term foster opportunities are also available. Information about adoptable animals is available at hstc1.org/Adopt , and foster information is available at hstc1.org/foster . Prospective adopters may call 772-223-8822 . Foster inquiries may be sent to catfoster@hstc1.org or dogfoster@hstc1.org , or made by calling 772-600-3220 . The Humane Society will also offer public microchipping services from 10 a.m. Registration is available at hstc1.org/Clinic . The booming market for Pokémon cards is creating new opportunities for collectors, but Martin County deputies say it is also drawing scammers who are selling counterfeits through online marketplaces. The Martin County Sheriff’s Office is investigating two separate cases involving fake Pokémon cards after victims reported losing a combined $1,200 in deals arranged through Facebook Marketplace. In the first case, deputies said a collector met a seller at a local gas station in Hobe Sound to trade nine Pokémon cards and cash. Investigators said the seller rushed through the transaction and left before the cards could be inspected. Once home, the victim realized the cards were counterfeit, and the seller blocked him online. Ten days later, deputies said another collector reported a similar experience in Stuart. That victim traded collectible Pokémon card boxes and sent money through Zelle in exchange for two cards that were later determined to be fake. Patrick Sutherland, who organizes Peetry's Card Show from the Treasure Coast to South Florida, said the trading card market has surged in value. The market for even specifically just Pokémon or trading cards in general, it is the most lucrative market there is, Sutherland said. Sutherland said the rising value often comes down to nostalgia and scarcity. Once they're out of their print run, they are never recycled back in, he said. He said authentic cards often have specific textures, coloring and holographic features that can be difficult to counterfeit. If you rub your finger across it you can feel texture, Sutherland said. He also pointed to details on a Pokémon card box, similar to the ones involved in one of the scams, that can help collectors identify counterfeit products. These are intentionally made not to be symmetrical. If you can see this end is higher than this one, Sutherland said. Sutherland urged buyers to slow down and inspect items before completing a deal, warning that rushed transactions can be costly. Because the last thing we ever want, ever, ever, ever is for our kids. Our future collectors to ever incur any of these problems, he said. Sutherland said the safest place to buy, sell, or trade collectibles is at a card show, where experienced collectors and vendors can help spot counterfeits. Meanwhile, Martin County deputies said they are still working to identify the suspects in both fraud cases.

Two sheriff's deputies shot and killed an 18-year-old man who was attacking his father with a butcher knife during a welfare check Wednesday night, according to the sheriff.WATCH: What we know so far about the deputy-involved shootingThe incident began when the suspect's mother called authorities, telling them she believed her son had taken something and was acting strangely.Two deputies arrived at the home located at the 2900 block of Hope Valley Street at around 8:15 p.m. The deputies entered through the front door, where they found the father and son in a violent struggle over a butcher knife with an approximately 5-inch blade.One deputy deployed a taser, which was ineffective. Deputies also gave verbal commands ordering the suspect to drop the knife. The suspect did not comply with either measure.The sheriff said the suspect had the father pinned to the ground in a stabbing position when the second deputy fired 3 shots, striking and incapacitating the suspect. The entire encounter lasted approximately 90 seconds.The 18-year-old was taken to a local hospital where he died from his injuries.The father was taken to a hospital with a superficial wound to his hands. Authorities have not yet determined whether the injury was caused by the knife or shrapnel from the rounds fired by the deputy.The sheriff said the deputies likely saved the father's life."It was obvious that this kid — actually he's not a kid, he's 18 — was going to stab this father, so the deputies took the action that they had to take to disable the son," the sheriff said. "For all intents and purposes, the deputies probably saved the dad's life because this was a very violent struggle over this knife, and they did what they had to do."The suspect's mother told dispatchers her son had a history of mental illness and had been acting irrationally prior to the call. The sheriff said the suspect had no prior contact with the sheriff's office outside of a mental health-related incident in 2025.The Florida Department of Law Enforcement and the state attorney's office are investigating the shooting. The state attorney will determine whether the deputies acted properly.Both deputies have been placed on administrative leave, which the sheriff described as standard policy regardless of the circumstances of a use-of-force incident."It doesn't indicate that they did anything wrong at all," the sheriff said.The Florida Department of Law Enforcement, the Palm Beach County State Attorney’s Office and PBSO’s Violent Crimes Division are actively investigating the incident.The suspect's name has not been released under Marsy's Law.

Palm Beach County schools face declining enrollment affecting budget, teacher pay and staffing as voters prepare for November property tax referendum.WATCH BELOW: 'The budget and enrollment go together in lock step,' Superintendent Mike Burke tells WPTV's Joel LopezAs Palm Beach County students return to classrooms Monday, the School District of Palm Beach County confronts a mounting enrollment crisis that is impacting the budget by $100 million, according to Superintendent Mike Burke. The district faces another potential decline of 2,900 students this year while preparing for a critical November referendum that could determine funding for teacher raises and school safety programs.The financial impact of declining enrollment has become increasingly severe for Palm Beach County schools. Last year's loss of approximately 7,000 students, with the nearly 3,000 loss this year translates directly into a $100 million budget reduction, Burke told WPTV."The budget and enrollment go together in lock step," Burke said, explaining how state funding formulas tie district revenue directly to student counts. "We are funded on a per student basis and when the enrollment goes down, the money goes down."This year's projected decline of 2,900 additional students threatens to compound existing financial pressures, affecting everything from teacher compensation to program offerings.District leaders point to the upcoming property tax referendum as a potential solution to mounting budget challenges. The November ballot measure would fund school choice programs, teacher raises, and enhanced safety initiatives across Palm Beach County schools."Each year we hope to add more programs," Burke said, referring to school choice options that allow students to attend schools outside their assigned zones.The referendum funding has already supported visible improvements in campus security, according to School Police Chief Sarah Mooney. Tax dollars have funded updated technology, emergency devices, and metal detectors across district schools.“We're really fortunate to be in Palm Beach County, because we enjoyed the support of our local voters,” Burke said.Burke pointed to the district’s voter-approved property tax referendum, first introduced in 2018, as a key reason Palm Beach County has been able to remain competitive when it comes to teacher pay and school programs.“It was actually my recommendation as CFO that we go to the voters for a one mil property tax Levy or allow us to pay our teachers more so that's been in place,” Burke said. “It's been approved by voters twice by law we have to go back every four years so it's time to go back to the voters.”The referendum will once again appear before voters in November. According to Burke, half of the funding generated from the levy goes directly toward teacher salaries.“Half of that levy goes straight to teacher pay and we call it referendum supplements,” Burke explained.He said teachers receive additional pay based on experience.“After one year their salary goes up $1,000 if they have 5 to 9 years additional $5,000 added to their base salary and then 10 more years of experience $10,000,” Burke said. Our teachers in Palm Beach County are some of the best paid in the state and better paid in our surrounding counties in South Florida.”Even with financial concerns, Burke says the district recently reached an agreement with the CTA at the end of July on teacher raises tied to new state funding that was passed.“I'm pleased report that we have settled,” Burke said. “The state has provided about $10 million for us through the states Teacher salary increase allocation.”Burke said state lawmakers placed strict guidelines on how those funds could be distributed limiting it to classroom teachers with 10 more years of experience teaching in Florida.“We made that offer to classroom teachers, but counselors, media specialist, and we had to put some local money behind that but we were able to offer 2.187% for members of the Teacher group to have 10 more years experience.Metal detectors installed with referendum funding have already intercepted weapons on campus, Mooney confirmed. Two guns were detected after school hours began — one carried by a visitor and another by a student — though neither incident posed an active threat to school safety."The most important thing we have is the people on our campuses," Mooney said, emphasizing how funding improvements enhance overall school security.Union negotiations for additional teacher raises face uncertainty as enrollment numbers continue declining. Burke acknowledged that future compensation discussions depend heavily on stabilizing student enrollment and securing referendum funding."The union wants to come back to the table and continue to negotiate for more, and we're really going to have to see how things go with our enrollment," Burke explained.The district has already lost 19 Haitian staff members following the expiration of Temporary Protected Status protections, raising concerns about potential student departures from Haitian families in Palm Beach County.District officials are monitoring enrollment impacts tied to federal immigration policy changes that may prompt additional families to leave the area.Facing continued enrollment pressure, Palm Beach County schools have created a dedicated enrollment office and expanded marketing efforts to attract students from outside the county.The recruitment strategy represents a significant shift as the district competes with neighboring school systems and private school options for students in South Florida's competitive education market.Burke emphasized that district priorities for the new school year include improving early literacy outcomes and expanding school choice programs, contingent on voter approval of the November referendum.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. The Martin County Sheriff’s Office is reporting a rise in DUI arrests, including an increase in incidents occurring during the day. Body camera footage from Wednesday shows deputies responding to a single-vehicle crash on I-95 near Martin Highway. Deputies said an intoxicated driver collided with a guardrail, abandoned the wrecked car in the center lane of the interstate, and fled the scene. The driver was taken into custody and faces several charges, including DUI, possession of heroin, and driving without a license. Sheriff John Budensiek said the county recorded five DUI arrests as of Thursday morning. Among the incidents was a wrong-way driver on Kanner Highway, a driver on A1A who hit a railroad crossing at high speed and rolled her car, and another driver with no license or insurance. "And then while we are getting ready to talk to you today yet again, we had another DUI in Hobe Sound: a driver slumped over the wheel, so our DUI units went down there, and he's sitting in our jail right now," Budensiek said. According to the sheriff’s office, DUI charges have increased every year since 2022, and this year is currently on pace to continue the trend. The sheriff’s office reported the following DUI arrest numbers: 2022 -- 506 DUI charges 2023 -- 532 DUI charges 2024 -- 537 DUI charges 2025 -- 540 DUI charges 2026 -- 349 (year-to-date) "All the information we're putting out there, you would think that DUI is becoming a thing of the past, but they're not — we're seeing more and more of them, and lately we're seeing more daytime DUIs, which is extremely concerning," Budensiek said. He said the aggressive driving unit will continue monitoring roadways day and night to combat impaired and dangerous drivers. "So, I would suggest, as sheriff, if you intend to drink at all, catch you a rideshare to wherever you are going to go drinking and catch it back home," Budensiek said. He also credited members of the public who call and report suspicious activity. After that visit, the owner put up a fence.Todd said she also stopped letting the dogs outside, but he can still hear them barking in the house. For Todd, what's out of sight is not out of mind — let alone out of sound or smell."It's just sad. Lucie County Sheriff's Office Patrol Operations Bureau has led to the arrest of a suspect connected to a series of burglaries in the St. Lucie Village area, deputies said.On Wednesday deputies responded to the 2900 block of North Indian River Drive after receiving a report of a suspicious person. Upon arrival, deputies located Daniel Eugene Holmes, 42, who was going through trash near the roadway. Deputies said they also observed a bicycle in Holmes' possession with fishing equipment attached to it.During their investigation, deputies determined Holmes matched the description of a person of interest developed during an ongoing burglary investigation in St. Through additional investigative efforts, deputies established probable cause linking Holmes to other reported crimes in the area, deputies said.Holmes was arrested on charges of two counts of burglary of a conveyance, and loitering and prowling."This case highlights the value of proactive patrol and the attention to detail our deputies demonstrate every day," Sheriff Richard Del Toro said in a post to Facebook. "What began as a call about suspicious activity quickly developed into an investigation that solved multiple crimes and removed a repeat offender from our community. We remain committed to aggressively investigating property crimes and holding those responsible accountable."Deputies said the investigation remains active and additional information will be provided as appropriate.

The Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission, and its partners, announced the results and winners of the 2026 Florida Python Challenge on Wednesday.A total of 907 participants from 30 states, Canada and Vietnam collectively removed 280 invasive Burmese pythons from South Florida during the 10-day competition.Tom Rahill won the Ultimate Grand Prize of $10,000 after removing 96 Burmese pythons from Everglades National Park. Rahm Levinson removed the longest python of the competition, a 16-foot, 5-inch snake, also from Everglades National Park.A highlight of this year's event was the return of Everglades National Park as a partner and one of eight official competition locations."The number of invasive pythons removed from the Everglades during the 2026 Florida Python Challenge is a major victory for Florida's native wildlife and a testament to what can be accomplished through strong partnerships and public participation," FWC Chairman Rodney Barreto said in a news release.The 2026 Florida Python Challenge was hosted by the FWC and the South Florida Water Management District, in close partnership with the National Park Service and the Fish & Wildlife Foundation of Florida."Congratulations to the 2026 winners of the Florida Python Challenge! Removing Burmese pythons from this ecosystem is critical to the survival of the native species that call this area home," South Florida Water Management District Governing Board Member "Alligator Ron" Bergeron said in the news release.FWC said the 10-day event is designed to raise awareness about invasive species and engage the public in Everglades conservation through the removal of invasive Burmese pythons.Ultimate Grand Prize — Awarded to the participant who removes the most pythons.$10,000 — Tom Rahill — 96 pythonsProfessionalMost Pythons Prize — $2,500 — Christina Kraus — 36 pythonsMost Pythons Runner-Up Prize — $1,500 — Taylor Stanberry — 34 pythonsLongest Python Prize — $1,000 — Rahm Levinson — 16 feet, 5 inchesNoviceMost Pythons Prize — $2,500 — Bart Shreve — 9 pythonsMost Pythons Runner-Up Prize — $1,500 — Michael Marousky — 4 pythonsLongest Python Prize — $1,000 — Vincent Poole — 8 feet, 2 inchesMilitary — Active Duty and VeteranMost Pythons Prize — $2,500 — Stephen Payton, U.S. Army — 3 pythonsMost Pythons Runner-Up Prize — $1,500 — Jonathan Miller, U.S. Air Force — 2 pythonsLongest Python Prize — $1,000 — Jeffery "Heath" Roser, U.S. Army — 8 feet, 7 inchesThis story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Beachgoers at Jupiter's Carlin Park have been waiting years for a new restaurant to fill the space left behind by the Lazy Loggerhead Cafe, which closed in 2022.WATCH BELOW: 'This is my mom and dad's favorite restaurant for years,' Greg Ryerson tells WPTV's Jon ShainmanThe Ryerson family of Wellington stopped to look at the blue building at the top of a small rise during a recent visit to the park."This is my mom and dad's favorite restaurant for years, and they were really disappointed when it closed," Greg Ryerson said.A coming soon sign continues to fade from the elements. A road rage incident that escalated into a four-vehicle crash at a major Port St. Lucie intersection has left multiple people hospitalized and one man arrested.The crash occurred Wednesday evening around 6:45 p.m. at the intersection of South U.S. Highway 1 and SE Lyngate Drive/SE Tiffany Avenue, according to Port St. Lucie police.Police say Kevin Lonergan, 54, was driving a black Ford Super Duty pickup truck and pursuing a red Harley-Davidson motorcycle northbound on U.S. Highway 1 during an ongoing road rage incident.Witness statements and dash-camera footage revealed the motorcycle rider entered the intersection against a red traffic signal and collided with a black Chevrolet Silverado, ejecting the rider from the bike. Lonergan's pickup truck then also ran the red light, struck the motorcycle rider who was on the ground, and collided head-on with a blue Toyota RAV4.The 31-year-old motorcycle rider suffered serious injuries, including a brain bleed and facial fractures. He lost consciousness following the crash and remains hospitalized in stable condition at Lawnwood Medical Center. Two occupants of the RAV4 were also transported to Lawnwood Medical Center, while the driver of the Silverado was taken to St. Police arrested Lonergan on two counts of reckless driving causing serious bodily injury and one count of reckless driving causing injury.The intersection was shut down until 2 a.m.

A 76-year-old woman was arrested after police said she used counterfeit barcode stickers to pay deeply reduced prices for merchandise at a Target store in Port St. Officers responded Tuesday to the Target in Tradition after store loss-prevention employees detained Joan McKeon, according to the Port St. Investigators said McKeon entered the store carrying barcode stickers for lower-priced products. She allegedly placed or scanned those barcodes at self-checkout instead of using the barcodes attached to the merchandise she selected. During the most recent incident, police said an item priced at $32.99 was scanned as a $1.29 purchase. Officers searching McKeon’s purse found 28 barcode stickers, some bearing the names of other retailers, including TJ Maxx, Publix and Burlington, police said. Investigators planned to contact those businesses as part of the continuing investigation. As Florida students head back to school, drivers should brush up on school zone safety rules to protect kids and avoid costly penalties. WATCH: Reminders for drivers as students head back to schoolMost urban school zones drop to 20 mph, with some areas requiring speeds as low as 15 mph. These reduced limits are active from 30 minutes before school starts until 30 minutes after dismissal. Drivers will know when zones are active by watching for flashing yellow lights or permanent signs.Speed cameras automatically issue $100 tickets to drivers caught exceeding limits by 10 mph or more, and all handheld devices are completely banned in active school zones. Breaking these rules can result in doubled fines, points on your driver's license, and higher insurance premiums. The bottom line: slow down, put the phone away, and stay alert in school zones.

VERO BEACH — Youth Guidance received a $7,500 grant from the TD Charitable Foundation to expand academic enrichment opportunities for children and teens across Indian River County. The funding supported 93 students with limited resources through tutoring by certified teachers, book clubs, and enrichment activities, including cooking, woodworking, teen leadership, and more. Youth Guidance reported that 96% of students in its math intervention group improved their assessment scores by at least 20% between pre- and post-testing. All students participating in the organization’s summer literacy intervention group increased their oral reading fluency, while 93% of students who attended Youth Guidance for at least 40 hours during the spring 2026 semester maintained a school attendance rate of 90% or higher. Kyrstyn’s progress illustrates the effect of the academic support, according to Youth Guidance. When she joined the organization’s reading intervention program last summer, she struggled with confidence in her reading ability. Kyrstyn’s progress shows the impact of academic support. When she first joined Youth Guidance’s reading intervention program last summer, she struggled with reading confidence. With assistance from Youth Guidance’s certified teachers and the Read Naturally program, her reading fluency increased by 62%, from 58 to 94 words per minute. She has since reached grade-level proficiency and takes pride in meeting her daily reading goals. The grant helped young people overcome challenges, develop strong academic foundations, and gain the skills and supportive relationships that prepare them for lifelong success. The partnership between Youth Guidance, TD Bank and the TD Charitable Foundation supports local students through academic enrichment, encouragement and opportunities designed to help them succeed. Founded in 1973, Youth Guidance serves Indian River County youth through mentoring relationships designed to build trust, self-esteem and pathways toward academic and career success. Its programs include the Pathways Afterschool Program, Summer Enrichment Program and Pre-Apprenticeship Program. A fourth person has been arrested in connection with the death of a 3-month-old baby who allegedly died from severe dehydration and malnutrition. Lucie County Sheriff's Office announced Tuesday that the child's biological father, 45-year-old Jason Gunter, was taken into custody by the United States Marshals Service at his home in Mechanicsville, Virginia. Detectives had obtained an arrest warrant for Gunter in connection with the ongoing investigation into the child's death. He has been charged with felony child neglect causing great harm and is awaiting extradition to St. The arrest comes after three others were previously charged in the case: the child's mother, 27-year-old Nicole Maxwell; the child's grandfather, Robert Maxwell; and Robert Maxwell's girlfriend, 38-year-old Vikki Koon. See also: Body found in ocean off Boca Raton coast, investigation underway All three were charged with aggravated manslaughter of a child and aggravated child abuse. Each was held on a $1.5 million bond. Investigation Began After Baby Was Brought to Hospital The investigation began on Aug. 20, 2025, when Koon and Robert Maxwell brought 3-month-old Robert Gunter to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital in Fort Pierce. Medical staff immediately observed signs that the infant had been dead for some time, including rigor mortis, fixed pupils and skin discoloration. He was pronounced dead at 11:35 a.m. after resuscitation efforts failed. Detectives assigned to the case conducted interviews with family members at the hospital before serving search warrants and beginning what would become a months-long investigation. Caregivers Allegedly Noticed Warning Signs According to a 37-page arrest affidavit, the infant had been primarily living with Koon and Robert Maxwell after Gunter moved to Virginia. During interviews, detectives learned caregivers had noticed numerous warning signs in the days leading up to the child's death. Investigators say Koon admitted the baby was often fed only a few times a day and claimed he sometimes drank as little as two bottles daily. She told detectives she noticed the child was becoming increasingly thin, pale and lethargic. She also described frequent vomiting, excessive sleeping and a decrease in wet diapers. Despite those concerns, detectives say no one sought emergency medical treatment. Text messages obtained during the investigation showed family members repeatedly warning both parents that something was wrong. 12, 2025, messages sent to Nicole Maxwell stated, "The baby's got nothing to eat. I don't know what to give him." Days later, additional messages warned that the baby was sick, covered in marks and sleeping constantly. Other messages urged Gunter to come to Florida because something was wrong with the infant. According to detectives, neither parent took action that resulted in immediate medical care for the child. Search Warrant Revealed Conditions Inside Home When investigators executed a search warrant at the mobile home on Silverstream Circle where the baby had been staying, they documented what they described as an "extreme environmental hazard." The affidavit details a residence filled with clutter, moldy food, exposed electrical wiring, live rodents and widespread cockroach infestations. Detectives reported finding baby bottles containing curdled milk and observed insects crawling in and around a collapsed playpen. Vomit-like substances were also found on a couch and nearby flooring. Crime scene investigators noted the home appeared extremely dirty and poorly maintained, with evidence suggesting the playpen was not actively being used by the infant despite statements from caregivers. Autopsy Findings Led to Homicide Ruling An autopsy later revealed the extent of the infant's condition. According to the Medical Examiner's Office, Robert Gunter weighed 11 pounds, 12 ounces at a pediatric appointment on July 24, 2025. Less than a month later, at the time of his death, he weighed only 9 pounds, 3.5 ounces, placing him below the first percentile for children his age. The autopsy found evidence of severe dehydration and malnutrition, including poor skin elasticity, loss of body fat, sunken features, elevated sodium levels, organ damage and an absence of food contents in the stomach and upper intestinal tract. Examiners also documented numerous lesions and insect bites across the infant's body. The Medical Examiner ultimately determined the child died from dehydration and malnutrition and classified the manner of death as homicide, writing that the infant was dependent on caregivers for nutrition and hydration and that the failure to provide those necessities directly caused his death. Father's Role Under Scrutiny Investigators say Gunter was aware of concerns about the child's condition. The criminal complaint states that messages sent to Gunter warned that the baby had marks on his body, was sleeping excessively and appeared ill. Detectives also recovered messages discussing food shortages and concerns the infant was not being properly cared for. Despite those warnings, investigators allege Gunter did not return to Florida, seek immediate intervention or contact emergency services. A separate text message recovered from his phone stated: "The baby is starving." Detectives included that message among evidence supporting criminal charges. Sheriff's officials said the investigation remains active as the case moves through the court system. Meanwhile, two other children connected to the home were placed in a safe environment with assistance from the Florida Department of Children and Families.

Lucie Wednesday released the emotional 911 call from a neighbor after a weekend murder-suicide at a home on Southeast Oxmoor Terrace. I think my neighbor was shot," the caller said during the 911 call. Authorities identified the victim as 50-year-old Elizabeth Ortega, a communications officer for the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office. Investigators believe Ortega was shot and killed by her longtime boyfriend, 50-year-old Ralph Varela Jr., who then shot and killed himself. According to police, Ortega had recently ended their 30-year relationship, but the two were still living together while Varela searched for a new place to live. The neighbor who called 911 said she had been in her backyard with her children when they heard the gunshots. "You heard the gunshot?" the dispatcher asked. There was, like, six of them. And I thought it was maybe on the other side of the street because we do have people that shoot off fireworks all the time. But this one made my house rattle," the caller said. When asked if she saw the gun, the caller responded, "No. We heard it a couple of minutes ago, and I made my kids come inside because it sounded really, really close." The caller said she did not know her neighbors' names but mentioned she often heard them yelling. "Her and her husband were fighting?" the dispatcher asked. "I don't know if they're fighting. They're just always cursing at each other," the caller said. Police arrived at the scene and began their investigation, which they are calling a murder-suicide. The debate over constructing massive artificial intelligence data centers is intensifying across South Florida ahead of the August primary elections, as proposals like the controversial "Project Tango" in Palm Beach County draw both interest and opposition. While Florida currently has no hyperscale AI centers, WPTV's Michael Hoffman looked into communities where they do operate, revealing a consistent pattern of resident complaints about noise and environmental impacts, issues one local expert calls "legitimate concerns."The conversation is becoming a central issue for voters as multiple municipalities in WPTV's five-county viewing area explore or enact moratoriums on data center construction. Developers are seeking to bring the powerful technology hubs to the state, but they face growing pushback from communities worried about the local impact.WATCH WPTV'S COVERAGE BELOW:In Dowagiac, Michigan, the soundtrack of daily life has changed. Residents living near a large-scale data center report a constant, industrial hum from cooling fans that operate 24 hours a day, 365 days a year."The fan noise just exceeds such a level to where we can't even enjoy being outside for more than a few minutes without either of us getting a headache," resident Lindy Valenzuela told WXYZ.This experience is not unique. Across the country, the issue has united residents across political party lines who say the quality of life in their neighborhoods has been permanently altered. This is a primary concern for opponents of Project Tango, a data center proposed for western Palm Beach County that has sparked public outcry.While Florida has more than 100 data centers, none are of the hyperscale variety required for modern AI, according to a map of U.S. These larger centers bring unique challenges.Mehran Basiratmand, the Director of Innovations and Programs at Florida Atlantic University and former policy board chairperson for the state’s largest data center, said public sentiment is clear."The noise level, the water consumption, electricity impact to basically surrounding neighborhood is creating a lot of concerns," Basiratmand said. He affirmed that these concerns have a legitimate basis.Basiratmand noted the difficult balance between technological advancement and community responsibility."Our demand is growing. AI is front and center, but I think we need to also be equally responsible for the limited resources that is currently at our disposal," he said.In response to proposals and resident feedback, a number of local governments are taking action. Several cities and counties in the region are either discussing or have already passed temporary bans, or moratoriums, on the approval of new data centers.These measures are designed to give officials time to study the potential impacts and develop zoning and regulatory frameworks that could mitigate issues like noise and resource consumption before developers break ground. The ongoing discussions ensure that the future of AI infrastructure will be a key topic for voters at the polls.

Hundreds of police officers and residents gathered in West Palm Beach for National Night Out, an annual event aimed at strengthening the relationship between law enforcement and the community.West Palm Beach Police Chief Tony Araujo said events like these are essential to building trust and giving residents a direct line to the department.WATCH WPTV'S COVERAGE BELOW:"Once they get to meet you and see what you're about, and they see a face beyond the uniform and the badge, it's important," Araujo said.The event featured games, activities, and backpack giveaways ahead of the upcoming school year, providing support to families across the city. Among those who attended were the Johnsons, who came with their grandmother after losing their home to an alleged arson fire."She doesn't really have the money," Nikka Johnson said. "We're getting school supplies, backpacks and clothes," Johnson said.Araujo said the conversations at events like these help officers understand what residents are dealing with day to day."The recurring issue in most communities that are close to downtown is about the homeless; traffic is always an issue," Araujo said.So far this year, West Palm Beach police have responded to at least 4 shootings across the city, at least 3 hit-and-run fatal crashes, more than 160 burglarized vehicles, and made at least 48 prostitution-related arrests, according to the city website.Mesha Burt attended with her two children and said the event helps her feel more connected to the officers working in the neighborhood."They've been pretty good about patrolling our streets, trying to keep it a little quieter than its been," Burt said.Araujo said community outreach remains a cornerstone of the department's policing strategy."This is just one of many events that we partake in," Araujo said.
