cards.headline: Martin County Sheriff says fence blocks investigation of property where neighbors report 15 to 20 dogs
cards.teaser: Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek said his office is legally blocked from investigating a property where neighbors report hearing and smelling up to 20 dogs after the owner put up a fence.
cards.body:
Thomas Todd and his wife said they believe there are between 15 and 20 dogs on a property next door to their Martin County home. Todd said when the wind picks up, the smell coming from next door is overwhelming, a combination of garbage and animal feces and urine. Todd first raised his concerns at a public event in Jensen Beach in May.

Public records show Martin County Animal Control officers and sheriff's deputies have visited the home at least 11 times since 2020, all related to concerns about the dogs and their owner. One incident report from 2020 describes accounts of as many as 25 dogs inside the home. On multiple occasions, authorities noted feces on the floor and furniture. The owner eventually stopped allowing law enforcement inside and put up a fence.

Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek said the fence has created a legal barrier to further investigation. Budensiek said deputies do not have a lawful way to enter the property unless there is visible evidence of mistreatment. In the most recent incident report from July 2025, the owner told deputies she had 7 dogs, then redacted and said that she only had five dogs.
cards.article_text: Thomas Todd, and his wife, have a neighbor they're worried about — not because of anything they can see, but because of what they can hear and smell. WATCH BELOW: 'She really has legally walled us off from investigating,' Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek tells Chief Investigative Reporter Jamie Ostroff The couple sent video of dogs barking from behind a fence next door at their Martin County home. Todd said he believes there are between 15 and 20 dogs on the property. I visited the Todds' home on a calm, July afternoon. But when the wind picks up, Todd said the smell coming from next door is overwhelming. "It's a combination of garbage and animal feces and urine," Todd said. "I mean, I don't know how somebody could live in that." Todd first raised his concerns at a WPTV Let's Hear It event in Jensen Beach in May. When asked what a solution would look like, his answer was simple: "Save those dogs. Get them out of there." Public records obtained by WPTV show Martin County Animal Control officers and sheriff's deputies have visited the home at least 11 times since 2020 — all related to concerns about the dogs and their owner. The owner is not being named because she has never been charged with a crime. One incident report from 2020 describes accounts of as many as 25 dogs inside the home. On multiple occasions, authorities noted feces on the floor and furniture. Records show the owner did clean up after initial visits and told animal control she had re-homed some of the dogs, but she eventually stopped allowing law enforcement inside. Multiple reports note that deputies were not allowed to see the dogs when they visited the home. A code enforcement officer took photos through the glass front door in 2023, noting "a dog with feces on it." After that visit, the owner put up a fence. Todd said she also stopped letting the dogs outside, but he can still hear them barking in the house. For Todd, what's out of sight is not out of mind — let alone out of sound or smell. And there's nothing anybody can do or will do," Todd said. Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek said the fence has created a legal barrier to further investigation. "You can't even see into the property anymore," Budensiek said. "So, she really has legally walled us off from investigating exactly what's going on inside." When asked whether deputies have a lawful way to enter the property and look for themselves, Budensiek said they do not — unless there is visible evidence of mistreatment. "If there was something that we could see from the outside that -- you know -- dogs are being mistreated, malnourished, not taken care of — we would absolutely get a search warrant and go in there," Budensiek said. Florida statutes require that confined animals be provided "a sufficient quantity of good and wholesome food and water." Budensiek said that standard appears to be met based on what deputies can observe. "We saw recently — as recently as last week — that there's food boxes that are out there, empty food boxes, so we know the animals from the outside look to be being taken care of," Budensiek said. I attempted to reach the owner by phone and left three voicemails. In the most recent incident report — from July 2025 — the owner told deputies she had 7 dogs, then "redacted and said that she only had five dogs," according to the report. Todd said he does not believe that statement. "Seems like from everything I've been told, the law's on her side," Todd said. Since I visited the Todds last month, they say they continue to hear the dogs and have continued to follow up with the sheriff's office. They have also seen animal control in front of the owner's house a few times since this story began — but deputies have not gone in. Budensiek acknowledged the neighbors' frustration but said there is little more his office can do. "I know the neighbors are worried and, and we'll still respond out there for complaints. But again, it's not illegal to be a bad neighbor," Budensiek said. We want to be your voice and help you find solutions. While we hold our monthly Let's Hear It meet-ups, we know many are not able to attend, but we still want to hear from you and start taking action to get you answers. You can e-mail us at LetsHearIt@wptv.com. This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. hero.headline: Florida House Speaker Daniel Perez resigns after Senate confirms him as ambassador to Brazil
hero.body:
Florida House Speaker Daniel Perez has resigned from the Florida House of Representatives after the U.S. Senate confirmed his nomination as Ambassador to the Federative Republic of Brazil. Perez announced his resignation in a letter to House members, saying President Donald J. Trump asked him to serve in the ambassadorial role. His resignation from the Florida House takes effect Friday, Aug. 21, and he will take the oath of office as ambassador later this month.

Under House Rule 2.5(d), Speaker pro tempore Wyman Duggan will assume the duties, powers, and prerogatives of the Speaker. Perez stated in his resignation letter that he has notified Speaker-designate Sam Garrison that his team may take control of House operations on Sept. 8 to allow more time to prepare for the start of his term. The transition creates a brief window where Duggan will serve as acting speaker before Garrison assumes the role.

In his resignation letter, Perez reflected on his tenure leading the chamber. He described serving in the House and as Speaker as the honor of his life. Perez told members they have been on a sometimes thrilling and sometimes tumultuous journey together during his time in leadership.

Perez expressed hope that House members feel, as he does, that they have done right by the House and the people of Florida as they look back on this term. The resignation marks the end of his service in the Florida Legislature as he prepares to represent the United States in Brazil. Perez becomes the latest Florida state legislator to leave office for a federal appointment under the Trump administration.

hero.headline: St. Lucie Mets split doubleheader with Daytona, rally for 11-10 win in 10 innings
hero.body:
The St. Lucie Mets split a doubleheader with the Daytona Tortugas on Wednesday at Clover Park, falling 8-4 in the opener before rallying for an 11-10 victory in 10 innings in the nightcap. The twin bill made up a June 20 rainout. John Smith III delivered a two-run single in the bottom of the 10th inning, scoring Wyatt Vincent and Vladi Gomez after Daytona had taken a 10-9 lead in the top of the inning.

The Mets forced extra innings after erasing a three-run deficit in the seventh. Gomez's two-strike, bases-loaded double tied the game 6-6 with two outs. Both teams scored in the eighth before trading two-run homers in the ninth. Daytona's Dylan King put the Tortugas ahead 9-7, but Julio Zayas answered with a game-tying two-run homer for the Mets.

Gomez finished 4 for 5 with three doubles, two RBIs and two runs. Smith III went 2 for 5 with three RBIs, while Zayas was 3 for 4 with a home run, two RBIs and two runs scored. Daytona prospect Aaron Watson earned the win in his Single-A debut, limiting the Mets to two runs over five innings despite allowing eight hits.

In the first game, the Tortugas took control early, capitalizing on two Mets throwing errors in the first inning before scoring four runs in the fourth, highlighted by Adolfo Sanchez's solo home run. The Mets collected 10 hits in the loss. Elian Peña went 2 for 4 with a double and two RBIs, while Aiden Robbins and Bohan Adderley each had two hits. Kuhio Aloy recorded the first hit of his professional career with a fifth-inning single. The Mets now stand at 14-22 in the second half and 47-55 overall, while Daytona is 23-13 and 44-58.

hero.headline: Fort Pierce Kings Landing developers short $15 million, city commissioners divided on next steps
hero.body:
The Kings Landing development in Fort Pierce faces another delay as Live Oak Development, the secondary developer on the project, told city commissioners they are $15 million short of the $60 million needed to complete the Marriott hotel and restaurant portion of the project. Live Oak Development CEO Paul Bertozzi said the shortfall is due in part to rising construction costs. City leaders said developers initially asked the city to cover the gap through a loan or grant, but Commissioner Michael Broderick said that request was denied.

Live Oak Development is now asking for 180 days to find the money through private sources. Bertozzi told commissioners the outreach has already begun. Commissioners are debating whether the city should reclaim the property. Broderick said he believes trying to reclaim the property through legal action would be expensive and time-consuming. He said he would rather give developers the time they are asking for.

Commissioner Chris Dzadovsky said he does not want to wait. Jon Nolli, owner of Funky Cuda in Fort Pierce, said he has been waiting on the development and is ready for it to be finished. Nolli said he even has plans to open businesses inside Kings Landing, including a beer garden and a deli, but the delays are wearing on him.

The city commission has scheduled a special meeting on September 14 to discuss next steps.

hero.headline: Road rage on U.S. 1 in Port St. Lucie ends in four-vehicle crash, Port St. Lucie man arrested
hero.body:
A road rage confrontation between a pickup truck and a motorcycle on U.S. 1 Wednesday escalated into a four-vehicle crash that left four people injured and a Port St. Lucie man in jail. Officers with the Port St. Lucie Police Department responded around 6:45 p.m. to the intersection of South U.S. Highway 1 and SE Lyngate Drive/SE Tiffany Avenue, where investigators determined that a red Harley-Davidson motorcycle and a black Ford Super Duty pickup truck were involved in an ongoing road-rage incident.

Detectives say the pickup, driven by 54-year-old Kevin Lonergan, was pursuing the motorcycle as both vehicles traveled northbound on U.S. 1 and approached the intersection. According to witness statements and dash-camera video, the motorcycle entered the intersection against a red light and collided with a black Chevrolet Silverado, throwing the 31-year-old rider from the bike. Police say Lonergan then entered the intersection against the red signal, struck the ejected motorcyclist, and crashed head-on into a blue Toyota RAV4.

The motorcyclist and two people inside the RAV4 were taken to Lawnwood Medical Center. The Silverado driver was transported to St. Lucie Medical Center. Investigators say the motorcyclist suffered serious injuries, including a brain bleed and facial fractures, and lost consciousness after the crash. He remains hospitalized in stable condition.

Based on witness statements, dash-camera video and the investigation, police arrested Lonergan for two counts of reckless driving causing serious bodily injury and one count of reckless driving causing injury. After being medically cleared, Lonergan was booked into the St. Lucie County Jail. The intersection remained closed for hours while investigators processed the scene before all lanes reopened around 2 a.m. Officer Brittany McNally said the case serves as a reminder that allowing anger to dictate actions behind the wheel can put multiple innocent lives at risk.

cards.teaser: A 42-year-old man linked to several burglaries in the St. Lucie Village community was arrested by St. Lucie County Sheriffs Office deputies.

Daniel Eugene Holmes, 42, was arrested on August 5 after officers found him going through trash near the road at the 2900 block of North Indian River Drive, according to a St. Lucie County Sheriffs Office Facebook posting. During their investigation, deputies determined Holmes matched the description of a person of interest developed during an ongoing burglary investigation in St. Lucie Village. Through additional investigative efforts, deputies established probable cause linking Holmes to other reported crimes in the area.

Holmes was charged with two counts of burglary of a conveyance and one count of loitering and prowling. He also had a bicycle with fishing equipment attached. Holmes was taken to the St. Lucie County Jail, where he remained as of August 6 on a $31,000 bond. Sheriff Richard Del Toro said the case highlights the value of proactive patrol and the attention to detail deputies demonstrate every day.

hero.headline: Vero Beach High School marching band prepares for school year with nearly 90 years of tradition
hero.body:
The Vero Beach High School Fighting Indians Band is preparing for the new school year as students practice at band camp just days before classes resume. The program was founded in 1934 as part of the Federal Music Project during the Great Depression.

Band director Sean Srigley is an alumnus of Vero Beach High School who was in the band himself. Annabel Robbins plays flute piccolo and serves as a drum major, while Brady, an incoming senior, is the woodwind captain and section leader. Brady said being in charge of many students is scary because he has to make sure they are all doing well.

The band has performed in the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade in 1988, marching through the streets of New York City and playing Alexander's Ragtime Band for millions of television viewers. The program has also performed in the Tournament of Roses Parade, the Fiesta Bowl Parade, the Orange Bowl and Carnegie Hall. The program has earned decades of Superior ratings and national recognition.

Students practice on the football field in the Florida heat, demonstrating discipline and dedication as they prepare music and drill routines. Srigley said the band at Vero Beach High School is right there with the school's academics and athletics, having marched in every big parade in America.
hero.article_text: This week I'm at Vero Beach High School where students are getting ready to go back to school, and I decided to do something I've never done before – I joined the marching band! I crashed band camp at Vero Beach High School just a few days before school started, and let me tell you, it was an incredible experience.WATCH: The first time I stepped onto that practice field, I could feel the history before I even picked up my instrument. This wasn't just another high school band – this was a tradition stretching back to 1934, when the Fighting Indians Band was founded as part of the Federal Music Project during the Great Depression. Every student who had ever worn that uniform had helped build an incredible legacy.I got to meet some amazing students who are keeping that tradition alive, like Annabel Robbins who plays flute piccolo and is a drum major. Brady, an incoming senior, is the woodwind captain and section leader."It's kind of scary, you know," Brady said. "You're in charge of a lot of kids, so you got to make sure they're all doing good.The band director, Sean Srigley, has a special connection to this program that goes way back. "I'm actually alumni of Vero Beach High School. I was in the band myself," Srigley explained. "The cool thing about Vero is we've got awesome academics, awesome athletics. Our band is right there with them. We've marched in pretty much every big parade you could have in America."And he's not exaggerating! This band has an absolutely incredible resume. They performed in the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade in 1988, marching through the streets of New York City and playing "Alexander's Ragtime Band" for millions of television viewers. That single performance became one of the defining moments in the program's history and remains a source of pride for every new generation of members.But that's not all – they've also performed in the Tournament of Roses Parade, the Fiesta Bowl Parade, the Orange Bowl and even Carnegie Hall! The program has earned decades of Superior ratings and national recognition while representing our Treasure Coast with pride.After learning about all this amazing history, it was time for me to get to work. But honestly, that wasn't really my thing, so I tried the drums next.But joining the marching band for practice meant more than just learning music and drill. It meant discipline and the ability to stand for a long time in that Florida heat – something these kids do with incredible dedication.As I marched onto the football field, I couldn't help but imagine all the students who had stood in that same place before me. Some had gone on to march through Manhattan in the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade. Others had performed in famous bowl games or international parades.As I left Vero Beach High School that day, I was thankful for the opportunity to be part of something so special, even for just one practice. These students aren't just making music – they're carrying on a legacy that's been building for nearly 90 years.

hero.headline: Fort Pierce Kings Landing development faces new delay as developers seek $15 million to finish Marriott project
hero.body:
Live Oak Development told Fort Pierce city commissioners they are $15 million short of the $60 million needed to complete the Marriott hotel and restaurant portion of the Kings Landing development. The secondary developer on the project cited rising construction costs as a portion of the cause for the shortfall. CEO Paul Bertozzi told commissioners construction costs continue to balloon across multiple industries.

City leaders said developers initially asked the city to cover the gap through a loan or grant. Commissioner Michael Broderick said that request was denied. The city does not have $15 million, and Broderick said he would not advocate the city investing that amount into a private enterprise. Live Oak Development is now asking for 180 days to find the money through private sources. Bertozzi told commissioners the outreach has already begun, including reaching out to friends and families and investment and private equity versus institutional investors.

Commissioners are divided on what to do next. Broderick said he believes trying to reclaim the property through legal action would be expensive and time-consuming. He said clawing the property back through reverter clauses would mean litigation for years and a ton of money, and he would rather give developers the 180 days they are asking for. Commissioner Chris Dzadovsky said he does not want to wait and thinks it is time to cut bait and move on.

Jon Nolli, owner of Funky Cuda in Fort Pierce, said he has been waiting on the development and is ready for it to be finished. Nolli said the completed project would benefit the surrounding area and he has plans to open businesses inside Kings Landing, including a beer garden and a deli. He said it has been taking so long that he does not even know if the trends have changed. The city commission has scheduled a special meeting on September 14 to discuss next steps.

cards.headline: Road rage crash in Port St. Lucie leaves motorcyclist with brain bleed, driver arrested
cards.teaser: A road rage incident that escalated into a four-vehicle crash at South U.S. Highway 1 and SE Lyngate Drive left a motorcyclist with serious injuries and multiple people hospitalized Wednesday evening.
cards.body:
The crash occurred around 6:45 p.m. Wednesday at the intersection of South U.S. Highway 1 and SE Lyngate Drive/SE Tiffany Avenue. Port St. Lucie police said Kevin Lonergan, 54, was driving a black Ford Super Duty pickup truck and pursuing a red Harley-Davidson motorcycle northbound on U.S. Highway 1 during an ongoing road rage incident.

Witness statements and dash-camera footage revealed the motorcycle rider entered the intersection against a red traffic signal and collided with a black Chevrolet Silverado, ejecting the rider from the bike. Lonergan's pickup truck then also ran the red light, struck the motorcycle rider who was on the ground, and collided head-on with a blue Toyota RAV4. The 31-year-old motorcycle rider suffered serious injuries, including a brain bleed and facial fractures. He lost consciousness following the crash and remains hospitalized in stable condition at Lawnwood Medical Center.

Two occupants of the RAV4 were also transported to Lawnwood Medical Center, while the driver of the Silverado was taken to St. Lucie Medical Center. Police arrested Lonergan on two counts of reckless driving causing serious bodily injury and one count of reckless driving causing injury. After being medically cleared, he was booked into the St. Lucie County Jail. The intersection was shut down until 2 a.m. Thursday.

hero.headline: Costco on Kanner Highway in Stuart closes after electrical fire, reopens with limited service
hero.body:
A Costco at 3173 South Kanner Highway in Stuart closed Thursday afternoon after an electrical fire and reopened later in the day with limited service, according to the Stuart Police Department. The fire was reported around 4 p.m. and was extinguished by Stuart and Martin County Fire Rescue personnel. The store closed out of an abundance of caution while fire personnel remained on scene to ensure the building was safe to reopen.

The store reopened Thursday evening but is operating with limited inventory. According to store management, only dry goods are available for purchase because the refrigeration unit is not operational. The Stuart Police Department urged shoppers and travelers to avoid the area during the closure.

Police said the store remained closed for an undetermined amount of time while fire rescue personnel inspected the building. Authorities said they would provide an update once Costco fully reopened. The cause of the electrical fire has not been disclosed.

cards.headline: Martin County Sheriff reports rise in daytime DUI arrests, calls trend 'extremely concerning'
cards.teaser: The Martin County Sheriff's Office recorded five DUI arrests as of Thursday morning, including several during daytime hours, prompting Sheriff John Budensiek to warn drivers about the rising trend.
cards.body:
The Martin County Sheriff's Office is reporting a rise in DUI arrests, including an increase in incidents occurring during the day. Sheriff John Budensiek said the county recorded five DUI arrests as of Thursday morning. Among the incidents was a wrong-way driver on Kanner Highway, a driver on A1A who hit a railroad crossing at high speed and rolled her car, and another driver with no license or insurance. Budensiek also reported a driver slumped over the wheel in Hobe Sound who was arrested and taken to jail.

Body camera footage from Wednesday shows deputies responding to a single-vehicle crash on I-95 near Martin Highway. Deputies said an intoxicated driver collided with a guardrail, abandoned the wrecked car in the center lane of the interstate, and fled the scene. The driver was taken into custody and faces several charges, including DUI, possession of heroin, and driving without a license.

According to the sheriff's office, DUI charges have increased every year since 2022. The office reported 506 DUI charges in 2022, 532 in 2023, 537 in 2024, 540 in 2025, and 349 year-to-date in 2026. Budensiek said the aggressive driving unit will continue monitoring roadways day and night to combat impaired and dangerous drivers. He suggested drivers who intend to drink should use a rideshare service.

The driver was taken into custody and faces several charges, including DUI, possession of heroin, and driving without a license. Sheriff John Budensiek said the county recorded five DUI arrests as of Thursday morning. Among the incidents was a wrong-way driver on Kanner Highway, a driver on A1A who hit a railroad crossing at high speed and rolled her car, and another driver with no license or insurance. "And then while we are getting ready to talk to you today yet again, we had another DUI in Hobe Sound: a driver slumped over the wheel, so our DUI units went down there, and he's sitting in our jail right now," Budensiek said. According to the sheriff’s office, DUI charges have increased every year since 2022, and this year is currently on pace to continue the trend. The sheriff’s office reported the following DUI arrest numbers: 2022 -- 506 DUI charges 2023 -- 532 DUI charges 2024 -- 537 DUI charges 2025 -- 540 DUI charges 2026 -- 349 (year-to-date) "All the information we're putting out there, you would think that DUI is becoming a thing of the past, but they're not — we're seeing more and more of them, and lately we're seeing more daytime DUIs, which is extremely concerning," Budensiek said. He said the aggressive driving unit will continue monitoring roadways day and night to combat impaired and dangerous drivers. "So, I would suggest, as sheriff, if you intend to drink at all, catch you a rideshare to wherever you are going to go drinking and catch it back home," Budensiek said. He also credited members of the public who call and report suspicious activity. cards.teaser: Body camera footage shows a North Carolina family explaining to a Martin County deputy how they were chased off the road near Kanner Highway, just west of I-95, over the weekend.
cards.body:
A North Carolina couple visiting Florida with their young son recounted to a Martin County sheriff's deputy how they were chased off the road near Kanner Highway, just west of I-95, over the weekend. The couple appeared visibly shaken as they explained what happened to them and the man's sister, who was driving ahead of them. The family said the suspect chased the man's sister for miles, prompting the wife to call 911.

The man explained that he and his wife tried to intervene, but the driver then turned his focus on them. The man's sister managed to escape, but the driver continued to follow him and his wife, eventually forcing them off the road. The driver, identified as Michael Spires, was taken into custody at a nearby gas station.

Sheriff John Budensiek said the family did not know what was coming next and are extremely grateful they did not get injured. Budensiek said the suspect did not have a gun and that the incident could have ended much worse.

hero.headline: Tom Rahill wins $10,000 grand prize in 2026 Florida Python Challenge after removing 96 snakes
hero.body:
The Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission and its partners announced the results of the 2026 Florida Python Challenge on Wednesday. Tom Rahill won the Ultimate Grand Prize of $10,000 after removing 96 Burmese pythons from Everglades National Park during the 10-day competition. A total of 907 participants from 30 states, Canada and Vietnam collectively removed 280 invasive Burmese pythons from South Florida.

Rahm Levinson removed the longest python of the competition, a 16-foot, 5-inch snake, also from Everglades National Park. A highlight of this year's event was the return of Everglades National Park as a partner and one of eight official competition locations. The event was hosted by the FWC and the South Florida Water Management District, in partnership with the National Park Service and the Fish & Wildlife Foundation of Florida.

In the professional category, Christina Kraus won $2,500 for most pythons with 36 snakes removed, and Taylor Stanberry won $1,500 as runner-up with 34 pythons. Rahm Levinson also won $1,000 for the longest python prize. In the novice category, Bart Shreve won $2,500 for removing nine pythons, Michael Marousky won $1,500 for four pythons, and Vincent Poole won $1,000 for an 8-foot, 2-inch snake. In the military category for active duty and veterans, Stephen Payton of the U.S. Army won $2,500 for three pythons, Jonathan Miller of the U.S. Air Force won $1,500 for two pythons, and Jeffery 'Heath' Roser of the U.S. Army won $1,000 for an 8-foot, 7-inch python.

FWC Chairman Rodney Barreto said the number of invasive pythons removed from the Everglades is a major victory for Florida's native wildlife and a testament to what can be accomplished through strong partnerships and public participation. South Florida Water Management District Governing Board Member 'Alligator Ron' Bergeron said removing Burmese pythons from the ecosystem is critical to the survival of native species that call the area home. The 10-day event is designed to raise awareness about invasive species and engage the public in Everglades conservation through the removal of invasive Burmese pythons.

hero.headline: Fort Pierce Kings Landing developers seek $15 million to finish Marriott project as city commissioners debate reclaiming property
hero.body:
Live Oak Development told Fort Pierce commissioners Thursday it is $15 million short of the $60 million needed to complete the Marriott hotel and restaurant portion of the Kings Landing development, prompting a divided debate among city leaders on whether to give the company more time or reclaim the property. The secondary developer on the project cited rising construction costs as a primary cause of the shortfall. CEO Paul Bertozzi said construction costs continue to balloon across multiple industries.

Live Oak Development initially asked the city to cover the gap through a loan or grant, according to city leaders. Commissioner Michael Broderick said the request was denied. The city does not have $15 million, nor would he advocate the city investing $15 million into a private enterprise, Broderick said. The developer is now requesting 180 days to find the money through private sources. Bertozzi told commissioners the outreach has already begun, including reaching out to friends and families and private equity investors versus institutional investors.

Commissioners are split on whether to reclaim the property or allow the extension. Broderick said trying to reclaim the property through legal action would be expensive and time consuming. Clawing the property back through reverter clauses is going to be litigation for years and a ton of money, Broderick said. He said he would rather give developers the 180 days they are asking for. Commissioner Chris Dzadovsky disagreed, saying it is time to cut bait and move on.

Jon Nolli, owner of Funky Cuda in Fort Pierce, said he has been waiting on the development and is ready for it to be finished. Nolli said the completed project would benefit the surrounding area and that he has plans to open businesses inside Kings Landing. He said he has a couple deposits on the commercial side for a beer garden and a deli, but the delays are wearing on him because the trends have changed. The city commission has scheduled a special meeting on September 14 to discuss next steps.

cards.headline: Martin County neighbors report dogs suffering next door as sheriff says legal barriers prevent investigation
cards.teaser: Thomas Todd and his wife say they are worried about 15 to 20 dogs living behind a fence at a neighboring property in Martin County, but the sheriff says a fence has created a legal barrier to investigation.
cards.body:
Public records obtained by WPTV show Martin County Animal Control officers and sheriff's deputies have visited the home at least 11 times since 2020, all related to concerns about the dogs and their owner. One incident report from 2020 describes accounts of as many as 25 dogs inside the home. On multiple occasions, authorities noted feces on the floor and furniture. Records show the owner did clean up after initial visits and told animal control she had re-homed some of the dogs, but she eventually stopped allowing law enforcement inside.

A code enforcement officer took photos through the glass front door in 2023, noting a dog with feces on it. After that visit, the owner put up a fence. Todd said she also stopped letting the dogs outside, but he can still hear them barking in the house. When the wind picks up, Todd said the smell coming from next door is overwhelming, a combination of garbage and animal feces and urine.

Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek said the fence has created a legal barrier to further investigation. You cannot even see into the property anymore, Budensiek said. She really has legally walled us off from investigating exactly what is going on inside. Budensiek said deputies do not have a lawful way to enter the property unless there is visible evidence of mistreatment. Florida statutes require that confined animals be provided a sufficient quantity of good and wholesome food and water. Budensiek said that standard appears to be met based on what deputies can observe. In the most recent incident report from July 2025, the owner told deputies she had seven dogs, then redacted and said that she only had five dogs.

"I mean, I don't know how somebody could live in that."Todd first raised his concerns at a WPTV Let's Hear It event in Jensen Beach in May. When asked what a solution would look like, his answer was simple: "Save those dogs. Get them out of there."Public records obtained by WPTV show Martin County Animal Control officers and sheriff's deputies have visited the home at least 11 times since 2020 — all related to concerns about the dogs and their owner. The owner is not being named because she has never been charged with a crime.One incident report from 2020 describes accounts of as many as 25 dogs inside the home. On multiple occasions, authorities noted feces on the floor and furniture. Records show the owner did clean up after initial visits and told animal control she had re-homed some of the dogs, but she eventually stopped allowing law enforcement inside. Multiple reports note that deputies were not allowed to see the dogs when they visited the home.A code enforcement officer took photos through the glass front door in 2023, noting "a dog with feces on it." After that visit, the owner put up a fence.Todd said she also stopped letting the dogs outside, but he can still hear them barking in the house. For Todd, what's out of sight is not out of mind — let alone out of sound or smell."It's just sad. And there's nothing anybody can do or will do," Todd said.Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek said the fence has created a legal barrier to further investigation."You can't even see into the property anymore," Budensiek said. "So, she really has legally walled us off from investigating exactly what's going on inside."When asked whether deputies have a lawful way to enter the property and look for themselves, Budensiek said they do not — unless there is visible evidence of mistreatment."If there was something that we could see from the outside that -- you know -- dogs are being mistreated, malnourished, not taken care of — we would absolutely get a search warrant and go in there," Budensiek said.Florida statutes require that confined animals be provided "a sufficient quantity of good and wholesome food and water." Budensiek said that standard appears to be met based on what deputies can observe."We saw recently — as recently as last week — that there's food boxes that are out there, empty food boxes, so we know the animals from the outside look to be being taken care of," Budensiek said.I attempted to reach the owner by phone and left three voicemails. She did not respond.In the most recent incident report — from July 2025 — the owner told deputies she had 7 dogs, then "redacted and said that she only had five dogs," according to the report.Todd said he does not believe that statement."Seems like from everything I've been told, the law's on her side," Todd said.Since I visited the Todds last month, they say they continue to hear the dogs and have continued to follow up with the sheriff's office. They have also seen animal control in front of the owner's house a few times since this story began — but deputies have not gone in.Budensiek acknowledged the neighbors' frustration but said there is little more his office can do."I know the neighbors are worried and, and we'll still respond out there for complaints. But again, it's not illegal to be a bad neighbor," Budensiek said.We want to be your voice and help you find solutions.While we hold our monthly Let's Hear It meet-ups, we know many are not able to attend, but we still want to hear from you and start taking action to get you answers. hero.teaser: Port St. Lucie police released the 911 call made by a neighbor who heard gunshots and saw Elizabeth Ortega lying motionless in her front yard before she was airlifted to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital, where she later died.
hero.body:
Port St. Lucie police released the 911 call made the night Elizabeth Ortega, 50, was shot and killed outside her home on the 2000 block of SE Oxmoor Terrace in Port St. Lucie. The suspect, Ralph Varela Sr., 50, was later found dead from a self-inflicted gunshot wound. In the 911 call, a neighbor described hearing five or six gunshots that were loud enough to rattle her house before her 4-year-old child spotted Ortega lying motionless in the front yard.

The caller told the dispatcher she did not go outside because she was frightened, and that Ortega and her husband were frequently heard arguing. The caller confirmed both vehicles belonging to the residents were still parked outside the home and that Ortega was not moving. Responding officers found Ortega suffering from multiple gunshot wounds. She was airlifted to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital, where she later died.

Police said Varela returned inside the home after the shooting, where officers later found him dead from what appeared to be a self-inflicted gunshot wound. Ortega's son, Ralph Varela Jr., is a firefighter with Palm Beach County Fire Rescue. The investigation remains active as detectives continue processing evidence and await final results from the Medical Examiner's Office.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie road rage crash leaves motorcyclist with brain bleed, driver arrested
cards.body:
A road rage incident escalated into a four-vehicle crash Wednesday evening at the intersection of South U.S. Highway 1 and SE Lyngate Drive in Port St. Lucie, leaving a motorcyclist with serious injuries and a 54-year-old driver under arrest. Kevin Lonergan was driving a black Ford Super Duty pickup truck and pursuing a red Harley-Davidson motorcycle northbound on U.S. Highway 1 during an ongoing road rage incident around 6:45 p.m., according to Port St. Lucie police.

Witness statements and dash-camera footage showed the motorcycle rider entered the intersection against a red traffic signal and collided with a black Chevrolet Silverado, ejecting the rider from the bike. Lonergan's pickup truck then also ran the red light, struck the motorcycle rider who was on the ground, and collided head-on with a blue Toyota RAV4, police said.

The 31-year-old motorcycle rider suffered serious injuries including a brain bleed and facial fractures. He lost consciousness following the crash and remains hospitalized in stable condition at Lawnwood Medical Center. Two occupants of the RAV4 were also transported to Lawnwood Medical Center, while the driver of the Silverado was taken to St. Lucie Medical Center.

Police arrested Lonergan on two counts of reckless driving causing serious bodily injury and one count of reckless driving causing injury. After being medically cleared, he was booked into the St. Lucie County Jail. The intersection was shut down until 2 a.m. Thursday while investigators processed the scene.

cards.headline: Martin County Sheriff reports rise in daytime DUI arrests
cards.teaser: The Martin County Sheriff's Office is reporting an increase in DUI arrests, including more incidents occurring during daytime hours, with five DUI arrests recorded as of Thursday morning.
cards.body:
The Martin County Sheriff's Office recorded five DUI arrests as of Thursday morning, prompting Sheriff John Budensiek to warn of a concerning rise in daytime impaired driving. Among the incidents was a wrong-way driver on Kanner Highway, a driver on A1A who hit a railroad crossing at high speed and rolled her car, and another driver with no license or insurance. Body camera footage from Wednesday shows deputies responding to a single-vehicle crash on I-95 near Martin Highway, where an intoxicated driver collided with a guardrail, abandoned the wrecked car in the center lane of the interstate, and fled the scene. The driver was taken into custody and faces charges including DUI, possession of heroin, and driving without a license.

According to the sheriff's office, DUI charges have increased every year since 2022. The office reported 506 DUI charges in 2022, 532 in 2023, 537 in 2024, 540 in 2025, and 349 year-to-date in 2026. Budensiek said the aggressive driving unit will continue monitoring roadways day and night to combat impaired and dangerous drivers. He credited members of the public who call and report suspicious activity.

cards.headline: St. Lucie County deputies arrest man in series of burglaries in St. Lucie Village
cards.teaser: Daniel Eugene Holmes, 42, was arrested after deputies responded to the 2900 block of North Indian River Drive and linked him to multiple burglaries in the St. Lucie Village area.
cards.body:
St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office deputies arrested Daniel Eugene Holmes, 42, on Wednesday after linking him to a series of burglaries in the St. Lucie Village area. Deputies responded to the 2900 block of North Indian River Drive after receiving a report of a suspicious person. Upon arrival, deputies located Holmes going through trash near the roadway and observed a bicycle in his possession with fishing equipment attached to it.

During their investigation, deputies determined Holmes matched the description of a person of interest developed during an ongoing burglary investigation in St. Lucie Village. Through additional investigative efforts, deputies established probable cause linking Holmes to other reported crimes in the area. Holmes was arrested on charges of two counts of burglary of a conveyance, and loitering and prowling. The investigation remains active.

cards.headline: Fourth arrest made in St. Lucie County child abuse case involving 3-month-old's death
cards.teaser: Jason Gunter, 45, was arrested in Virginia as the fourth suspect in the death of a 3-month-old infant who died in August 2025 in Fort Pierce.
cards.body:
Jason Gunter, 45, was arrested at his home in Mechanicsville, Virginia, by the U.S. Marshals Service on August 4 on an outstanding warrant obtained by St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office detectives. Gunter is believed to be the natural father of a 3-month-old infant who died in August 2025 in what investigators called one of the worst cases of child neglect they have seen. Gunter was charged with felony child neglect with great harm for his alleged role in the circumstances surrounding the child's death. He is being held without bond in the Hanover County Jail, awaiting extradition to St. Lucie County.

Also charged in the case are the biological mother, Nicole Marie Maxwell, 27, the child's grandfather, Robert Arthur Maxwell, 61, and Vikki Nicole Koon, 38, Robert Maxwell's girlfriend, each on charges of aggravated manslaughter of a child and aggravated child abuse. They are being held in the St. Lucie County Jail on $1.5 million bond each. On August 20, 2025, deputies responded to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital in Fort Pierce after a 3-month-old child was brought to the emergency room by the child's grandfather. The infant was pronounced dead on arrival. The boy died of dehydration and malnutrition in a mobile home in the 800 block of Silverstream Circle in Fort Pierce. Four other children in the home ranging in age from 2 to 10 years old were placed in foster care through the state Department of Children and Families.

cards.headline: Costco in Stuart closes after electrical fire
cards.teaser: A Costco located at 3173 S. Kanner Highway in Stuart was forced to close Thursday afternoon after an electrical fire.
cards.body:
A Costco in Stuart was forced to close Thursday afternoon after an electrical fire, the Stuart Police Department said. The incident was reported at around 4 p.m. Police said out of an abundance of caution the Costco located at 3173 S. Kanner Highway is currently closed following a fire that has been extinguished.

The store will remain closed for an undetermined amount of time while Stuart and Martin County Fire Rescue personnel remain on scene to ensure the building is safe to reopen. Authorities are urging individuals to avoid the area until further notice.

cards.headline: Martin County Sheriff warns of counterfeit Pokémon card scam
cards.teaser: Two Martin County residents lost more than $1,200 combined while buying counterfeit Pokémon trading cards they believed were authentic, prompting a warning from the sheriff's office.
cards.body:
The Martin County Sheriff's Office is warning residents after two people lost more than $1,200 combined while buying counterfeit Pokémon trading cards they believed were authentic. Deputies said the reports were made within the past few weeks. While Pokémon cards are often seen as collectibles, some rare cards can be worth hundreds or even thousands of dollars, making them a target for scammers and counterfeiters.

The sheriff's office said fake cards are being sold through online marketplaces, social media and other online sales platforms across the country. Officials encourage buyers to do their research before making a purchase and to be wary of deals that seem too good to be true. They also recommend checking a seller's reputation and having high-value cards authenticated by a reputable expert before handing over money. For added safety, the agency recommends meeting in one of its designated exchange parking spaces, which are monitored by cameras around the clock.

hero.headline: Fort Pierce Kings Landing developers seek $15 million to complete Marriott hotel after budget shortfall
hero.body:
The Kings Landing development in Fort Pierce is facing another delay as Live Oak Development, the secondary developer on the project, told city commissioners they are $15 million short of the $60 million needed to complete the Marriott hotel and restaurant portion of the project. CEO Paul Bertozzi said the shortfall is due in part to rising construction costs. City commissioners are divided on what to do next.

Developers initially asked the city to cover the gap through a loan or grant. Commissioner Michael Broderick said that request was denied. Broderick said the city does not have $15 million and he would not advocate the city investing that amount into a private enterprise. Live Oak Development is now asking for 180 days to find the money through private sources. Bertozzi told commissioners the outreach has already begun, with the company looking at friends and families and investment and private equity versus institutional investors.

Commissioners are debating about the city reclaiming the property. Broderick said he believes trying to reclaim the property through legal action would be expensive and time-consuming. He said clawing the property back through reverter clauses is going to be litigation for years and a ton of money. Broderick said he would rather give developers the time they are asking for, questioning what the city would lose by 180 days. Commissioner Chris Dzadovsky said he does not want to wait and thinks it is time to cut bait and move on.

Jon Nolli, owner of Funky Cuda in Fort Pierce, said he has been waiting on the development and is ready for it to be finished. Nolli said the completed project would benefit the surrounding area and he even has plans to open businesses inside Kings Landing including a beer garden and a deli. Nolli said the delays are wearing on him and the trends have changed during the wait. The city commission has scheduled a special meeting on September 14 to discuss next steps.

hero.headline: Indian River County sheriff's deputies shoot, kill 18-year-old attacking father with butcher knife during welfare check
hero.body:
Two Indian River County sheriff's deputies shot and killed an 18-year-old man who was attacking his father with a butcher knife during a welfare check Wednesday night. The incident began when the suspect's mother called authorities at approximately 8:17 p.m., telling them she believed her son had taken something and was acting strangely. When the two deputies arrived at the home, they heard screaming and entered through the front door, where they found the father and son in a violent struggle over a butcher knife with an approximately 5-inch blade.

One deputy deployed a Taser, which was ineffective. Deputies also gave verbal commands ordering the suspect to drop the knife. The suspect did not comply with either measure. The sheriff said the suspect had the father pinned to the ground in a stabbing position when the second deputy fired three shots, striking and incapacitating the suspect. The entire encounter lasted approximately 90 seconds. The 18-year-old was pronounced dead at the scene.

The father was transported to a hospital with a superficial wound to his hands. Authorities have not yet determined whether the injury was caused by the knife or shrapnel from the rounds fired by the deputy. The sheriff said the deputies likely saved the father's life. The suspect's mother told dispatchers her son had a history of mental illness and had been acting irrationally prior to the call. The sheriff said the suspect had no prior contact with the sheriff's office outside of a mental health-related incident in 2025.

The Florida Department of Law Enforcement and the state attorney's office are investigating the shooting. The state attorney will determine whether the deputies acted properly. Both deputies have been placed on administrative leave, which the sheriff described as standard policy regardless of the circumstances of a use-of-force incident. hero.headline: Family says roadside memorial for woman killed in St. Lucie County crash keeps being removed
hero.teaser: More than three years after Kaitlyn Kohler was struck and killed while crossing U.S. 1 in St. Lucie County, her family says the roadside memorial they created has been removed three separate times.
hero.body:
Kaitlyn Kohler, 27, was killed in May 2023 while crossing U.S. 1 in St. Lucie County. According to investigators, a St. Lucie County Sheriff's deputy was responding to assist with a traffic stop and was traveling about 100 mph without emergency lights or sirens activated when Kohler entered the crosswalk against a Do Not Walk signal. The deputy was later cleared of any criminal wrongdoing, and no criminal charges were filed.

Kohler's mother, Brandi Kohler, says the memorial has been removed three separate times after they received approval to have it there. "We just want to grieve in peace. We want to be able to grieve her and not have to keep fighting," Brandi Kohler said. She drives by the memorial twice a day and said, "I always smile at her beautiful face." The family says they have been informed that multiple complaints have led to requests for the memorial to be removed. Brandi said someone riding a motorcycle claimed debris from the site got into his wheel and he almost crashed, prompting the Florida Department of Transportation to call them.

On Tuesday, the memorial was removed once again. Brandi says they contacted a representative with FDOT who later acknowledged it should not have happened and that they would be putting the memorial back the following day. As of Wednesday morning, the memorial was returned to the site where the crash happened. "Just let us have our last piece of our daughter. This is the last piece of our daughter. Just let us have it in peace," Brandi said.

cards.headline: Father arrested in Virginia in Fort Pierce infant malnutrition death case
cards.body:
The U.S. Marshals Service arrested Jason Gunter, 45, at his home in Mechanicsville, Virginia, on Tuesday in connection with the death of his 3-month-old son who died from severe dehydration and malnutrition in Fort Pierce. The St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office charged Gunter with felony child neglect causing great harm, and he is awaiting extradition to St. Lucie County. He is the fourth person arrested in the case.

The investigation began on Aug. 20, 2025, when the infant, Robert Gunter, was brought to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital in Fort Pierce by his grandfather, Robert Maxwell, and Robert Maxwell's girlfriend, Vikki Koon. Medical staff observed signs the baby had been dead for some time, including rigor mortis, fixed pupils and skin discoloration. He was pronounced dead at 11:35 a.m. The infant weighed only 9 pounds, 3.5 ounces at death, down from 11 pounds, 12 ounces at a pediatric appointment on July 24, 2025. The Medical Examiner classified the death as homicide caused by dehydration and malnutrition.

Detectives say text messages warned Gunter that the baby had marks on his body, was sleeping excessively and appeared ill. One message stated "The baby is starving." Other messages sent to the child's mother, Nicole Maxwell, on Aug. 12, 2025, stated "The baby's got nothing to eat. I don't know what to give him." Despite these warnings, investigators allege Gunter did not return to Florida, seek intervention or contact emergency services.

Nicole Maxwell, 27, Robert Maxwell, 61, and Vikki Koon, 38, were previously charged with aggravated manslaughter of a child and aggravated child abuse. Each is being held on $1.5 million bond at the St. Lucie County Jail. When investigators executed a search warrant at the mobile home on Silverstream Circle in Fort Pierce where the baby had been staying, they documented clutter, moldy food, exposed electrical wiring, live rodents and widespread cockroach infestations. Two other children connected to the home were placed in a safe environment with assistance from the Florida Department of Children and Families.
cards.article_text: A fourth person has been arrested in connection with the death of a 3-month-old baby who allegedly died from severe dehydration and malnutrition. Lucie County Sheriff's Office announced Tuesday that the child's biological father, 45-year-old Jason Gunter, was taken into custody by the United States Marshals Service at his home in Mechanicsville, Virginia. Detectives had obtained an arrest warrant for Gunter in connection with the ongoing investigation into the child's death. He has been charged with felony child neglect causing great harm and is awaiting extradition to St. The arrest comes after three others were previously charged in the case: the child's mother, 27-year-old Nicole Maxwell; the child's grandfather, Robert Maxwell; and Robert Maxwell's girlfriend, 38-year-old Vikki Koon. See also: Body found in ocean off Boca Raton coast, investigation underway All three were charged with aggravated manslaughter of a child and aggravated child abuse. Each was held on a $1.5 million bond. Investigation Began After Baby Was Brought to Hospital The investigation began on Aug. 20, 2025, when Koon and Robert Maxwell brought 3-month-old Robert Gunter to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital in Fort Pierce. Medical staff immediately observed signs that the infant had been dead for some time, including rigor mortis, fixed pupils and skin discoloration. He was pronounced dead at 11:35 a.m. after resuscitation efforts failed. Detectives assigned to the case conducted interviews with family members at the hospital before serving search warrants and beginning what would become a months-long investigation. Caregivers Allegedly Noticed Warning Signs According to a 37-page arrest affidavit, the infant had been primarily living with Koon and Robert Maxwell after Gunter moved to Virginia. During interviews, detectives learned caregivers had noticed numerous warning signs in the days leading up to the child's death. Investigators say Koon admitted the baby was often fed only a few times a day and claimed he sometimes drank as little as two bottles daily. She told detectives she noticed the child was becoming increasingly thin, pale and lethargic. She also described frequent vomiting, excessive sleeping and a decrease in wet diapers. Despite those concerns, detectives say no one sought emergency medical treatment. Text messages obtained during the investigation showed family members repeatedly warning both parents that something was wrong. 12, 2025, messages sent to Nicole Maxwell stated, "The baby's got nothing to eat. I don't know what to give him." Days later, additional messages warned that the baby was sick, covered in marks and sleeping constantly. Other messages urged Gunter to come to Florida because something was wrong with the infant. According to detectives, neither parent took action that resulted in immediate medical care for the child. Search Warrant Revealed Conditions Inside Home When investigators executed a search warrant at the mobile home on Silverstream Circle where the baby had been staying, they documented what they described as an "extreme environmental hazard." The affidavit details a residence filled with clutter, moldy food, exposed electrical wiring, live rodents and widespread cockroach infestations. Detectives reported finding baby bottles containing curdled milk and observed insects crawling in and around a collapsed playpen. Vomit-like substances were also found on a couch and nearby flooring. Crime scene investigators noted the home appeared extremely dirty and poorly maintained, with evidence suggesting the playpen was not actively being used by the infant despite statements from caregivers. Autopsy Findings Led to Homicide Ruling An autopsy later revealed the extent of the infant's condition. According to the Medical Examiner's Office, Robert Gunter weighed 11 pounds, 12 ounces at a pediatric appointment on July 24, 2025. Less than a month later, at the time of his death, he weighed only 9 pounds, 3.5 ounces, placing him below the first percentile for children his age. The autopsy found evidence of severe dehydration and malnutrition, including poor skin elasticity, loss of body fat, sunken features, elevated sodium levels, organ damage and an absence of food contents in the stomach and upper intestinal tract. Examiners also documented numerous lesions and insect bites across the infant's body. The Medical Examiner ultimately determined the child died from dehydration and malnutrition and classified the manner of death as homicide, writing that the infant was dependent on caregivers for nutrition and hydration and that the failure to provide those necessities directly caused his death. Father's Role Under Scrutiny Investigators say Gunter was aware of concerns about the child's condition. The criminal complaint states that messages sent to Gunter warned that the baby had marks on his body, was sleeping excessively and appeared ill. Detectives also recovered messages discussing food shortages and concerns the infant was not being properly cared for. Despite those warnings, investigators allege Gunter did not return to Florida, seek immediate intervention or contact emergency services. A separate text message recovered from his phone stated: "The baby is starving." Detectives included that message among evidence supporting criminal charges. Sheriff's officials said the investigation remains active as the case moves through the court system. Meanwhile, two other children connected to the home were placed in a safe environment with assistance from the Florida Department of Children and Families.

cards.headline: St. Lucie County woman charged in alleged $7 million fraud from Southern Truss
cards.teaser: Laura Grasso and two other employees are accused of stealing approximately $7 million from Southern Truss over a seven-year period, with the money allegedly used for luxury vacations, jewelry and high-end vehicles.
cards.body:
The St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office recently searched the Indian River Estates home of Laura Grasso as part of its ongoing investigation into the Southern Truss fraud case. According to investigators, Grasso and two other employees are accused of stealing approximately $7 million from Southern Truss over a seven-year period. Detectives say the money was allegedly used for personal expenses, including luxury vacations, jewelry purchases and high-end vehicles.

Grasso is facing multiple charges, including grand theft and racketeering. Authorities say the search warrant was executed to gather additional evidence connected to the case as the investigation moves forward. The investigation remains active, and authorities have not released additional details about the evidence collected during the search. Southern Truss is a truss manufacturing company based in St. Lucie County.

cards.teaser: Marrissa Bailey was arrested Sunday at a MAX gas station on Orange Avenue in Fort Pierce after officers investigating a Walmart theft found narcotics and drug paraphernalia in her vehicle.
cards.body:
Fort Pierce Police Department officers were called to 1228 Orange Avenue on Sunday in reference to an investigation involving a white GMC Acadia connected to a late-July theft at Walmart. The vehicle was stopped at a MAX gas station on Orange Avenue, and the driver, Marrissa Bailey, 29, was identified as the suspect in the Walmart theft. Narcotics and drug paraphernalia were also found during the stop.

Bailey was arrested for grand theft, possession of cocaine and possession of drug paraphernalia. She was brought to the St. Lucie County Jail without incident.

hero.headline: North Carolina family run off road near I-95 in Martin County during chase
hero.body:
A North Carolina family visiting Florida was forced off Kanner Highway near Interstate 95 in Martin County over the weekend after a driver chased them for miles and pit-maneuvered them off the road. Body camera footage shows the couple and their young son walking out of the bushes to recount the incident to a Martin County Sheriff's deputy.

The man told deputies the suspect first chased his sister, who was traveling separately with her baby. His wife called 911 to report the chase. The man and his wife pulled over hoping the driver would move on, but he returned and turned his focus on them. The man's sister escaped, but the suspect continued following the couple and eventually forced them off the road.

Deputies arrested Michael Spires at a nearby gas station. Sheriff John Budensiek said the family was extremely grateful they were not injured and that the incident was not worse.

Budensiek said the suspect did not have a gun. He said it could have ended much worse.

hero.headline: Virginia man arrested as fourth suspect in St. Lucie County infant death case
hero.teaser: Jason Gunter, 45, was arrested at his home in Mechanicsville, Virginia, on charges of felony child neglect causing great harm in connection with the death of a 3-month-old infant in St. Lucie County last August.
hero.body:
Jason Gunter, 45, was arrested by the U.S. Marshals Service at his home in Mechanicsville, Virginia, on Tuesday on an outstanding warrant obtained by St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office detectives. Gunter is believed to be the natural father of a 3-month-old infant who died in August 2025. He was charged with felony child neglect with great harm for his alleged role in the circumstances surrounding the child's death. Gunter is being held without bond in the Hanover County Jail, awaiting extradition to St. Lucie County.

Also charged in the case are the biological mother, Nicole Marie Maxwell, 27, the child's grandfather, Robert Arthur Maxwell, 61, and Vikki Nicole Koon, 38, Robert Maxwell's girlfriend, each on charges of aggravated manslaughter of a child and aggravated child abuse. All three are being held in the St. Lucie County Jail on $1.5 million bond each. The investigation began on August 20, 2025, when deputies responded to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital in Fort Pierce after the 3-month-old child was brought to the emergency room by the child's grandfather. The infant was pronounced dead on arrival.

The boy died of dehydration and malnutrition in a mobile home in the 800 block of Silverstream Circle in Fort Pierce, which was in bad condition, according to investigators, who found an extreme bug infestation and a lack of food in the home. Four other children in the home, ranging in age from 2 to 10 years old, were placed in foster care through the state Department of Children and Families.

The arrest was made on an outstanding warrant obtained by St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office detectives. Gunter is charged with felony child neglect causing great bodily harm for his alleged role in the circumstances surrounding the infant's death. Authorities said Gunter is awaiting extradition to St. Lucie County, where he will face the charge. Lucie County Sheriff's Office remains committed to conducting thorough investigations, holding those responsible accountable under the law, and seeking justice for victims and their families," the agency said in a statement. cards.headline: Fort Pierce fraud investigation leads to search warrant at home of Southern Truss bookkeeper
cards.teaser: St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office deputies executed a search warrant at the Fort Pierce home of Laura Beth Grasso, the bookkeeper and comptroller accused of defrauding Southern Truss Companies of nearly $7 million.
cards.body:
St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office deputies executed a search warrant Tuesday morning at the Fort Pierce home of Laura Beth Grasso in the Indian River Estates neighborhood near Sunset Boulevard. Grasso was arrested July 16 along with Sheri Lynn Harrs and Tina Marie Mejia following what the sheriff's office described as a years-long scheme targeting Southern Truss Companies. Grasso has pleaded not guilty to the charges.

Investigators allege Grasso, who worked as the company's bookkeeper and comptroller, used her administrative access to bypass financial controls and funnel millions of dollars out of the business. Detectives say the money was spent on luxury vehicles, vacations, designer goods, jewelry and other personal expenses. Grasso faces charges of first-degree grand theft of $100,000 or more, organized fraud of $50,000 or more, conducting an enterprise through a pattern of racketeering activity, and money laundering of $100,000 or more. Grasso's bond was set at a combined $1.15 million across the four charges.

Tuesday's search follows an earlier warrant served on a vehicle connected to Grasso. A judge signed that warrant July 24, authorizing detectives to search a blue 2025 Chevrolet Tahoe registered to Grasso that had been towed to the sheriff's office evidence compound the day after her arrest. According to an inventory filed with the court, deputies found roughly $8,500 in cash, a jewelry organizer with jewelry, a Louis Vuitton purse and wallet, and a loaded Smith & Wesson M&P .40 Shield pistol in the glove box.
cards.article_text: A large law enforcement presence descended on a Fort Pierce neighborhood Tuesday morning as detectives executed a search warrant connected to an alleged fraud scheme that investigators say cost a local business nearly $7 million. Lucie County Sheriff's Office confirmed to CBS12 News that deputies are serving a search warrant as part of the ongoing investigation into the Southern Truss fraud case. Crime scene investigators were seen outside the home of Laura Beth Grasso in the Indian River Estates neighborhood near Sunset Boulevard. Grasso was arrested July 16 along with Sheri Lynn Harrs and Tina Marie Mejia following what the sheriff's office described as a years-long scheme targeting Southern Truss Companies. Grasso has pleaded not guilty to the charges, court records show. Investigators allege Grasso, who worked as the company's bookkeeper and comptroller, used her administrative access to bypass financial controls and funnel millions of dollars out of the business. Detectives say the money was spent on luxury vehicles, vacations, designer goods, jewelry and other personal expenses. Neighbors on Sunset Boulevard told CBS12 News they had long been suspicious of Grasso's lifestyle. They got 4 or 5 brand new trucks. They got food delivery every day, four different food deliveries. I mean, we always wondered what was going on over there," neighbor Greg Longhway said. Grasso faces charges of: First-degree grand theft of $100,000 or more Organized fraud of $50,000 or more Conducting an enterprise through a pattern of racketeering activity (RICO) Money laundering of $100,000 or more Harrs and Mejia each face charges of grand theft, organized fraud and racketeering. Grasso's bond was set at a combined $1.15 million across the four charges. Longhway said he watched deputies storm the house Tuesday morning. "Oh, they came ripping in, and the SWAT gear and everything with the guns pulled and hollering. Come out that search warrant. Come out with your hands up," he said. Prosecutors have asked a judge to hold a hearing on the legitimacy and source of any bail premium or collateral before allowing Grasso to be released from the St. Lucie County Jail, arguing in a court filing that a defendant should not be able to use money obtained through criminal activity to secure her release. Tuesday's search follows an earlier warrant served on a vehicle connected to Grasso. A judge signed that warrant July 24, authorizing detectives to search a blue 2025 Chevrolet Tahoe registered to Grasso that had been towed to the sheriff's office evidence compound the day after her arrest. According to an inventory filed with the court, deputies found roughly $8,500 in cash, a jewelry organizer with jewelry, a Louis Vuitton purse and wallet, and a loaded Smith & Wesson M&P .40 Shield pistol in the glove box. Longhway said the family largely kept to themselves. They've never said a word to anybody. They've been there for a year and a half, two years. They don't talk to anybody, which is fine; we don't care," Longhway said. "We figured something was up over there, though." The alleged scheme started to unravel after a tornado damaged the Southern Truss facility, according to the criminal complaint. With the plant largely shut down, the company's owner noticed operating costs staying suspiciously high, including fuel charges for a company jet that wasn't flying. When he confronted Grasso and told her outside forensic accountants were being brought in, investigators say server logs show she began logging into the company's financial system overnight to alter records. A forensic audit later recovered a secret "shadow ledger" on her computer, according to the complaint, tracking where the missing money had actually gone. Southern Truss also filed a civil lawsuit against the three women, alleging they carried out a coordinated scheme between 2018 and 2025 to divert company funds through unauthorized payroll payments, wire transfers and other transactions. The amended complaint alleges Grasso alone misappropriated at least $5 million, while Mejia and Harrs allegedly received hundreds of thousands more. The criminal case remains pending. Court records show a magistrate in June declined to pause the related civil case because of the criminal proceedings, instead ordering the defendants to respond to discovery by July 30 and complete depositions by Aug. Neighbors say they saw someone arrested by a SWAT team this morning. Lucie County Sheriff's Office has not confirmed any additional arrests or what investigators were searching for on Tuesday.

cards.headline: Martin County residents lose over $1,200 to fake Pokémon card scam
cards.teaser: The Martin County Sheriff's Office is warning residents after two people lost more than $1,200 combined while buying counterfeit Pokémon trading cards they believed were authentic.
cards.body:
The Martin County Sheriff's Office is warning residents after two people lost more than $1,200 combined while buying counterfeit Pokémon trading cards they believed were authentic. Deputies said the reports were made within the past few weeks. While Pokémon cards are often seen as collectibles, some rare cards can be worth hundreds or even thousands of dollars, making them a target for scammers and counterfeiters.

The sheriff's office said fake cards are being sold through online marketplaces, social media and other online sales platforms across the country. Officials encourage buyers to do their research before making a purchase and to be wary of deals that seem too good to be true. They also recommend checking a seller's reputation and having high-value cards authenticated by a reputable expert before handing over money. When buying cards in person, deputies advise taking time to inspect the items carefully and verify they are authentic.

The sheriff's office noted that recovering money can be difficult once a counterfeit item has been purchased. For added safety, the agency recommends meeting in one of its designated exchange parking spaces, which are monitored by cameras around the clock.

hero.headline: Early voting begins Saturday in Indian River County for August primary election
hero.body:
Early voting for Florida's August primary election begins Saturday in Indian River County and continues through Aug. 16. Voters can find a complete list of early voting locations and additional information by visiting voteindianriver.com.

The early voting period is also underway in neighboring counties across the Treasure Coast region. In Martin County, early voting runs Saturday, Aug. 8 through Aug. 16, with locations and additional information available at martinvotes.gov. St. Lucie County offers the same early voting schedule, running from Saturday, Aug. 8 through Aug. 16, with details available at stlucievotes.gov.

Palm Beach County is providing early voting during the same timeframe, from Saturday, Aug. 8 through Aug. 16. Voters in Palm Beach County can access a full list of early voting locations by visiting votepalmbeach.gov. Okeechobee County is also offering early voting from Saturday, Aug. 8 through Aug. 16, though specific hours were not immediately available. Voters seeking more information about Okeechobee County early voting can visit voteokeechobee.gov.

The early voting period gives voters across the region an opportunity to cast their ballots ahead of the primary election day. By offering multiple days and locations for early voting, election officials aim to provide flexibility for voters who may be unable to visit polling places on election day itself. Voters are encouraged to check their respective county election websites for the most current information about early voting locations, hours, and any requirements for casting ballots during the early voting period.

hero.headline: U.S. 1 closed in both directions near Tiffany Avenue in Port St. Lucie after crash
hero.body:
A traffic crash closed U.S. Highway 1 in both directions near Southeast Tiffany Avenue in Port St. Lucie on Thursday morning. The Port St. Lucie Police Department directed northbound U.S. 1 traffic to exit at Port St. Lucie Boulevard, while southbound U.S. 1 traffic was rerouted to Veterans Memorial Parkway.

The department asked travelers to avoid the area and use alternate routes while officers and emergency personnel worked at the scene. Police did not release information about injuries in the crash.

The closure affected one of the major north-south corridors through Port St. Lucie during morning hours. Emergency responders remained on scene Thursday morning to investigate and clear the roadway.

Police did not provide an estimated time for reopening the highway. Motorists traveling through Port St. Lucie were advised to plan for delays and consider alternative routes.

Upon arrival, officers found a plume of black smoke coming from a detached structure and three vehicles that were located in the back of the residence.

SLCFD says firefighters quickly brought the fire under control and prevented the fire from going into the home. The Fire Marshal's Office is investigating the cause of the fire. No injuries were reported, SLCFD says.
